children.title: Selection Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary roles representing chosen objects, options, or subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary indicators encoding whether individual candidates are selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of candidates. A family \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\in\{0,1\}^{I}\) consists of selection binaries when \(x_i=1\) means that candidate \(i\) is selected and \(x_i=0\) means that it is not selected. Thus the selected collection is represented by \(S(x)=\{i\in I:x_i=1\}\). Cardinality requirements are expressed by constraints such as \(\sum_{i\in I}x_i=k\), \(\sum_{i\in I}x_i\le k\), or \(\sum_{i\in I}x_i\ge k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each binary records whether one candidate is chosen; sums of these binaries impose exact, upper, or lower selection-cardinality requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S(x)=\{i\in I:x_i=1\}\) is the subset encoded by \(x\).

children.title: Assignment Incidence Binaries
children.top_down_role: Incidence roles linking entities to resources, positions, or categories.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Incidence Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary matrix encoding assignments between two finite index sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of entities and \(J\) a finite set of destinations, agents, or classes. Variables \(x=(x_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{I\times J}\) are assignment incidence binaries when \(x_{ij}=1\) means that entity \(i\) is assigned to \(j\). Requiring exactly one assignment for every entity is expressed by \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\); destination capacities may be expressed by \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i x_{ij}\le b_j\) for every \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each matrix entry records an entity-to-destination assignment; row equations enforce unique assignments, while weighted column inequalities impose destination capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{ij}=1\) holds exactly for the represented entity-destination incidences.

children.title: Network Incidence Binaries
children.top_down_role: Edge, arc, or node membership roles in discrete network structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Incidence Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary indicators encoding membership of arcs or edges in a chosen network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Variables \(x=(x_a)_{a\in A}\in\{0,1\}^{A}\) are network incidence binaries when \(x_a=1\) means that arc \(a\) belongs to the selected network and \(x_a=0\) otherwise. The chosen arc set is \(A(x)=\{a\in A:x_a=1\}\). For distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\), let \(\delta^+(v)\) and \(\delta^-(v)\) denote the arcs leaving and entering \(v\). The balance equations \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=1\) for \(v=s\), \(-1\) for \(v=t\), and \(0\) for \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) encode a binary unit \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow. These equations alone may permit additional directed cycles, so further restrictions are needed when the selected arcs must form a single directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each binary indicates whether an arc is selected. Node balances encode a binary unit flow from the source to the sink, but additional restrictions may be needed to exclude selected cycles and obtain a single path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A(x)=\{a\in A:x_a=1\}\) is the encoded arc subset, and the displayed balances make it a binary unit \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow that may include additional directed cycles.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering vertex v

children.title: Subset Membership Binaries
children.top_down_role: Membership roles for explicitly modeled selected subsets.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Membership Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characteristic-vector representation of an arbitrary subset of a finite ground set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite ground set and let \(S\subseteq E\). The subset-membership binary vector of \(S\) is \(x^S\in\{0,1\}^{E}\), defined by \(x^S_e=1\) if \(e\in S\) and \(x^S_e=0\) if \(e\notin S\). Conversely, every \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) determines the unique subset \(S(x)=\{e\in E:x_e=1\}\). Hence subsets of \(E\) and binary vectors indexed by \(E\) are in bijection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset is represented by its characteristic binary vector, and every binary vector uniquely determines the elements belonging to its represented subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\mapsto x^S\) is a bijection from \(2^E\) to \(\{0,1\}^{E}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The characteristic-vector bijection is precise and appropriate, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Activation-Indicator Binary Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: On–off states, fixed-charge triggers, and conditional-enforcement roles.

children.title: Activation-State Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary states governing whether modeled activities or components are active.

knowledge_statements.title: Activation-State Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary state variables controlling whether an indexed component is active.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) index components and let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\). The variable \(y_i\) is an activation-state binary when \(y_i=1\) denotes that component \(i\) is active and \(y_i=0\) denotes that it is inactive. If a nonnegative activity variable \(z_i\) has valid active-state upper bound \(U_i\), the linking constraint \(0\le z_i\le U_i y_i\) enforces \(z_i=0\) whenever \(y_i=0\), while permitting \(z_i\in[0,U_i]\) whenever \(y_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary records whether a component is active; an upper-bound link forces its associated nonnegative activity to zero in the inactive state.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le z_i\le U_i\) is valid when component \(i\) is active.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le z_i\le U_i y_i\) implies \(y_i=0\Rightarrow z_i=0\).

source_refs.locator: 2.10 Modeling Fixed Charges p. 66

source_witnesses.locator: 2.10 Modeling Fixed Charges p. 66

children.title: Conditional-Enforcement Indicators
children.top_down_role: Indicator roles controlling conditional constraint enforcement.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Enforcement Indicators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator variables imposing a constraint in one designated binary state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in X\), let \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(y\in\{0,1\}\). A conditional-enforcement indicator represents the implication \(y=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\). Its feasible set is \(\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y=1,\ g(x)\le0\}\cup\{(x,y):x\in X,\ y=0\}\). If a finite constant \(M\) satisfies \(g(x)\le M\) for every \(x\in X\), then the inequality \(g(x)\le M(1-y)\) is a valid mixed-integer formulation of the implication and is exact relative to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator activates a constraint when it equals one; a valid finite upper bound yields an exact big-M formulation over the stated base domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)\le M(1-y)\) is equivalent over \(X\times\{0,1\}\) to \(y=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\).

notation.meaning: base domain of continuous or mixed variables
valid upper bound on g over X

children.title: Fixed-Charge Trigger Binaries
children.top_down_role: Trigger roles associated with use-dependent or setup-dependent charges.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Trigger Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary triggers linking positive activity to payment of a fixed charge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_i\ge0\) be an activity with finite valid upper bound \(U_i\), let \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\), and let \(f_i\ge0\) be a fixed charge. The formulation \(0\le z_i\le U_i y_i\) with objective contribution \(f_i y_i+c_i(z_i)\) ensures that positive activity requires \(y_i=1\) and therefore incurs \(f_i\). If minimization and \(f_i>0\) make unnecessary activation suboptimal, an optimal solution satisfies \(y_i=1\) exactly when \(z_i>0\); otherwise the formulation guarantees only \(z_i>0\Rightarrow y_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linking inequality makes positive activity trigger a binary fixed cost; exact equivalence also requires conditions excluding costless or otherwise beneficial idle activation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_i>0\Rightarrow y_i=1\), so positive activity incurs the objective term \(f_i\).

notation.meaning: fixed charge and valid activity bound

children.title: Resource-Availability Indicators
children.top_down_role: Binary roles controlling the availability of capacities or resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Availability Indicators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary indicators controlling whether indexed resource capacity is usable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a finite set of resources and \(I\) a finite set of activities. For each \(r\in R\), let \(y_r\in\{0,1\}\) and let \(C_r\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be a finite resource capacity. For each \(i\in I\) and \(r\in R\), let \(x_i\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) be an activity level and \(a_{ir}\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) its per-unit consumption of resource \(r\). The variable \(y_r\) is a resource-availability indicator when \(y_r=1\) permits use of resource \(r\) and \(y_r=0\) forbids its use. The linking constraint \(\sum_{i\in I}a_{ir}x_i\le C_r y_r\) enforces zero total consumption when the resource is unavailable and the usual capacity bound when it is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator switches an indexed resource capacity on or off. Because all modeled consumptions are nonnegative, multiplying capacity by the binary forces total consumption to zero whenever the resource is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\ge0\) and \(a_{ir}\ge0\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(r\in R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(r\in R\), \(y_r=0\Rightarrow\sum_{i\in I}a_{ir}x_i=0\), while \(y_r=1\Rightarrow\sum_{i\in I}a_{ir}x_i\le C_r\).

notation.meaning: finite activity and resource index sets
consumption of resource r by activity i

children.title: Ordering-Precedence Binary Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Pairwise order, sequencing, orientation, and precedence roles.

children.title: Pairwise Ordering Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary roles representing relative order between pairs of objects.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Ordering Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary relation variables encoding which member of each pair precedes the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of distinct objects. For \(i,j\in I\) with \(i\ne j\), a pairwise ordering binary \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) has value one exactly when \(i\) precedes \(j\). A strict total order is encoded by antisymmetry equations \(y_{ij}+y_{ji}=1\) for all distinct \(i,j\), together with transitivity inequalities \(y_{ij}+y_{jk}-1\le y_{ik}\) for all distinct \(i,j,k\). Under these constraints, the relation \(i\prec j\iff y_{ij}=1\) is a strict total order on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each binary chooses the order of a pair; antisymmetry and transitivity constraints make all pairwise choices collectively represent a strict total order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(i\prec j\iff y_{ij}=1\) defines a strict total order when the displayed constraints hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pairwise variables and total-order constraints are mathematically coherent, but no citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Sequence-Position Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary roles assigning objects to positions in a sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequence-Position Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-matrix variables assigning each object to one sequence position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a set of \(n\) objects and let \(P=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be the positions of a sequence. Variables \(x=(x_{ip})\in\{0,1\}^{I\times P}\) are sequence-position binaries when \(x_{ip}=1\) means that object \(i\) occupies position \(p\). The equations \(\sum_{p\in P}x_{ip}=1\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ip}=1\) for every \(p\in P\) make \(x\) a permutation matrix and encode a unique ordering of all objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary matrix assigns every object to exactly one position and every position to exactly one object, thereby encoding a permutation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row and column equations make \(x\) encode a unique permutation of \(I\).

notation.meaning: indicator that object i occupies position p

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The permutation-matrix representation is precise and fits the leaf, but it lacks a source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Orientation Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary roles selecting a direction or orientation.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary variables choosing one of two mutually exclusive orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite set of objects, each having two admissible orientations labeled \(0\) and \(1\). A variable \(o_e\in\{0,1\}\) is an orientation binary when \(o_e=q\) means that object \(e\) uses orientation \(q\). Equivalently, if directed alternatives \((u_e,v_e)\) and \((v_e,u_e)\) represent the two orientations, then their incidence indicators may be defined by \(x_{u_ev_e}=o_e\) and \(x_{v_eu_e}=1-o_e\), which enforces selection of exactly one orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One binary chooses between two labeled orientations; complementary incidence expressions ensure that exactly one directed alternative is selected.
assumptions_latex: Each object has exactly two admissible orientations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{u_ev_e}+x_{v_eu_e}=1\), so exactly one orientation is represented for each \(e\in E\).

notation.meaning: incidences of the two directed alternatives

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-orientation encoding is plausible, but no source is supplied and the directed-alternative interpretation is application-dependent.

children.title: Temporal Precedence Binaries
children.top_down_role: Binary roles representing which activity precedes another.

knowledge_statements.title: Temporal Precedence Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scheduling indicators linking pairwise precedence choices to nonoverlap inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let activities \(i\) and \(j\) have start times \(s_i,s_j\), nonnegative durations \(p_i,p_j\), and a valid constant \(M\). A temporal precedence binary \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) selects the order of two activities that may not overlap. The inequalities \(s_i+p_i\le s_j+M(1-y_{ij})\) and \(s_j+p_j\le s_i+My_{ij}\) enforce \(i\) before \(j\) when \(y_{ij}=1\), and \(j\) before \(i\) when \(y_{ij}=0\). Validity requires \(M\) to dominate the maximum possible violation of each inactive inequality over the bounded scheduling domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary selects which of two nonoverlapping activities comes first; valid big-M inequalities enforce the chosen temporal order and relax the alternative.
assumptions_latex: Start times lie in a bounded scheduling domain.
\(M\) is valid for both inactive inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two inequalities imply either \(s_i+p_i\le s_j\) or \(s_j+p_j\le s_i\), according to \(y_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: start time and duration of activity i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disjunctive scheduling representation and validity condition on the big-M constant are appropriate, but no supporting citation with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Logical Truth Binaries
children.top_down_role: Truth values attached to propositions and compound logical conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Logical Truth Binaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary truth-value representation of propositions, including compound conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proposition \(P\), its logical truth binary is \(z_P\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(z_P=1\) if and only if \(P\) is true. For propositions \(P,Q\), consistent truth binaries obey \(z_{\neg P}=1-z_P\), \(z_{P\wedge Q}=z_Pz_Q\), and \(z_{P\vee Q}=z_P+z_Q-z_Pz_Q\). These equalities specify truth values; a mixed-integer formulation may replace nonlinear products by equivalent linear constraints over binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A logical truth binary equals one exactly when its proposition is true; binaries for negation, conjunction, and disjunction must reproduce their truth tables.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are propositions with definite truth values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_P=\mathbf 1[P]\), with the displayed Boolean identities for compound propositions.

notation.meaning: binary truth value assigned to proposition P

review_flags: Exact supporting locator for logical truth-variable modeling was not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and Boolean identities are mathematically correct and fit the logical-truth-binary container, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary linear representation of clauses and CNF formulas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact satisfaction equivalence for non-tautological clauses encoded by binary truth variables, extended row-wise to CNF; CNF conversion is asserted only as logical equivalence, not as a compact transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ encode truth values, with $x_j=1$ if and only if proposition $x_j$ is true. For $P,N\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $P\cap N=\varnothing$, the clause $C=\bigvee_{j\in P}x_j\vee\bigvee_{j\in N}\neg x_j$ is satisfied if and only if $\sum_{j\in P}x_j-\sum_{j\in N}x_j\ge 1-|N|$. Thus, for a CNF formula with one such clause per row, define $A_{ij}=1$ for a positive literal, $A_{ij}=-1$ for a negated literal, and $A_{ij}=0$ otherwise. Then the formula is satisfied if and only if $Ax\ge\mathbf 1-n(A)$, where $n(A)_i$ is the number of $-1$ entries in row $i$. Every propositional formula is logically equivalent to a formula in conjunctive normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode true and false as 1 and 0. A clause with positive literals indexed by P and negated literals indexed by N is satisfied exactly when its binary vector satisfies the corresponding signed covering inequality. Applying one inequality to each clause gives an exact binary linear-system representation of a CNF formula. Every propositional formula has a logically equivalent CNF representation, although no bound on the representation size is claimed.
assumptions_latex: A_{ij}=1,-1,0\text{ according as }x_j\text{ occurs positively, negatively, or not at all in clause }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is satisfied}\iff \sum_{j\in P}x_j-\sum_{j\in N}x_j\ge 1-|N|,\qquad \bigwedge_{i=1}^m C_i\text{ is satisfied}\iff Ax\ge\mathbf 1-n(A).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logical inequality systems, disjunctive sets, and disjunctive programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite formulas whose atomic statements are linear inequalities, equations, or systems thereof.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For propositions \(A,B\) with solution sets \(S_A,S_B\), \[A\Rightarrow B\equiv(\neg A)\vee B,\qquad S_{A\land B}=S_A\cap S_B,\qquad S_{A\vee B}=S_A\cup S_B.\] A set \(S_\varphi=\{x:\varphi(x)\}\) is disjunctive when its defining formula includes a disjunction, and optimization over \(S_\varphi\) is disjunctive programming. Conjunction-only linear systems define convex polyhedral sets, whereas disjunction is the connective capable of producing a nonconvex union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear inequalities and equations may be treated as true-or-false propositions, with conjunction corresponding to intersection and disjunction to union. An implication is equivalent to the disjunction of the negated antecedent and the consequent. A set defined by a formula containing a disjunction is a disjunctive set, and optimization over such a set is disjunctive programming. Conjunction-only linear systems are convex polyhedral, while a disjunction can produce a nonconvex set, though not every disjunction necessarily does so.
assumptions_latex: A,B\text{ are propositions represented by linear inequalities, equations, or finite systems thereof.}
\text{The connectives have their standard propositional semantics.}
\text{Non-disjunctive linear formulas are interpreted as conjunctions of linear constraints.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\Rightarrow B\equiv(\neg A)\vee B,\quad S_{A\land B}=S_A\cap S_B,\quad S_{A\vee B}=S_A\cup S_B;\qquad \vee\text{ permits nonconvex feasible sets and defines the disjunctive setting.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Integer Dependence and Separation Alternatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded integral refinement of a theorem of alternatives for finite families of bounded integer vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k>0\), \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\{0,\pm1,\ldots,\pm a_1\}^m\), and \(M_1=(ma_1)^{m+1}\). The following are equivalent: (a) there exist \(\beta_j\in\mathbb R_+\), not all zero, with \(\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jv_j=0\); (b) there exist integers \(\beta_j\in[0,M_1]\), not all zero, with \(\sum_{j=1}^k\beta_jv_j=0\); (c) no \(h\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \(h^Tv_j>0\) for every \(j\); and (d) no \(h\in\{0,\pm1,\ldots,\pm M_1\}^m\) satisfies \(h^Tv_j\ge1\) for every \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded integer vectors, nontrivial nonnegative real dependence is equivalent to bounded nontrivial nonnegative integer dependence and to the absence of either a real strict separator or a bounded integer separator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(a)}\iff\text{(b)}\iff\text{(c)}\iff\text{(d)}

children.title: Unit-Count Variables
children.top_down_role: Integer quantities representing numbers of individual units.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Count Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer multiplicity measured in individual, indivisible units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a set of item types. A unit-count variable \(x_i\) records the number of individual units of type \(i\in I\) selected, produced, assigned, or installed. Its domain is \(x_i\in\mathbb Z_+\), or \(x_i\in\{0,\ldots,U_i\}\) when a finite upper bound \(U_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) is known. If one unit contributes \(a_i\) units of a resource, its aggregate contribution is \(a_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-count variable is a nonnegative integer counting individual items; multiplying it by a per-unit coefficient gives the aggregate contribution.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is an index set and each counted unit is indivisible.
\(U_i\), when present, is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) and the modeled aggregate equals \(a_i x_i\).

notation.meaning: number of individual units of type i
optional upper bound on the unit count

children.title: Batch-Multiplicity Variables
children.top_down_role: Integer quantities representing repeated batches, lots, or runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Multiplicity Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer multiplicity measured in indivisible batches of fixed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let batch type \(i\) contain \(q_i\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\) physical units per batch. A batch-multiplicity variable \(b_i\in\mathbb Z_+\) records the number of complete batches selected or produced. The corresponding physical quantity is \(x_i=q_i b_i\); hence feasible quantities belong to \(q_i\mathbb Z_+\). With at most \(B_i\) batches, the domain becomes \(b_i\in\{0,\ldots,B_i\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch-multiplicity variable counts complete batches, so the resulting physical quantity is an integer multiple of the fixed batch size.
assumptions_latex: \(q_i\) is a positive integer batch size.
\(B_i\), when present, is a nonnegative integer.

knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Level Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer indices for ordered stages in a sequential process or development plan.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb Z_+\), and let stages \(0,1,\ldots,K\) be ordered so that reaching stage \(k\) requires completion of every preceding stage. A stage-level variable \(s\in\{0,\ldots,K\}\) denotes the highest attained stage. Equivalently, for each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), define \(y_k=\mathbf 1[s\ge k]\in\{0,1\}\). Then \(1\ge y_1\ge y_2\ge\cdots\ge y_K\ge0\) and \(s=\sum_{k=1}^K y_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stage-level variable gives the highest completed sequential stage and is equivalently represented by nested binary indicators for attainment of each positive stage.
assumptions_latex: Stages are finite and sequentially ordered.
Attaining a stage entails attaining every earlier stage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\in\{0,\ldots,K\}\), equivalently \(s=\sum_{k=1}^K y_k\) with \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\) and \(y_k\ge y_{k+1}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K-1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Level Variables

assumptions_latex: The capacity catalog is finite and strictly increasing.
Exactly one capacity level is selected.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact direct, ordered-unary, binary, mixed-radix, and hybrid representations of a bounded integer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\{L,L+1,\ldots,U\}\), where \(L,U\in\mathbb Z\), \(L\le U\), and \(N=U-L\). A direct representation retains this domain. An ordered-unary representation is \(x=L+\sum_{j=1}^{N}y_j\), with \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) and \(y_j\ge y_{j+1}\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}\); empty sums apply when \(N=0\). A binary representation is \(x=L+\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}2^j b_j\), where \(p=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), \(b_j\in\{0,1\}\), and \(\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}2^j b_j\le N\). For a mixed-radix representation, choose radices \(r_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\), weights \(w_0=1\) and \(w_j=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}r_i\), and enough digits that \(\prod_{j=0}^{p-1}r_j\ge N+1\); then impose \(d_j\in\{0,\ldots,r_j-1\}\), \(x=L+\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}w_jd_j\), and \(\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}w_jd_j\le N\). More generally, a hybrid finite-digit encoding is exact precisely when its permitted digit assignments attain every offset in \(\{0,6e6,N\}\) and no other offset.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded integer can be retained directly or encoded exactly by ordered unary digits, binary digits with a range constraint, mixed-radix digits with complete positional weights and a range constraint, or any hybrid digit system whose attainable offsets are exactly the bounded range.
assumptions_latex: All encoding digits have the stated finite integer domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each displayed construction represents exactly \(\{L,L+1,\ldots,U\}\); a general hybrid construction is exact if and only if its attainable offsets are exactly \(\{0,1,\ldots,U-L\}\).

notation.meaning: mixed radix, digit, and positional weight

children.title: Unbounded Integer Domains
children.top_down_role: Integer domains requiring recession, finite-generation, and representability considerations.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Integer Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why finite bounded-integer encodings do not represent genuinely unbounded integer domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is unbounded when, for every \(M>0\), some \(x\in D\) satisfies \(\lVert x\rVert>M\). No representation using only finitely many variables with finite domains can map surjectively onto such a \(D\), because its assignment set is finite. For example, \(D=\mathbb Z_+\) cannot be represented exactly by a fixed finite binary expansion. Exact modeling therefore retains an unbounded integer variable or uses an alternative representation with unbounded generators or dynamically extendable structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely unbounded integer domain cannot be encoded exactly by a fixed finite collection of bounded digits because those digits have only finitely many assignments.
assumptions_latex: The proposed encoding uses finitely many variables, each with a finite domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No such finite bounded-domain encoding is surjective onto \(D\).

notation.meaning: any norm on the finite-dimensional ambient space

children.title: Semicontinuous Variables

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuous Variables
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A zero state separated from a closed nonzero operating interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given real bounds \(0<L\le U<\infty\), a semicontinuous variable \(x\) has domain \(\{0\}\cup[L,U]\). Thus \(x\) is either inactive at zero or, when active, is at least \(L\) and at most \(U\). An exact mixed-integer representation introduces \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \(Lz\le x\le Uz\): \(z=0\) forces \(x=0\), while \(z=1\) permits precisely \(x\in[L,U]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semicontinuous variable is either zero or lies within a nonzero interval; one binary variable gives an exact bounded formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{0\}\cup[L,U]\) if and only if some \(z\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \(Lz\le x\le Uz\).

notation.meaning: positive operating lower and upper bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semicontinuous variable and node-bound reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inactive-or-interval domain and its simplification under local search-tree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A semicontinuous variable \operatorname{sc}(x,\ell,u), with \ell>0, has domain x\in\{0\}\cup[\ell,u]. At a search node, imposing a local lower bound x\geq\ell' with \ell'>0 excludes the inactive value and yields \max\{\ell,\ell'\}\leq x\leq u. Imposing a local upper bound x\leq u' with u'<\ell leaves only x=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semicontinuous variable is either zero or lies in a positive interval. A positive local lower bound removes the zero alternative and makes it an ordinary bounded variable; a local upper bound below the active interval fixes it to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\geq\ell'>0\Rightarrow \max\{\ell,\ell'\}\leq x\leq u,\qquad x\leq u'<\ell\Rightarrow x=0.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Finite-Domain Encodings

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compact binary encoding assigns each \(v_i\in V\) a distinct code \(c(v_i)\in\{0,1\}^q\), where \(q=\lceil\log_2 m\rceil\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded improving move under bounded subdeterminants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded augmentation theorem; the corrupted norm subscript is normalized to the infinity norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb R^m$, and $c\in\mathbb R^{1\times n}$. Suppose every square subdeterminant of $A$ has absolute value at most $\Delta$. If $z\in\mathbb Z^n$ is feasible but not optimal for $\max\{cx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}$, then there exists $z'\in\mathbb Z^n$ such that $Az'\le b$, $cz'>cz$, and $\lVert z-z'\rVert_\infty\le n\Delta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every subdeterminant of an integral constraint matrix is bounded by Delta, every feasible nonoptimal integer solution has a strictly improving feasible integer solution within infinity-norm distance n Delta.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is not optimal for }\max\{cx:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists z'\in\mathbb Z^n:\ Az'\le b,\ cz'>cz,\ \lVert z-z'\rVert_\infty\le n\Delta

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for Exact Single-Equation Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when an affine rational system admits a containing hyperplane with exactly the same nonnegative integer points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S=\{x\in\mathbb{Q}^n:Ax=b\}$ be an affine subspace. There exists an affine hyperplane $H\supseteq S$ such that $H\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^n=S\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^n$ if and only if either $S$ is itself an affine hyperplane or the cone generated by the columns of $A$ is pointed. In particular, if $\operatorname{rank}(A)\geq2$, a linear combination of the equations $Ax=b$ has exactly the same nonnegative integer solutions as the full system if and only if the column cone of $A$ is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine rational system can be replaced, on nonnegative integer points, by one containing hyperplane exactly when the original affine space is already a hyperplane or the cone generated by the columns of its coefficient matrix is pointed. When the matrix has rank at least two, this reduces to pointedness of the column cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists H\supseteq S:\ H\text{ affine hyperplane and }H\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^n=S\cap\mathbb{Z}_+^n\bigr)\iff\bigl(S\text{ is an affine hyperplane}\ \lor\ \operatorname{cone}(A_{\cdot1},\ldots,A_{\cdot n})\text{ is pointed}\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aggregation Problem for Nonnegative Integer Equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The linear combination sought must preserve exactly the nonnegative integer solution set; its existence is not asserted unconditionally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a system $Ax=b$ over $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n$, the aggregation problem is to find a multiplier vector $\lambda$ such that
\[
\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\mid Ax=b\}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\mid \lambda^\top Ax=\lambda^\top b\}.
\]
When such a multiplier exists, solving the system over nonnegative integers reduces to solving the single aggregated equation over the same domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The aggregation problem seeks a linear combination of a system's equations whose single equation has exactly the same nonnegative integer solutions as the original system. Existence of such a combination is not automatic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Find }\lambda\text{ such that }\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\mid Ax=b\}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_+^n\mid \lambda^\top Ax=\lambda^\top b\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong and weak formulations of uncapacitated facility location
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two mixed-binary linear formulations with disaggregated and aggregated facility-opening links.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the strong formulation is
\[
\max_{x,y}\ \sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in N}c_{ij}y_{ij}-\sum_{j\in N}f_jx_j
\]
subject to \(\sum_{j\in N}y_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(y_{ij}\le x_j\) for every \(i\in I,j\in N\), \(y\in\mathbb R_+^{mn}\), and \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). The weak formulation has the same objective, assignment equations, and variable domains, but replaces the disaggregated links by \(\sum_{i\in I}y_{ij}\le m x_j\) for every \(j\in N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong UFL formulation assigns every customer fully and permits assignment to a facility only when that facility is open. The weak formulation replaces the individual assignment-opening inequalities by one aggregated inequality per facility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{UFL}:\ y_{ij}\le x_j\ (i\in I,j\in N),\qquad \mathrm{WUFL}:\ \sum_{i\in I}y_{ij}\le m x_j\ (j\in N),

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-form optimum of the weak UFL linear relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes an optimal solution of the LP relaxation when all facility costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(I=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(f_j\ge0\) for every \(j\in N\), and relax the binary restrictions in WUFL to linear-programming bounds. For every \(i\in I\), choose
\[
j_i\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{j\in N}\left(c_{ij}-\frac{f_j}{m}\right).
\]
Then the relaxation has an optimal solution satisfying
\[
y^*_{i j_i}=1,\qquad y^*_{ij}=0\quad(j\ne j_i),
\]
and
\[
x_j^*=\frac1m\sum_{i\in I}y^*_{ij}\qquad(j\in N).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every opening cost is nonnegative, an optimal solution of the weak-formulation LP relaxation assigns each customer entirely to a facility maximizing adjusted profit c_ij minus f_j/m. Each facility variable equals the fraction of customers assigned to it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(x^*,y^*)\in\operatorname{Opt}(\operatorname{LP}(\mathrm{WUFL})):\ y^*_{i j_i}=1,\ y^*_{ij}=0\ (j\ne j_i),\ x_j^*=m^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}y^*_{ij}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sherali–Adams lift-and-project procedure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of the lifted polyhedron R_t and projected relaxation S_t.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given Ax\ge b and 1\le t\le n: (1) generate (Ax-b)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j)\ge0 for every disjoint I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} satisfying 1\le|I|+|J|\le t; (2) use x_j^2=x_j, replace each nonempty square-free monomial \prod_{i\in I}x_i by y_I, and set y_\varnothing=1, thereby obtaining R_t\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathcal P_n}; (3) project R_t onto the x-space and denote the resulting polytope by S_t.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate all allowed product inequalities, reduce square factors using binary identities, replace square-free monomials by subset-indexed variables, set the empty-set variable to one, and project the resulting polyhedron onto the original variables. This projection is S_t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_t\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathcal P_n},\qquad S_t=\operatorname{proj}_x(R_t).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-size certificates for mixed-integer linear feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the mixed-integer linear-set definition, the nonemptiness certificate result, and the explicitly conjectural boundary for emptiness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\le b\}\), where \((A,G,b)\) is rationally encoded. Then \(S\) is a mixed-integer linear set. If \(S\ne\varnothing\), it contains a feasible point whose encoding size is polynomial in the encoding size of \((A,G,b)\); consequently, its nonemptiness has a polynomially verifiable certificate and belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). No evident analogous polynomially checkable certificate is known for emptiness, and membership of the emptiness problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\) is conjectured to fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational mixed-integer linear set consists of nonnegative integer and continuous vectors satisfying rational linear inequalities. If it is nonempty, it has a polynomial-size feasible witness, so nonemptiness is in NP. Emptiness has no evident analogous polynomially checkable certificate and is conjectured not to be in NP.

children.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models with convex continuous nonlinear substructure.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity refers to the continuous relaxation of a minimization-form MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,p,m,q\in\mathbb Z_+\), let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be convex sets, let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be convex functions, and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\). A convex mixed-integer nonlinear program has the form
\[\min\{f(x,y):g_i(x,y)\le 0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ Ax+By=b,\ (x,y)\in X\times(Y\cap\mathbb Z^p)\}.\]
Replacing \(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^p\) by \(y\in Y\) produces a convex continuous optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex MINLP is a minimization model whose integrality-relaxed domain and feasible region are convex, whose relaxed objective and inequality functions are convex, and whose equality constraints are affine.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The continuous relaxation is a convex optimization problem.}\)

notation.meaning: decision vector constrained to be integral in the MINLP

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvexity is classified through the continuous relaxation of a minimization-form MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a mixed-integer nonlinear minimization model with continuous variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), integer-constrained variables \(y\in\mathbb Z^p\), and a prescribed continuous relaxation of the restrictions on \(y\). Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) be the feasible set of that relaxation and let \(f:R\to\mathbb R\) be its objective. The model is nonconvex if \(R\) is not convex or, when \(R\) is convex, if \(f\) is not convex on \(R\). Nonlinear constraints, nonlinear equalities, and interactions involving relaxed integer variables fall in this class only when they create one of these failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex MINLP is a minimization model whose continuous relaxation has a nonconvex feasible set or, on a convex relaxed feasible set, a nonconvex objective. A nonlinear equality or discrete interaction qualifies only when it causes such a failure.

The integer restrictions have a prescribed continuous relaxation with feasible set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\).
\(f:R\to\mathbb R\) is the relaxed minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The continuous relaxation is not a convex optimization problem.}\)

children.title: Forward Implication Patterns
children.top_down_role: One-way dependence from a triggering proposition to a required consequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Implication Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary encoding of implication between two reified propositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let binary variables \(y,z\in\{0,1\}\) indicate the truth of propositions \(P\) and \(Q\), respectively. The forward implication \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is represented exactly by
\[y\le z.\]
Indeed, the inequality excludes only the truth assignment \((y,z)=(1,0)\), which is precisely the unique assignment on which \(P\Rightarrow Q\) is false. It imposes no converse requirement when \(Q\) is true.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary truth indicators, the forward implication from P to Q is exactly the inequality y ≤ z.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\Rightarrow Q\iff y\le z\).

children.title: Reverse Implication Patterns
children.top_down_role: One-way dependence expressed in the reverse semantic direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Implication Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary encoding of the converse implication between reified propositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let binary variables \(y,z\in\{0,1\}\) indicate the truth of propositions \(P\) and \(Q\). The reverse implication \(Q\Rightarrow P\), viewed relative to the ordered pair \((P,Q)\), is represented exactly by
\[z\le y.\]
The inequality excludes only \((y,z)=(0,1)\), the unique assignment on which \(Q\Rightarrow P\) is false. It does not impose the forward implication \(P\Rightarrow Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For binary truth indicators, the reverse implication from Q to P is exactly the inequality z ≤ y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\Rightarrow P\iff z\le y\).

children.title: Logical Equivalence Patterns

knowledge_statements.title: Logical Equivalence Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equivalence of two propositions represented by binary truth indicators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y,z\in\{0,1\}\) reify propositions \(P\) and \(Q\). Logical equivalence requires both directed implications and therefore has the exact linear representation
\[y\le z,\qquad z\le y,\]
or, equivalently,
\[y=z.\]
Consequently, precisely the assignments \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\) are feasible, matching the truth table of \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two reified propositions are logically equivalent exactly when their binary truth indicators are equal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\iff y=z\).

children.title: Partial-Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where only one logical direction is supported by the intended semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Equivalence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single implication is insufficient to encode logical equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary truth indicators \(y,z\), the constraint \(y\le z\) encodes only \(P\Rightarrow Q\), not \(P\Leftrightarrow Q\), because \((y,z)=(0,1)\) remains feasible. Symmetrically, \(z\le y\) leaves \((y,z)=(1,0)\) feasible. Thus an equivalence formulation must enforce both directions, unless some independent model constraint already implies the omitted direction; without such an implication, the formulation is only a partial equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One directional implication does not establish equivalence; the omitted direction must be enforced or independently implied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\le z\not\Rightarrow y=z\) and \(z\le y\not\Rightarrow y=z\).

children.title: Compound Boolean Pattern Taxonomy

children.title: Conjunctive Requirement Patterns
children.top_down_role: Compound conditions requiring simultaneous satisfaction of component propositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive Requirement Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary reification of a finite conjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\in\{0,1\}\) reify propositions \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\), with \(m\ge1\), and let \(y\in\{0,1\}\) reify their conjunction. The equivalence \(y=1\iff Q_1\land\cdots\land Q_m\) is represented exactly by
\[y\le z_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad y\ge\sum_{i=1}^m z_i-(m-1).\]
The upper inequalities enforce every requirement when \(y=1\); the lower inequality forces \(y=1\) when all requirements hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary conjunction indicator is bounded above by every child and below by their sum minus m−1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=1\iff \bigwedge_{i=1}^m(z_i=1)\).

children.title: Inclusive Disjunction Patterns
children.top_down_role: Alternative conditions permitting one or more component propositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Inclusive Disjunction Patterns
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary reification of a finite inclusive disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\in\{0,1\}\) reify propositions \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\), with \(m\ge1\), and let \(y\in\{0,1\}\) reify their inclusive disjunction. The equivalence \(y=1\iff Q_1\lor\cdots\lor Q_m\) is represented exactly by
\[y\ge z_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad y\le\sum_{i=1}^m z_i.\]
Multiple \(z_i\) may equal one; hence this is inclusive rather than exclusive disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inclusive-OR indicator dominates every child and is bounded above by the sum of all child indicators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=1\iff \bigvee_{i=1}^m(z_i=1)\).

notation.meaning: truth indicator for the inclusive disjunction

children.title: Compound Logic Trees
children.top_down_role: Nested combinations of logical operators organized as expression trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Compound Logic Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive exact encoding of a finite Boolean syntax tree using auxiliary binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite rooted Boolean tree whose leaves have binary truth indicators and whose internal nodes are unary NOT nodes or nonempty AND or OR nodes. Process the internal nodes from leaves to root and introduce a binary variable \(y_v\) for every node \(v\). For a NOT node \(v=\neg u\), impose \(y_v=1-y_u\). For an AND node with child set \(C(v)\), impose \(y_v\le y_u\) for every \(u\in C(v)\) and \(y_v\ge\sum_{u\in C(v)}y_u-|C(v)|+1\). For an OR node, impose \(y_v\ge y_u\) for every \(u\in C(v)\) and \(y_v\le\sum_{u\in C(v)}y_u\). Finally, impose \(y_r=1\) for the root \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encode a finite Boolean tree containing only NOT, AND, and OR nodes from the leaves upward with exact binary constraints, and require the root indicator to equal one.
assumptions_latex: The Boolean expression is a finite rooted tree.
Every internal node is a unary NOT node or an AND or OR node with at least one child.
Every leaf and auxiliary node indicator is binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The formulation is feasible exactly for leaf assignments satisfying the root formula.}\)

notation.meaning: truth indicator associated with node v
nonempty child set of an AND or OR node v

children.title: Operator-Nesting Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Semantic distinctions arising when compound operators are nested or regrouped.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Nesting Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided encodings are unsafe when an auxiliary proposition occurs in negative polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\) represent \(z_1\land z_2\) inside the nested formula \(y\Rightarrow\neg w\). If only \(w\le z_1\) and \(w\le z_2\) are imposed, together with \(y+w\le1\), then \((y,z_1,z_2,w)=(1,1,1,0)\) is feasible although \(y\Rightarrow\neg(z_1\land z_2)\) is false. Therefore a one-sided child encoding cannot generally be substituted beneath negation or another antitone context; exact reification, including \(w\ge z_1+z_2-1\), is required unless model-specific implications supply the missing direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-sided auxiliary encoding can fail under negation; nested operators generally require exact reification or an independently implied missing direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated one-sided formulation admits a truth assignment forbidden by \(y\Rightarrow\neg(z_1\land z_2)\).

children.title: Exclusive Choice Logic Family

children.title: Mutually Exclusive Choices
children.top_down_role: Alternative decisions that cannot be active simultaneously.

knowledge_statements.title: Mutually Exclusive Choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise mutual exclusion for a finite family of binary choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For binary choice indicators \(y_1,
\ldots,y_m\in\{0,1\}\), with \(m\ge2\), the choices are mutually exclusive when no distinct pair can be simultaneously selected:
\[y_i+y_j\le1\qquad(1\le i<j\le m).\]
Because the variables are binary, these pairwise inequalities are equivalent to the compact condition
\[\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\le1.\]
The all-zero assignment remains admissible, so mutual exclusion alone does not require any choice to be selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary choices are mutually exclusive exactly when their sum is at most one; selecting no choice remains allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_i+y_j\le1\ (i<j)\iff\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\le1\).

children.title: Exactly-One Choices
children.top_down_role: Alternative sets requiring one selected member.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactly-One Choices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection condition requiring one and only one binary alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For binary choice indicators \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\in\{0,1\}\), with \(m\ge1\), exactly one alternative is selected precisely when
\[\sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1.\]
Equivalently, the formulation combines the at-most-one constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\le1\) with the coverage constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^m y_i\ge1\). Thus both simultaneous selections and the all-zero assignment are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one binary choice is selected when the sum of all selection indicators equals one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one choice is selected \(\iff\sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic definition of a binary-state conditional constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in X\), a conditional constraint with designated state \(z=1\) has semantics \[z=1\Longrightarrow g(x)\le 0.\] Its feasible set in coordinates \((z,x)\) is \[\bigl(\{0\}\times X\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{1\}\times\{x\in X:g(x)\le 0\}\bigr).\] Thus the condition restricts \(x\) when the designated state is active and imposes no restriction beyond \(x\in X\) when it is inactive.

children.title: Use-Triggered Charges
children.top_down_role: Charges incurred when a modeled asset or option is used.

knowledge_statements.title: Use-Triggered Charges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed positive charge triggered by any positive use in a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\times\{0,1\}\) be a feasible set containing the linking constraints \[0\le x_j\le U_jz\qquad(j=1,\ldots,n).\] Adding \(Fz\), with \(F>0\), to a minimized objective \(c(x)+Fz\) incurs the fixed charge whenever \(x\ne 0\), because positive use forces \(z=1\). If \((0,1)\in\mathcal F\) implies \((0,0)\in\mathcal F\), then every optimal solution with \(x=0\) has \(z=0\), since changing only \(z\) from one to zero reduces the objective by \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linking bounds force the binary indicator, and hence the fixed charge, whenever use is positive. If deactivation remains feasible when use is zero, every optimum deactivates the indicator and avoids the charge in that case.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb{R}_+^n\times\{0,1\}\) is the feasible set and includes \(0\le x_j\le U_jz\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\), where every \(U_j\ge 0\) is finite.
The objective \(c(x)+Fz\) is minimized over \(\mathcal F\), where \(c:\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(F>0\).
The remaining constraints permit deactivation at zero use: \((0,1)\in\mathcal F\Longrightarrow(0,0)\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible \((x,z)\in\mathcal F\) satisfies \(x\ne 0\Longrightarrow z=1\), and every optimum satisfies \(x=0\Longrightarrow z=0\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set for the use variables and binary indicator.
Vector of nonnegative quantities whose positive use triggers the charge.
Finite upper bound linking component j to the use indicator.
Objective contribution independent of the binary use indicator.
Positive fixed charge incurred upon activation.

knowledge_statements.title: Entry-Triggered Charges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary transition formulation for a charge incurred exactly when an inactive state becomes active.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_{t-1},x_t,e_t\in\{0,1\}\), where \(x_t\) denotes activity and \(e_t\) denotes entry at time \(t\). Exact entry semantics are imposed by \[e_t\ge x_t-x_{t-1},\qquad e_t\le x_t,\qquad e_t\le 1-x_{t-1}.\] Thus \(e_t=1\) if and only if \((x_{t-1},x_t)=(0,1)\). For an entry charge \(f_t\ge0\), the corresponding objective term is \(f_t e_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The entry indicator equals one exactly for a zero-to-one activity transition, so multiplying it by the entry fee charges each activation event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_t=1\iff (x_{t-1},x_t)=(0,1)\), with charge \(f_t e_t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Setup-State Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary readiness state that permits operation and carries a setup-dependent cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether a facility, machine, or process is set up, and let \(x\) denote its operating level. Given a valid capacity bound \(U\ge0\), setup-state semantics are \[0\le x\le Us.\] Consequently, positive operation implies \(s=1\), while \(s=0\) forces \(x=0\). A nonnegative setup charge \(f\) is represented by the objective term \(fs\); the state \(s=1\) permits but does not require positive operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A setup indicator enables bounded operation and incurs its fixed charge; being set up permits operation but does not force use.
assumptions_latex: \(U\ge0\) is a valid upper bound and \(f\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le x\le Us\), so \(s=0\Rightarrow x=0\), with setup charge \(fs\).

knowledge_statements.title: Activation-Cost Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear coupling between a binary activation decision, bounded activity, and a fixed objective charge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\{0,1\}\) activate a nonnegative activity \(x\), whose valid active-state bounds are \(0\le L\le U\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an ambient set, let \(x\in X\), and let \(C_1,C_2\subseteq X\) be the feasible sets of two alternative constraint systems. The either-or disjunction is \[[x\in C_1]\ \lor\ [x\in C_2],\] equivalently \(x\in C_1\cup C_2\). The disjunction is inclusive unless exclusivity is imposed separately: a point in \(C_1\cap C_2\) satisfies both branches and remains feasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Big-M formulation of an either–or linear disjunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary formulation of two bounded linear alternatives, with two-job nonoverlap as an application.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let y\in\mathbb{R}^n satisfy 0\le y\le u. If M\ge \max\{a^iy-b_i:0\le y\le u\} for each i\in\{1,2\}, then \((a^1y\le b_1)\lor(a^2y\le b_2)\) is represented by a^iy-b_i\le M(1-x_i)\ (i=1,2),\ x_1+x_2=1,\ x_i\in\{0,1\},\ 0\le y\le u. When x_i=1, alternative i is enforced; the bound on M makes an unselected alternative redundant over the bounded domain. For two jobs sharing a nonpreemptive machine, the alternatives may be t_2\ge t_1+p_1 and t_1\ge t_2+p_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded domain, an either–or pair of linear inequalities can be represented using two binary variables that sum to one and a sufficiently large big-M constant. The selected binary enforces its inequality, while the other inequality becomes redundant. Mutually exclusive job-precedence orders are a scheduling specialization.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Alternative Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive feasible-set representation in which selecting a branch activates a subordinate disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a parent disjunction have branch sets \(C_i\subseteq X\). Suppose branch \(i\) contains subordinate alternatives \(D_{ij}\subseteq X\), indexed by \(j\in J_i\). Its nested feasible set is \[\bigcup_i\left(C_i\cap\bigcup_{j\in J_i}D_{ij}\right)=\bigcup_i\bigcup_{j\in J_i}(C_i\cap D_{ij}).\] Thus a subordinate alternative is relevant only inside its selected parent branch; flattening is set-theoretically valid when every resulting branch retains both the parent and subordinate constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested disjunction selects a parent branch and then one of its subordinate branches; flattening must retain constraints from both levels.
assumptions_latex: \(C_i,D_{ij}\subseteq X\) and each \(J_i\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_i(C_i\cap\bigcup_{j\in J_i}D_{ij})=\bigcup_i\bigcup_{j\in J_i}(C_i\cap D_{ij})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchical Choice Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree semantics for conditional choices across multiple levels of a disjunctive hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=(V,E)\) be a finite rooted tree with root \(r\), and assign \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\) to every node. A hierarchical exactly-one choice structure satisfies \[y_r=1,\qquad \sum_{w\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}y_w=y_v\] for every nonleaf node \(v\). Hence each active internal node selects exactly one child, while every child of an inactive node is inactive. The active nodes form one root-to-leaf path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary choices on a rooted tree select one child of every active internal node, producing a single active root-to-leaf path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_r=1\) and \(\sum_{w\in\operatorname{ch}(v)}y_w=y_v\) make the active nodes a root-to-leaf path.

children.title: Subordinate Choice Coupling
children.top_down_role: Dependencies linking higher-level selections to lower-level alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Subordinate Choice Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear consistency condition coupling a parent selection to its immediate subordinate alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_p\in\{0,1\}\) represent selection of a parent branch and let \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\) represent its subordinate alternatives for \(j\in J(p)\). Exact subordinate-choice coupling is \[\sum_{j\in J(p)}y_j=y_p.\] If \(y_p=0\), every subordinate trigger is zero; if \(y_p=1\), exactly one subordinate trigger is one. For an at-most-one subordinate choice, the corresponding condition is \(\sum_{j\in J(p)}y_j\le y_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The children sum to the parent indicator, so an active parent selects exactly one child and an inactive parent selects none.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j\in J(p)}y_j=y_p\) enforces exact subordinate selection.

notation.meaning: set of subordinate choices under parent p

children.title: Hierarchy-Consistency Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where subordinate choices conflict with their governing selections.

knowledge_statements.title: Hierarchy-Consistency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of ancestor implications alone to enforce required subordinate selection in a hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) have two subordinate alternatives with binary indicators \(y_p,y_1,y_2\). The ancestor implications \[y_1\le y_p,\qquad y_2\le y_p\] prevent a child from being active under an inactive parent, but they do not require an active parent to choose a child: \((y_p,y_1,y_2)=(1,0,0)\) satisfies both inequalities. Exact-one hierarchy consistency therefore additionally requires \(y_1+y_2=y_p\); at-most-one semantics requires only \(y_1+y_2\le y_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Child-to-parent implications forbid orphan children but permit an active parent with no selected child; equality is needed for mandatory subordinate choice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_i\le y_p\) alone is insufficient for exact choice; \(y_1+y_2=y_p\) is required.

children.title: Generalized Disjunctive Models
children.top_down_role: Boolean and algebraic structures maintained as a distinct modeling layer.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) and every \(D_k\) are finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pair \((x,Y)\) is feasible exactly when the global constraints and Boolean formula hold, each block has at least one true proposition, and every true proposition enforces its attached algebraic system.

notation.meaning: continuous decision point and its ambient set
Boolean proposition selecting disjunct i of block k

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) and every \(D_k\) be finite nonempty index sets, let \(x\in X\), let \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}^q\), and let \(r_{ik}:X\to\mathbb{R}^{q_{ik}}\) for \(k\in K\) and \(i\in D_k\). Let \(Y_{ik}\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}\), and let \(\Omega(Y)\) be a propositional formula coupling these Boolean variables. A generalized disjunctive model requires \[g(x)\le0,\qquad \Omega(Y)=\mathrm{true},\qquad \bigvee_{i\in D_k}Y_{ik}\quad(k\in K),\] together with \[Y_{ik}\Rightarrow r_{ik}(x)\le0\quad(k\in K,\ i\in D_k),\] where vector inequalities are componentwise. Thus every selected disjunct enforces its attached algebraic system. Exactly-one or other cardinality rules may be included explicitly in \(\Omega(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized disjunctive model combines global algebraic constraints, Boolean branch propositions, branch-specific constraint systems, and explicit logical relations. Every true branch proposition enforces its attached constraints, while separate Boolean rules determine permitted selection cardinalities.

children.title: Sparse-Choice SOS1 Regime

children.title: SOS1 Support Semantics
children.top_down_role: Solver-recognized sparse supports permitting at most one active member.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Support Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based semantics of a type-1 special ordered set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((z_1,[0mldots,z_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\) be an ordered collection of variables. It is a special ordered set of type 1 if \[\left|\{i\in\{1,[0mldots,n\}:z_i\ne0\}\right|\le1.\] Thus the zero vector is allowed, and otherwise exactly one member may be nonzero. The ordering weights identify the members and their order for solver handling, but they do not alter this at-most-one-nonzero feasible-set semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS1 collection permits at most one nonzero member; all members may be zero, and ordering weights do not change feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\) is SOS1-feasible iff \(|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\le1\).

notation.meaning: member variable of the SOS1 collection
set of indices of nonzero components

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended SOS1 support semantics is standard and the definition kind fits, but no source is supplied. The statement also contains corrupted LaTeX tokens such as [0mldots, so it cannot be accepted as a well-formed mathematical record.

children.title: At-Most-One Support Semantics
children.top_down_role: Generic sparse-choice structures permitting zero or one active member.

knowledge_statements.title: At-Most-One Support Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality predicate defining at-most-one nonzero support without solver-specific ordering metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(z_1,[0mldots,z_n)\inodal{R}^n\), define \(\operatorname{supp}(z)=\{i:z_i\ne0\}\). The at-most-one support condition is \[|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\le1.\] If binary indicators \(y_i\) encode nonzero eligibility and valid bounds satisfy \(-M_i y_i\le z_i\le M_i y_i\), then \(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\le1\) is a sufficient mixed-integer representation. It is exact in the projected \(z\)-space when each \(M_i\) validly bounds \(|z_i|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At most one component may be nonzero. Binary eligibility indicators and valid magnitude bounds provide a standard mixed-integer representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i y_i\le1\) and \(-M_i y_i\le z_i\le M_i y_i\) project to \(|\operatorname{supp}(z)|\le1\).

notation.meaning: indices of nonzero components of z
valid absolute bound on component i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The intended support-cardinality condition and bounded binary representation are mathematically standard, but the record has no citation and contains corrupted LaTeX, including [0mldots and the undefined command \rodal. A specific source and repaired statement are required.

children.title: Weighted SOS1 Ordering
children.top_down_role: Ordering metadata attached to members of an SOS1 support.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted SOS1 Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Role of reference weights in an SOS1 declaration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be declared SOS1 with pairwise distinct reference weights \(w_1,\ldots,w_n\). The weights induce the ordering obtained by sorting \(w_i\), but SOS1 feasibility is exactly \[|\{i:x_i\ne 0\}|\le 1.\] Consequently, changing the weights or their order without changing their distinctness does not change the feasible support family; weights may affect branching or solver processing only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct weights order SOS1 members for solver processing, but feasibility requires only that at most one member be nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le 1\), independently of the ordering induced by \(w\).

notation.meaning: The set of indices whose variables are nonzero.
Reference weight attached to SOS1 member i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SOS1 feasibility claim is standard, but the assertions about reference-weight invariance and solver processing require an authoritative SOS locator.

children.title: SOS1 Recognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation choices affecting whether SOS1 structure remains visible.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS1 Recognition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between an SOS1 restriction and an ordinary linear inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For continuous nonnegative variables, the linear constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\le 1\) does not enforce SOS1 support. Indeed, for \(n\ge 2\), the vector with \(x_1=x_2=1/2\) and all other components zero satisfies the inequality but has two nonzero components. The inequality implies SOS1 only under additional domain restrictions, such as \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\), or when SOS1 is separately declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sum-at-most-one row enforces SOS1 for binary variables, but not for unrestricted nonnegative continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i x_i\le 1\not\Rightarrow |\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le 1\).

notation.meaning: Indices of nonzero components of x.

children.title: Adjacent-Choice SOS2 Regime
children.top_down_role: Ordered structures allowing activity on adjacent members.

children.title: SOS2 Support Semantics
children.top_down_role: Solver-recognized ordered supports permitting activity on neighboring members.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Support Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent support definition of an SOS2 set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) have members ordered by pairwise distinct weights \(w_1<\cdots<w_n\). The vector \(x\) satisfies the SOS2 restriction if there exists \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) such that \[\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}.\] Thus zero, singleton, and two-member supports are permitted, while a two-member support must consist of adjacent members in the weight ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS2 vector has at most two nonzero members, and any two nonzero members must be adjacent in weight order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is SOS2 exactly when \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}\) for some \(j\).

notation.meaning: Indices of nonzero components of x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated SOS2 convention is mathematically precise, but its defining support semantics and treatment of weights require an authoritative source.

children.title: Adjacent-Pair Activity
children.top_down_role: Choice structures restricted to one member or a neighboring pair.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjacent-Pair Activity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent support characterization for an ordered SOS2 family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an ordered family \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), SOS2 activity is equivalent to membership of the support in one edge of the path on vertices \(1,\ldots,n\). Explicitly, \[\operatorname{supp}(x)\in\bigcup_{j=1}^{n-1}2^{\{j,j+1\}}.\] Hence two positive or negative nonzero components may be simultaneously active only at consecutive positions; the restriction concerns support and does not prescribe their signs or magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS2 supports are precisely subsets of adjacent pairs in the path defined by the member ordering.
assumptions_latex: The members are indexed in their SOS2 weight order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\{j,j+1\}\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct reformulation of standard SOS2 semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a correct path-graph reformulation under the stated SOS2 convention, but that convention remains unsupported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Breakpoint Weight Ordering
children.top_down_role: Ordering metadata used to position members within an SOS2 support.

knowledge_statements.title: Breakpoint Weight Ordering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition for weights defining SOS2 adjacency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate member \(x_i\) with breakpoint weight \(w_i\). A valid unambiguous SOS2 ordering requires pairwise distinct weights; after relabeling, they satisfy \[w_1<w_2<\cdots<w_n.\] Two members are adjacent exactly when their ranks in this sorted sequence differ by one. Coincident weights fail to determine a unique adjacency relation unless an additional tie-breaking order is explicitly supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct breakpoint weights define SOS2 adjacency by sorted rank; tied weights require an explicit tie-breaking order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_i\ne w_j\) for \(i\ne j\) yields a strict total order and well-defined adjacent pairs.

notation.meaning: Breakpoint or reference weight attached to member i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Distinct weights define a strict ordering, but whether tied SOS2 weights are invalid or handled by solver-specific tie breaking requires authoritative documentation.

children.title: SOS2 Recognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation choices affecting visibility of adjacency structure.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Recognition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-combination equations do not themselves impose SOS2 adjacency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 3\) and impose only \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\). These constraints do not enforce SOS2 support: \(\lambda_1=\lambda_3=1/2\), with every other component zero, is feasible but activates two nonadjacent ordered members. Therefore a convex-combination formulation requires an explicit SOS2 declaration or additional integer constraints that enforce adjacency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex constraints permit nonadjacent positive weights, so SOS2 adjacency needs an explicit declaration or an equivalent integer formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda\ge 0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\) do not imply SOS2 support.

notation.meaning: Convex-combination weight of ordered member i.

children.title: Higher-Order Ordered Supports
children.top_down_role: Ordered-support structures beyond the two standard special ordered set types.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Ordered Supports
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A generalized consecutive-support structure extending SOS1 and SOS2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an ordering of \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) and an integer \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A consecutive support of order \(k\) is a vector \(x\) for which there exists \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n-k+1\}\) satisfying \[\operatorname{supp}(x)\subseteq\{j,j+1,\ldots,j+k-1\}.\] Thus at most \(k\) members may be nonzero, and all active members lie in one consecutive block. The cases \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) recover the support patterns of SOS1 and SOS2, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-k consecutive support places every nonzero member within one block of at most k consecutive ordered positions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{supp}(x)\) is contained in a length-\(k\) interval of the member ordering.

notation.meaning: Maximum length of the active consecutive block.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consecutive-block definition is coherent, but it is not established that this particular construction exhausts or canonically defines the broader Higher-Order Ordered Supports topic.

knowledge_statements.title: Set Covering Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical binary formulation for minimum-cost set cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) be required elements and let \(S_1,\ldots,S_n\subseteq U\) have costs \(c_j\). Define \(A_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(i\in S_j\). The minimum-cost set covering problem is represented by \[\min\left\{\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j: \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\ge 1\ \text{for every }i\in U,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.\] A feasible vector selects sets whose union contains every element of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary variables select minimum-cost subsets, with one covering inequality requiring each ground element to belong to a selected subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\ge\mathbf{1}\) holds exactly when the selected sets cover \(U\).

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that set j is selected.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incidence-Matrix Formulations of Set Covering, Packing, and Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the set-theoretic definitions, their exact 0-1 incidence formulations, and the assignment specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(M_j\subseteq M\) for \(j\in N\). For \(F\subseteq N\), define \(x_j=1\) iff \(j\in F\), and let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(a_{ij}=1\) iff \(i\in M_j\). Then \[F\text{ covers }M\iff Ax\ge\mathbf1,\qquad F\text{ is a packing}\iff Ax\le\mathbf1,\qquad F\text{ partitions }M\iff Ax=\mathbf1.\] Set covering seeks a minimum-cost cover, whereas set packing seeks a maximum-weight packing. A square assignment problem is a set-partitioning problem whose columns each contain one job and one person.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a family of subsets, selecting columns covers, packs, or partitions the ground set exactly when its binary incidence vector satisfies Ax at least one, at most one, or equal to one, respectively. Covering is typically minimum-cost and packing maximum-weight; square assignment is a set-partitioning specialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ covers }M\iff Ax\ge\mathbf1;\quad F\text{ packs }M\iff Ax\le\mathbf1;\quad F\text{ partitions }M\iff Ax=\mathbf1.
