knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cuts, Edge Boundaries, and Vertex Degree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General graph-theoretic definitions used as preliminaries for graph-based covering formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with nonnegative edge weights \(w_e\) for \(e\in E\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(\delta(S):=\{uv\in E:u\in S,\ v\notin S\}\). A set \(F\subseteq E\) is a cut if \(F=\delta(S)\) for some \(S\subseteq V\), and it is proper if this holds for some \(\varnothing\neq S\subset V\). For \(v\in V\), \(\delta(v):=\delta(\{v\})\), and \(\deg(v):=|\delta(v)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vertex subset S, its edge boundary consists of edges with one endpoint in S and the other outside. A cut is such an edge boundary, and it is proper when S is nonempty and not all of V. The edges incident to a vertex v form delta(v), whose cardinality is the degree of v.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta(S)=\{uv\in E:u\in S,\ v\notin S\}\), \(F\) is a cut iff \(F=\delta(S)\) for some \(S\subseteq V\), \(F\) is proper iff this holds for some \(\varnothing\neq S\subset V\), \(\delta(v)=\delta(\{v\})\), and \(\deg(v)=|\delta(v)|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Set Packing Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical binary formulation for weighted set packing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), where column \(j\) represents an object and row \(i\) represents a resource or incompatibility class. With profit \(c_j\), weighted set packing is represented by \[\max\left\{\sum_{j=1}^n c_jx_j: \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}x_j\le 1\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\right\}.\] Each row prohibits simultaneous selection of two columns containing that row's element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set packing maximizes selected profit while each incidence row permits at most one selected object.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible selections are exactly \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\le\mathbf{1}\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set packing–stable set correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence obtained from the column-intersection graph of a binary packing matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}, define the intersection graph G_A on the n columns of A by joining distinct u,v whenever a_{iu}=a_{iv}=1 for some row i. Then S^P(A)=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\leq\mathbf1\}=\operatorname{stab}(G_A). Conversely, for every undirected graph G=(V,E), its stable-set characteristic vectors are exactly \{x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}:x_u+x_v\leq1\ \forall uv\in E\}, which is a set-packing family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary vectors satisfying a set-packing matrix are exactly the stable-set vectors of the matrix's column-intersection graph. Conversely, every graph stable-set family is a set-packing family defined by its edge constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^P(A)=\operatorname{stab}(G_A).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Packing, partitioning, and covering set systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite set systems, their characteristic-vector formulations, weighted optimization models, and incidence-matrix notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let E=\{1,\ldots,n\}, let \mathcal F=\{F_1,\ldots,F_m\}\subseteq 2^E, and let x^S\in\{0,1\}^n be the characteristic vector of S\subseteq E. The set S is a packing, partitioning, or covering of \mathcal F exactly when |S\cap F_i|\leq1, |S\cap F_i|=1, or |S\cap F_i|\geq1, respectively, for every i. Thus S^P=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{j\in F_i}x_j\leq1\ \forall i\}, S^T=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{j\in F_i}x_j=1\ \forall i\}, and S^C=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_{j\in F_i}x_j\geq1\ \forall i\}. For weights w, the canonical problems maximize w^\top x over S^P and minimize w^\top x over S^T or S^C. If A is the incidence matrix of \mathcal F, these families are respectively \{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\leq\mathbf1\}, \{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax=\mathbf1\}, and \{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\geq\mathbf1\}; the same definitions apply to any 0,1 matrix A.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite family of sets, a selected set is a packing, partitioning, or covering when it meets every family member at most once, exactly once, or at least once. Characteristic vectors give binary incidence-matrix systems with Ax at most, equal to, or at least the all-ones vector; the standard weighted models maximize packing weight and minimize partitioning or covering weight.
assumptions_latex: A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\text{ is the incidence matrix of }\mathcal F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^P=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\leq\mathbf1\},\quad S^T=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax=\mathbf1\},\quad S^C=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:Ax\geq\mathbf1\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Set Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-inequality formulation of the maximum-weight stable-set problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite simple graph \(G=(V,E)\) with vertex weights \(c_v\), introduce \(x_v\in\{0,1\}\). The maximum-weight stable-set problem has formulation \[\max\left\{\sum_{v\in V}c_vx_v:x_u+x_v\le 1\ \text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\right\}.\] Its binary feasible vectors are exactly the incidence vectors of stable sets of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable set is represented by binary vertex variables and one at-most-one inequality for every graph edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary feasible vectors are exactly incidence vectors of stable sets of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Binary indicator that vertex v is selected.

children.title: Conflict-Graph Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict-Graph Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflict graph induced by a binary packing matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), its conflict graph is the simple graph \(G_A=(V,E)\) with \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \[\{j,k\}\in E\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j\ne k\ \text{ and }\ A_{ij}=A_{ik}=1\ \text{ for some row }i.\] Thus vertices represent selectable columns, and an edge joins precisely two columns that cannot both occur in a binary solution of \(Ax\le\mathbf{1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conflict graph joins two packing columns whenever they share a row and therefore cannot both be selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_A\) records every pairwise incompatibility induced by \(Ax\le\mathbf{1}\).

notation.meaning: Vertices corresponding to columns of A.

children.title: Packing-to-Graph Correspondence

knowledge_statements.title: Packing-to-Graph Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between binary packings and stable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\), and let \(G_A\) be the graph whose vertices are the columns of \(A\), with two distinct columns adjacent exactly when they contain a 1 in a common row. For every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), define \(S(x)=\{j:x_j=1\}\). Then \[Ax\le\mathbf{1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S(x)\text{ is a stable set of }G_A.\] Consequently, weighted set packing with objective \(c^Tx\) is represented as the maximum-weight stable-set problem on \(G_A\) with vertex weights \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary feasible packings correspond exactly to stable sets in the graph joining columns that share an incidence row.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le\mathbf{1}\iff S(x)\) is stable in \(G_A\).

notation.meaning: Conflict graph of the packing matrix.
Set of columns selected by x.

children.title: Set Partitioning Formulations
children.top_down_role: Selection of subsets forming exact assignments or decompositions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j=1\) exactly for the selected subsets, and \(Ax=\mathbf{1}\) makes every element belong to exactly one selected subset.

notation.meaning: Incidence matrix: entry \(A_{rj}\) equals one when subset \(j\) contains element \(r\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite weighted set-partitioning model.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each column \(j\in J\) represent a subset of the ground set \(R\), with incidence coefficient \(A_{rj}\). The weighted set-partitioning formulation is
\[
\min\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=\mathbf{1},\ x\in\{0,1\}^{J}\right\}.
\]
For every \(r\in R\), the equality \(\sum_{j\in J}A_{rj}x_j=1\) requires exactly one selected subset containing \(r\). Replacing the objective by maximization, or omitting it when only feasibility matters, does not alter the defining exact-partition constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select binary-indexed subsets so that every ground element is contained in exactly one selected subset, optionally optimizing total selection cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Set Partitioning Formulations

children.title: Satisfiability Formulations
children.top_down_role: Clause-based binary models and generalized set-covering interpretations.

assumptions_latex: \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is a finite Boolean variable set.
Each clause \(k\in K\) has disjoint positive and negative index sets \(P_k,N_k\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment satisfies every clause if and only if its binary vector satisfies all displayed covering inequalities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CNF satisfiability as a generalized set-covering feasibility system.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Generalized Set Covering: The Satisfiability Problem p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Represent truth by \(x_i=1\) and falsity by \(x_i=0\). A clause \(k\), containing positive literals indexed by \(P_k\) and negated literals indexed by \(N_k\), is satisfied exactly when
\[
\sum_{i\in P_k}x_i+\sum_{i\in N_k}(1-x_i)\ge 1.
\]
Consequently, a conjunctive-normal-form formula is satisfiable if and only if the binary feasibility system consisting of this inequality for every \(k\in K\), together with \(x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\), has a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each CNF clause becomes a covering inequality requiring at least one literal to be true; the formula is satisfiable exactly when the binary system is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Satisfiability Formulations

children.title: Bipartite Assignment Formulations
children.top_down_role: One-to-one and capacitated assignment structures on bipartite systems.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite vertex classes and \(E\subseteq I\times J\).
\(d_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) and \(b_j\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\) are required assignments and capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary feasible points encode bipartite assignments meeting every left-side requirement without exceeding any right-side capacity.

notation.meaning: Indicator that left vertex \(i\) is assigned to right vertex \(j\).
Required number of assignments incident to \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite capacitated assignment, including one-to-one assignment as a special case.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each admissible pair \((i,j)\in E\), let \(x_{ij}\) indicate assignment. The capacitated bipartite assignment system is
\[
\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}=d_i\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}\le b_j\quad(j\in J),\qquad
x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\]
With costs \(c_{ij}\), one optimizes \(\sum_{(i,j)\in E}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). The one-to-one perfect-assignment formulation is obtained when \(d_i=b_j=1\), \(|I|=|J|\), and every right-side inequality is imposed as equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary edge variables assign each left vertex its required number of partners while respecting right-vertex capacities; unit equalities give one-to-one assignment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual assignment algorithm on the zero-reduced-cost graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for maximum-weight assignment on a complete balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain dual-feasible potentials \((u,v)\) with \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-u_i-v_j\le0\). On the equality graph \(\bar E=\{(i,j):\bar c_{ij}=0\}\), compute or continue a maximum-cardinality matching. If it has size \(n\), return it as an optimal assignment. Otherwise, for the terminally labeled sets \(V_1^+,V_2^+\), set \(\delta=\min\{-\bar c_{ij}:i\in V_1^+,\ j\in V_2\setminus V_2^+\}\), update \(u_i\leftarrow u_i-\delta\) for \(i\in V_1^+\) and \(v_j\leftarrow v_j+\delta\) for \(j\in V_2^+\), and resume matching augmentation on the updated equality graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal-dual assignment algorithm alternates between augmenting a matching in the graph of tight edges and changing dual potentials when no perfect tight-edge matching is available. A perfect matching in the tight-edge graph is returned as an optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: G=(V_1,V_2,E)\text{ is complete bipartite with }V_1=\{1,\ldots,n\}\text{ and }V_2=\{1',\ldots,n'\}.
\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-u_i-v_j\le0\quad\forall i,j\text{ initially and after each dual update}.
M\text{ and }V_1^+,V_2^+\text{ are obtained from the maximum-cardinality matching procedure on the equality graph}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |M^*|=n\implies M^*\text{ is an optimal maximum-weight assignment};\quad |M^*|<n\implies\text{the stated dual update is performed before resuming augmentation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Assignment cost invariance under row-column potential shifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective transformation for balanced one-to-one assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) and \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\), define \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-u_i-v_j\). Every assignment \(x\) satisfies \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}-\sum_{i,j}\bar c_{ij}x_{ij}=\sum_i u_i+\sum_j v_j\). Consequently, an assignment is optimal for \(c\) if and only if it is optimal for \(\bar c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting arbitrary row and column potentials from an assignment cost matrix changes the value of every feasible assignment by the same constant, namely the sum of all potentials. Therefore the set of optimal assignments is unchanged.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is an assignment satisfying }\sum_jx_{ij}=1\ \forall i\text{ and }\sum_ix_{ij}=1\ \forall j.
u_i,v_j\in\mathbb R\text{ are arbitrary and }\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-u_i-v_j.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}=\sum_{i,j}\bar c_{ij}x_{ij}+\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j,\qquad \operatorname*{argmax}_{x}c^Tx=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x}\bar c^Tx.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-programming formulations of bipartite matching and assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight bipartite matching, its balanced perfect-assignment specialization, and the assignment LP dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(V_1,V_2,E)\) with edge weights \(c_e\), maximum-weight matching can be solved as \(\max\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}x_e\le 1\ (i\in V_1\cup V_2),\ x_e\ge0\}\), whose total-unimodular constraint structure yields an integral optimum. When \(|V_1|=|V_2|=n\) and a matching of cardinality \(n\) is required, the assignment formulation is \(\max\sum_{i,j=1}^n c_{ij}x_{ij}\) subject to \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\), \(\sum_ix_{ij}=1\), and \(x_{ij}\ge0\). Its dual is \(\min\{\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j:u_i+v_j\ge c_{ij}\ \forall i,j,\ u_i,v_j\in\mathbb R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree-constrained bipartite-matching LP has an integral optimum because of total unimodularity. Requiring a perfect matching between two sets of size n gives the assignment LP, whose dual uses unrestricted row and column potentials whose sums dominate the edge weights.
assumptions_latex: G=(V_1,V_2,E)\text{ is bipartite and }c_e\in\mathbb R\text{ for every }e\in E.
\text{For the assignment specialization, }|V_1|=|V_2|=n\text{ and a matching of cardinality }n\text{ is required.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\ge0}\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e:\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}x_e\le1\ \forall i\right\}\text{ has an integral optimum, and the assignment specialization has dual }\min\left\{\sum_i u_i+\sum_jv_j:u_i+v_j\ge c_{ij}\ \forall i,j\right\}.

children.title: Generalized Assignment Formulations
children.top_down_role: Assignments coupled to capacities or heterogeneous resource consumption.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite machine set and \(J\) a finite job set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each feasible binary vector assigns every job to one machine and respects the machine-dependent resource capacities.

notation.meaning: Indicator that job \(j\) is assigned to machine \(i\).
Resource consumed by job \(j\) on machine \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard minimization form of the generalized assignment problem.

source_refs.locator: 2.8 The Generalized Assignment Problem p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The generalized assignment problem has the binary formulation
\[
\min\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\quad(j\in J),\qquad
\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}x_{ij}\le b_i\quad(i\in I),
\qquad x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The assignment equalities select exactly one machine for each job. The capacity inequalities couple assignments through heterogeneous consumptions, since both the cost \(c_{ij}\) and consumption \(a_{ij}\) may depend on the chosen machine-job pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every job to exactly one machine while machine-specific job consumptions remain within capacities, minimizing total assignment cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Assignment Formulations

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized assignment 0–1 formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary generalized assignment model with exact assignment constraints and assignment-specific resource consumption under capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given coefficients \(c_{ij}\), resource consumptions \(t_{ij}\), and capacities \(T_j\), the generalized assignment problem is
\[
\max_{x\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}}\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}=1\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{ij}x_{ij}\le T_j\quad(j=1,\ldots,n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized assignment problem maximizes total assignment value using binary variables. Each item is assigned to exactly one agent, and the resource consumption of the items assigned to each agent cannot exceed its capacity.
assumptions_latex: c_{ij},\ t_{ij},\ T_j\ \text{are given for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ j=1,\ldots,n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j=1}^{n}x_{ij}=1\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^{m}t_{ij}x_{ij}\le T_j\ \forall j,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\right\}

children.title: Graph Matching Formulations
children.top_down_role: Edge-selection models for pairings in bipartite and general graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Binary vectors satisfying the degree inequalities are exactly incidence vectors of matchings in \(G\).

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident to vertex \(v\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical binary incidence formulation of graph matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer formulation valid for matchings in bipartite and general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Associate a binary variable \(x_e\) with each edge \(e\in E\). The matching formulation is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e:
\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\ \text{for every }v\in V,
\ x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\right\}.
\]
The degree inequalities prevent two selected edges from sharing a vertex. Replacing every degree inequality by equality gives a perfect-matching formulation. The same integer system applies to bipartite and nonbipartite graphs, although their linear relaxations differ and additional inequalities are needed to describe the general-graph matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select weighted edges so that no two share a vertex; degree equalities instead require a perfect matching.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perfect matching polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the perfect matching polytope and records the nonnegativity and degree equations necessarily satisfied by its points; bipartite sufficiency is separated into the following corollary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the perfect matching polytope is \(P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M\in\{0,1\}^E:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }G\}\subseteq\mathbb R^E\). Every \(x\in P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)\) satisfies \(x_e\ge0\) for all \(e\in E\) and \(x(\delta(v))=1\) for every \(v\in V\), where \(x(F)=\sum_{e\in F}x_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perfect matching polytope is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of perfect matchings. Every point in it is nonnegative and assigns total incident-edge weight one to each vertex.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }G\},\qquad P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x\ge0,\ x(\delta(v))=1\ \forall v\in V\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality of a shortest Hungarian augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One cardinality-increasing iteration of the Hungarian method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(U\cup W,E) be weighted bipartite with |U|=|W|=n, and let M be minimum-weight among all matchings of cardinality k<n. Let S and T be the uncovered vertices in U and W. If D_M has no directed S-to-T path, then G has no perfect matching. Otherwise, let P be a shortest such path under the signed lengths \ell_e=w_e on unmatched arcs and \ell_e=-w_e on matched reverse arcs, and set N=M\triangle P. Then |N|=k+1, w(N)=w(M)+\ell(P), and N has minimum weight among all cardinality-(k+1) matchings. Because D_M has no negative-length circuit, P can be computed in polynomial time by Bellman--Ford.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a minimum-weight matching of size k, failure to find a directed path between uncovered sides certifies that no perfect matching exists. Otherwise, symmetric difference with a shortest signed alternating path produces a minimum-weight matching of size k+1, with its weight increased by the path length. The path is computable in polynomial time because the auxiliary digraph has no negative cycle.
assumptions_latex: G=(U\cup W,E)\text{ is a weighted bipartite graph}
M\text{ is minimum-weight among cardinality-}k\text{ matchings}
S\subseteq U,\ T\subseteq W\text{ are the vertices uncovered by }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\nexists\,S\text{-to-}T\text{ path in }D_M\bigr)\Rightarrow G\text{ has no perfect matching};\quad P\text{ shortest}\Rightarrow N=M\triangle P,\ |N|=k+1,\ w(N)=w(M)+\ell(P),\ N\text{ is minimum-weight at cardinality }k+1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Augmentation along an augmenting path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of alternating and augmenting paths and the cardinality effect of symmetric-difference augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in \(G=(V,E)\). A path \(P\) is \(M\)-alternating when its edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\); it is \(M\)-augmenting when, additionally, both end vertices are uncovered by \(M\). For every \(M\)-augmenting path, \(|P\setminus M|=|P\cap M|+1\), and \(N=M\triangle P=(M\setminus P)\cup(P\setminus M)\) is a matching satisfying \(|N|=|M|+1\). Consequently, the existence of an \(M\)-augmenting path implies that \(M\) is not maximum-cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating path switches between unmatched and matched edges. If both endpoints are unmatched, symmetric difference with the path produces a valid matching containing one more edge, so the original matching is not maximum-cardinality.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching in }G=(V,E)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N=M\triangle P\text{ is a matching},\qquad |N|=|M|+1,\qquad M\text{ is not maximum-cardinality}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds description of the matching polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact edge-variable formulation for matchings that need not be perfect in an arbitrary undirected graph.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching variants and the weighted 0–1 b-matching formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines matching, b-matching, perfect matching, edge-covering variants, and the weighted binary incidence formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) satisfying \(\deg_M(i)\le 1\) for every \(i\in V\). Given positive integers \(b_i\), a \(b\)-matching satisfies \(\deg_M(i)\le b_i\); it is perfect when every such inequality holds with equality. In a 0–1 \(b\)-matching each edge is selected at most once, whereas an integer \(b\)-matching permits nonnegative integer edge multiplicities. Requirements \(\deg_M(i)\ge b_i\) instead define node covering by edges. With edge weights \(c_e\), the weighted 0–1 \(b\)-matching problem is \(\max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{|E|}\}\), where \(A\) is the node–edge incidence matrix and \(x_e=1\) means that edge \(e\) is selected. Unit weights give the cardinality problem; for perfect matchings, a minimum-weight objective can also be considered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching selects edges so that each vertex meets at most one selected edge. A b-matching allows at most b_i selected incident edges at vertex i, and it is perfect when all those bounds hold with equality. Edge use may be binary or have nonnegative integer multiplicity. Lower degree requirements instead define node covering by edges. The weighted binary b-matching model maximizes total edge weight subject to node–edge incidence constraints and binary edge variables. Unit weights give a cardinality problem, while perfect matchings may also be minimized by weight.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ is the node--edge incidence matrix of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{c^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{|E|}\}\text{ formulates the weighted 0--1 }b\text{-matching problem.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the matching-assignment representation supported by the extract, not the figure-dependent branching rules of the larger TSP branch-and-bound procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $V=\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and construct the bipartite graph $G_B=(V^L\cup V^R,E^*)$ with $V^L=V$, $V^R=\{m+1,\ldots,2m\}$, and, for each edge $e=(i,j)\in E$, edges $e^L=(i,m+j)$ and $e^R=(j,m+i)$ satisfying $c_{e^L}=c_{e^R}=c_e$. If $y^0$ is the characteristic vector of an optimal perfect matching in $G_B$, then $x_e^0=y_{e^L}^0+y_{e^R}^0$ is an optimal integer $2$-matching in $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate each original edge in opposite directions across two copies of the vertex set. An optimal perfect matching in the resulting bipartite graph maps to an optimal integer 2-matching by summing the two copied-edge indicators.
assumptions_latex: y^0\text{ is the characteristic vector of an optimal perfect matching in }G_B
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_e^0=y_{e^L}^0+y_{e^R}^0\quad\forall e\in E,\qquad x^0\text{ is an optimal integer }2\text{-matching in }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of the degree relaxation for perfect matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insufficiency of nonnegativity and vertex-degree equations for perfect matchings in general non-bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }G\} and R(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x_e\ge 0\ (e\in E),\ x(\delta(v))=1\ (v\in V)\}. Every perfect-matching incidence vector belongs to R(G), so P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)\subseteq R(G). For general non-bipartite graphs this inclusion need not be equality; there exist graphs with P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\varnothing but R(G)\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity and one incident selected edge at each vertex form a valid relaxation of the perfect matching polytope, but they are insufficient for general non-bipartite graphs and can be feasible even when no perfect matching exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)\subseteq R(G),\quad\text{and equality can fail; in particular, }P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\varnothing\text{ while }R(G)\ne\varnothing\text{ is possible}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of Integer b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-capacity and odd-set description of the integer b-matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blossom relative to a matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blossom identified from two alternating-tree paths of opposite parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching. Suppose an alternating-tree search yields two alternating paths to a vertex, one of even length and one of odd length. Tracing the paths toward the root to their intersection identifies a set \(U\subseteq V\) of odd cardinality and an even vertex \(b(U)\), called its base, such that \(|M\cap E(U)|=\lfloor |U|/2\rfloor\). The subgraph \((U,E(U))\) is called a blossom relative to \(M\). Every \(u\in U\setminus\{b(U)\}\) is incident to an edge of \(M\cap E(U)\), and \(b(U)\) is either the tree root or is adjacent to a matching edge in the tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two alternating-tree paths of opposite parity identify an odd vertex set U whose induced subgraph is a blossom. Its odd-set bound is tight, every nonbase vertex is matched internally, and its even base is either the root or is adjacent to a tree matching edge.
assumptions_latex: \text{An alternating-tree search yields two alternating paths of opposite parity to a vertex}
U\subseteq V\text{ and }b(U)\text{ are obtained by tracing the paths to their intersection}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |U|\text{ is odd},\quad |M\cap E(U)|=\left\lfloor\frac{|U|}{2}\right\rfloor,\quad (U,E(U))\text{ is a blossom with base }b(U)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary-digraph and maximum-flow reductions for bipartite matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-cardinality matching in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(U\cup W,E) be bipartite and M a matching. Form D_M by orienting each e\in E\setminus M from U to W and each e\in M from W to U. If S\subseteq U and T\subseteq W are the vertices uncovered by M, then an M-augmenting path in G is equivalent to a directed S-to-T path in D_M, and may therefore be found by breadth-first or depth-first search. Alternatively, add vertices s,t, arcs su, uw, wt, capacities c_{su}=c_{wt}=1 and c_{uw}=\infty. Integral s-t flows correspond to bipartite matchings, with flow value equal to matching cardinality, so maximum matching reduces to maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Orient unmatched edges from the left side to the right side and matched edges in reverse. Augmenting paths are exactly directed paths from an uncovered left vertex to an uncovered right vertex, so graph search finds them. A second construction reduces maximum bipartite matching to maximum flow using unit capacities next to the source and sink and infinite capacities on original edges; integral flow value equals matching size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is an }M\text{-augmenting path}\iff P\text{ is a directed }S\text{-to-}T\text{ path in }D_M;\qquad \max |M|=\max\operatorname{val}(x)\text{ in the stated flow network}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Hull of Binary Perfect 2-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Description by degree equations, binary-edge bounds, and inequalities indexed by odd node-disjoint edge sets in cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(G=(V,E)\), the convex hull of binary perfect \(2\)-matchings is the set of \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{E}\) satisfying
\[
x(\delta(v))=2\quad\forall v\in V,\qquad x_e\le1\quad\forall e\in E,
\]
and, for every \(H\subsetneq V\) and every odd-cardinality node-disjoint edge set \(\widehat E\subseteq\delta(H)\),
\[
\sum_{e\in\widehat E}(1-x_e)+x(\delta(H)\setminus\widehat E)\ge1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary perfect 2-matching polytope is described by degree-two equations, bounds from zero to one, and the stated cut inequality for each odd node-disjoint edge subset of a proper cut.
assumptions_latex: \widehat E\subseteq\delta(H)\text{ is an odd-cardinality set of node-disjoint edges}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{bin}}^{\mathrm{perf}}(G))=\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(v))=2\ \forall v,\ \sum_{e\in\widehat E}(1-x_e)+x(\delta(H)\setminus\widehat E)\ge1\ \forall(H,\widehat E)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Procedure for shrinking a blossom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction of a blossom during alternating-tree search, including matching and label updates and nested contractions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a blossom \((U,E(U))\) relative to a matching \(M\), with base \(b(U)\), construct a reduced graph \(\widetilde G\) by replacing \(U\) with a pseudonode \(B(U)\). Join each vertex outside \(U\) that was adjacent to a vertex of \(U\) to \(B(U)\). The resulting incident edges are nonmatching, except that a matching edge adjacent to \(b(U)\), if present, remains matching; the remainder of the graph and matching is unchanged, producing \(\widetilde M\). Give \(B(U)\) the label of \(b(U)\), redirect to \(B(U)\) the predecessor labels of vertices outside \(U\) that were labeled from vertices in \(U\), record \((B(U),b(U),U)\), and continue the labeling process on \(\widetilde G\). Subsequent contractions may contain existing pseudonodes, which are treated as ordinary vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a blossom by a pseudonode, preserve its external adjacency and any matching edge at its base, transfer and redirect the search labels, record the contracted blossom, and continue the labeling search. Nested blossom contractions are permitted.
assumptions_latex: b(U)\text{ is the base of the blossom}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The construction yields a reduced graph }\widetilde G\text{ with matching }\widetilde M\text{ on which labeling and nested contraction can continue}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating-tree cardinality matching algorithm for bipartite graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Labeling algorithm that searches successively for augmenting paths from exposed roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(V,E)\), initialize an arbitrary matching \(M\), with all vertices unlabeled and unscanned. If an exposed unlabeled vertex exists, choose one as a root \(r\), label it even, and grow an alternating tree. From an even vertex, label every unlabeled neighbor odd; from a nonexposed odd vertex, label its matching mate even. If an odd exposed vertex is reached, use predecessor labels to recover the augmenting path from \(r\), augment \(M\), remove all labels, and restart. If no exposed unlabeled vertex remains, return \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any matching in a bipartite graph, grow labeled alternating trees from exposed roots. Augment whenever an exposed odd vertex is reached, and return the matching once every exposed vertex has already been processed by the search.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is initialized as an arbitrary matching in }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure returns the current matching when no exposed unlabeled vertex remains}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree, blossom, and odd-cut constraints for matching polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity, exactness boundary, and equivalent odd-set representations for matching and perfect-matching polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E), let P_M(G) be its matching polytope, and write E[U]=\{uv\in E:u,v\in U\}. Every x\in P_M(G) satisfies x\geq0 and x(\delta(v))\leq1 for all v\in V. If G is bipartite, these constraints describe P_M(G) exactly. They are insufficient for general graphs: for a triangle, (1/2,1/2,1/2) is a vertex of the degree relaxation but is not in the matching polytope. For every odd U\subseteq V, every x\in P_M(G) satisfies x(E[U])\leq(|U|-1)/2. The perfect-matching polytope is obtained by imposing x(\delta(v))=1 for all v; on this face, the blossom inequality for odd U is equivalent to x(\delta(U))\geq1. If U or V\setminus U is a singleton, this odd-cut inequality is implied by a degree equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegativity and degree constraints exactly describe the matching polytope of a bipartite graph, but not that of a general graph; the half-valued triangle point demonstrates the failure. Every matching also satisfies a blossom inequality for each odd vertex set. On the perfect-matching face, blossom inequalities are equivalent to odd-cut inequalities, and odd cuts with a singleton shore are redundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ bipartite}\Rightarrow P_M(G)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E:x(\delta(v))\leq1\ \forall v\};\quad x(E[U])\leq\frac{|U|-1}{2}\ \forall x\in P_M(G),\ |U|\text{ odd};\quad x(\delta(v))=1\ \forall v\Rightarrow\left[x(E[U])\leq\frac{|U|-1}{2}\iff x(\delta(U))\geq1\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Labeling Algorithm for Bipartite Maximum-Cardinality Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternating-path search from exposed vertices in one bipartition, with augmentation or termination when the labeling search is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a bipartite graph \(G=(V_1,V_2,E)\) and a matching \(M\), label every exposed vertex of \(V_1\) by \(*\). Repeatedly scan labeled unscanned vertices: from \(i\in V_1\), label every unlabeled \(j\in V_2\) such that \((i,j)\in E\setminus M\); from \(i\in V_2\), if \(i\) is exposed, recover the alternating path \(P\) by backtracking the labels and set \(M\leftarrow(M\cup P)\setminus(M\cap P)\), erase all labels, and restart; if \(i\) is matched, label its matched neighbor in \(V_1\). If no labeled unscanned vertex remains, terminate and denote the labeled and unlabeled sets by \(V_1^+,V_2^+\) and \(V_1^-,V_2^-\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label the exposed vertices on the first side and search along alternating unmatched and matched edges. Reaching an exposed vertex on the second side yields an augmenting path; update the matching by symmetric difference, clear the labels, and restart. If the search is exhausted, terminate with each bipartition divided into labeled and unlabeled vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either augments }M\text{ along a discovered alternating path or terminates with the partition }(V_1^+,V_1^-,V_2^+,V_2^-).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Description of the Bipartite PMS Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Original-space description by bounds, bipartition balance, and Hall-type neighborhood inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be bipartite with $V=V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2$. For $S\subseteq V_1$, let $N_G(S)=\{j\in V_2:(i,j)\in E\text{ for some }i\in S\}$, and write $x(U)=\sum_{i\in U}x_i$. Then
\[
P_{\mathrm{PMS}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{V}:0\leq x_i\leq1\ (i\in V),\ x(V_1)-x(V_2)=0,\ x(S)-x(N_G(S))\leq0\ (S\subseteq V_1)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perfectly matchable subgraph polytope of a bipartite graph is exactly the set of vertex vectors satisfying unit bounds, equal selected totals on the two sides, and every Hall-type neighborhood inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{PMS}}(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^V:x(V_1)=x(V_2),\ \forall S\subseteq V_1,\ x(S)\leq x(N_G(S))\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hungarian-method iteration and signed auxiliary lengths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-weight perfect matching in a balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(U\cup W,E) be a weighted bipartite graph with |U|=|W|=n. The Hungarian method performs at most n iterations. At iteration k, 0\le k\le n-1, it maintains a matching M of cardinality k having minimum weight among all cardinality-k matchings and reduces construction of an optimal cardinality-(k+1) matching to a shortest-path problem in D_M. Each unmatched-edge arc directed from U to W has length \ell_e=w_e, and each matched-edge arc directed from W to U has length \ell_e=-w_e.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a balanced weighted bipartite graph, the Hungarian method uses at most n iterations. Its kth iteration starts with a minimum-weight matching of size k and reduces finding a minimum-weight matching of size k+1 to a shortest-path problem in the alternating auxiliary digraph, assigning weight w to unmatched forward arcs and minus w to matched reverse arcs.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is minimum-weight among matchings of cardinality }k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating and Augmenting Paths Relative to a Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The source uses an alternating-path convention that begins at an exposed vertex with an unmatched edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $M\subseteq E$ be a matching and let $P=v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_p,v_p$ be a path. The path $P$ is alternating relative to $M$ if $e_i\in E\setminus M$ for every odd $i$, $e_i\in M$ for every even $i$, and $v_0$ is exposed by $M$. It is augmenting if, in addition, $p$ is odd and $v_p$ is exposed by $M$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the source's convention, an alternating path starts at an exposed vertex and alternates between unmatched and matched edges, beginning with an unmatched edge. It is augmenting when it has odd length and ends at another exposed vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is alternating}\iff\left[(\forall i\leq p)(i\text{ odd}\Rightarrow e_i\in E\setminus M)\land(\forall i\leq p)(i\text{ even}\Rightarrow e_i\in M)\land v_0\text{ is exposed}\right];\quad P\text{ is augmenting}\iff\left[P\text{ is alternating}\land p\text{ is odd}\land v_p\text{ is exposed}\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching definitions and node-edge incidence formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of matching and perfect matching, together with the binary formulation of maximum-cardinality and perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, with every edge joining two distinct vertices. A matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) of pairwise disjoint edges, and it is perfect if every vertex belongs to exactly one edge of \(M\). Let \(A_G\in\{0,1\}^{V\times E}\) be the node-edge incidence matrix, where \((A_G)_{ve}=1\) exactly when \(v\in e\). Then maximum-cardinality matching is formulated as \(\max\{\sum_{e\in E}x_e:A_Gx\leq\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^E\}\), and \(G\) has a perfect matching if and only if \(A_Gx=\mathbf 1\) has a solution \(x\in\{0,1\}^E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching consists of pairwise disjoint edges and is perfect when every vertex is covered exactly once. Binary edge variables with degree-at-most-one constraints formulate maximum-cardinality matching, while degree equalities characterize perfect-matching feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}x_e:A_Gx\leq\mathbf 1,\ x\in\{0,1\}^E\right\},\qquad G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff\exists x\in\{0,1\}^E:\ A_Gx=\mathbf 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching Polytope Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear description of the matching polytope of a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\),
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:x\geq0,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\ \forall v\in V,\ \sum_{e\in E[U]}x_e\leq\frac{|U|-1}{2}\ \forall U\subseteq V\text{ with }|U|\text{ odd}\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every finite undirected graph, the convex hull of its matching incidence vectors is exactly the set of nonnegative edge vectors satisfying all degree constraints and all odd-set blossom inequalities.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\}=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:x\geq0,\ x(\delta(v))\leq1\ \forall v\in V,\ x(E[U])\leq\frac{|U|-1}{2}\ \forall U\subseteq V\text{ with }|U|\text{ odd}\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating paths, exposed vertices, and augmenting paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a matching, together with the cardinality effect of augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a matching \(M\), a path is alternating relative to \(M\) if its edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\). A vertex is exposed relative to \(M\) if it is incident to no edge of \(M\). An alternating path whose two endpoints are exposed is augmenting relative to \(M\). If \(P\) is such a path, replacing the matching edges of \(P\) by its nonmatching edges yields \(M'=M\triangle E(P)\), which is a matching with \(|M'|=|M|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating path alternates between matching and nonmatching edges. An exposed vertex meets no matching edge, and an augmenting path is alternating with both endpoints exposed. Reversing edge membership along an augmenting path increases the matching cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ augmenting relative to }M\implies M'=M\triangle E(P)\text{ is a matching and }|M'|=|M|+1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hall Characterization of Perfectly Matchable Induced Subgraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient conditions for an induced bipartite subgraph to have a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}V_2,E)$ be bipartite and let $W\subseteq V_1\cup V_2$. For $S\subseteq W\cap V_1$, define $N_{G[W]}(S)=\{j\in W\cap V_2:(i,j)\in E\text{ for some }i\in S\}$. Then $G[W]$ has a perfect matching if and only if $|W\cap V_1|=|W\cap V_2|$ and $|S|\leq |N_{G[W]}(S)|$ for every $S\subseteq W\cap V_1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An induced bipartite subgraph has a perfect matching exactly when its two vertex classes have equal size and every subset of the first class has at least as many neighbors within the induced subgraph.
assumptions_latex: N_{G[W]}(S)=\{j\in W\cap V_2:\exists i\in S,\ (i,j)\in E\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G[W]\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff\left(|W\cap V_1|=|W\cap V_2|\ \land\ \forall S\subseteq W\cap V_1,\ |S|\leq |N_{G[W]}(S)|\right).

children.title: Quadratic Assignment Formulations
children.top_down_role: Assignment structures with pairwise interaction costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Assignment Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Koopmans-Beckmann quadratic assignment formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic assignment problem is
\[
\min\left\{
\sum_{i,k\in I}\sum_{j,\ell\in J}f_{ik}d_{j\ell}x_{ij}x_{k\ell}
+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }i\in I,
\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ \text{for every }j\in J,
\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \text{for every }(i,j)\in I\times J
\right\}.
\]
The two assignment systems enforce a bijection, while each product \(x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\) activates the pairwise cost for facilities \(i,k\) placed at locations \(j,\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bijective facility-location assignment minimizes linear placement costs plus pairwise flow-distance costs activated by pairs of assignment variables.
assumptions_latex: \(f_{ik},d_{j\ell},c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) are given interaction, distance, and linear costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary feasible points are bijections of facilities to locations, and the quadratic objective charges every assigned facility pair for its induced interaction.

notation.meaning: Indicator that facility \(i\) is assigned to location \(j\).
Interaction or flow from facility \(i\) to facility \(k\).
Distance or pair cost from location \(j\) to location \(\ell\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic assignment as a binary quadratic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-to-one facility-to-location assignment with pairwise flow-distance interaction costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(n\) facilities and \(n\) locations, flows \(f_{k\ell}\), distances \(d_{ij}\), and binary assignment variables \(x_{ki}\), the quadratic assignment problem is represented by \[\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}}\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{n}d_{ij}f_{k\ell}x_{ki}x_{\ell j}\] subject to \[\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{ki}=1\quad(k=1,\ldots,n),\qquad \sum_{k=1}^{n}x_{ki}=1\quad(i=1,\ldots,n).\] Hence it is a \(0\)-\(1\) quadratic, and therefore polynomial, program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each facility is assigned to exactly one location and each location receives exactly one facility. The objective minimizes total flow-weighted distance and is quadratic in the binary assignment variables.
assumptions_latex: x_{ki}\in\{0,1\}\text{ indicates that facility }k\text{ is assigned to location }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{QAP}=\min\left\{\sum_{i,j,k,\ell=1}^{n}d_{ij}f_{k\ell}x_{ki}x_{\ell j}:\sum_i x_{ki}=1\ \forall k,\ \sum_k x_{ki}=1\ \forall i,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}\right\}.

children.title: Binary Knapsack Formulations
children.top_down_role: Single-resource selection models with binary item decisions.

assumptions_latex: \(a_i\ge0\), \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(b\ge0\) are given for finitely many items.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible binary vector selects each item at most once and has aggregate resource use at most \(b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical zero-one single-resource knapsack model.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite item set \(N\), the binary knapsack formulation is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i:
\sum_{i\in N}a_ix_i\le b,
\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\text{ for every }i\in N\right\}.
\]
The variable domain permits either zero or one copy of each item. The single inequality aggregates all selected-item consumption against one capacity. A minimization variant may reverse the modeling interpretation, but binary multiplicity and the single resource constraint define this formulation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose at most one copy of each item to maximize profit while total consumption remains within one resource capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Knapsack Formulations

children.title: Bounded-Integer Knapsack Formulations
children.top_down_role: Single-resource models with bounded integer item multiplicities.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible vector chooses an integer number of copies between zero and its item-specific upper bound while satisfying the single capacity.

notation.meaning: Number of copies selected of item type \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-resource knapsack with finite integral item multiplicities.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite item-type set \(N\), the bounded-integer knapsack formulation is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i:
\sum_{i\in N}a_ix_i\le b,
\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z},\ 0\le x_i\le u_i\text{ for every }i\in N\right\}.
\]
Each \(x_i\) counts copies of type \(i\), and the finite integral bound \(u_i\) limits its multiplicity. Setting every \(u_i=1\) recovers the binary knapsack formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose bounded integer quantities of item types to maximize profit without exceeding one shared resource capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Knapsack Formulations

children.title: Unbounded-Integer Knapsack Formulations
children.top_down_role: Single-resource models permitting unrestricted nonnegative item multiplicities.

assumptions_latex: \(a_i\ge0\), \(p_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(b\ge0\) are given for finitely many item types.
Any type with \(a_i=0\) and \(p_i>0\) is excluded to ensure a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible vectors select arbitrary nonnegative integer multiplicities subject only to the aggregate capacity.

notation.meaning: Number of copies selected of item type \(i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded multiplicities under one resource constraint.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite item-type set \(N\), the unbounded-integer knapsack formulation is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i:
\sum_{i\in N}a_ix_i\le b,
\ x_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\text{ for every }i\in N\right\}.
\]
No item-specific upper bound is imposed, so \(x_i\) may represent any nonnegative integer multiplicity consistent with capacity. When all \(a_i>0\), capacity implicitly bounds every feasible \(x_i\); zero-consumption positive-profit types would instead make the maximization problem unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose unrestricted nonnegative integer quantities of item types under one capacity; positive-profit zero-consumption types must be excluded for boundedness.

assumptions_latex: \(N=B\mathbin{\dot\cup}D\mathbin{\dot\cup}U\) is a finite partition of item types.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mixed-multiplicity knapsack formulation is
\[
\max\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{i\in N}a_ix_i\le b,
\]
with domains
\[
x_i\in\{0,1\}\ (i\in B),\qquad
x_i\in\mathbb{Z},\ 0\le x_i\le u_i\ (i\in D),\qquad
x_i\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}\ (i\in U).
\]

children.title: Multidimensional Knapsack Formulations
children.top_down_role: Selection models with several coupled resource budgets.

assumptions_latex: \(N\) is a finite item set and \(R\) a finite resource set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible binary selection respects every resource budget simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary multidimensional knapsack with finitely many resource budgets.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The binary multidimensional knapsack formulation is
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i:
\sum_{i\in N}a_{ri}x_i\le b_r\text{ for every }r\in R,
\ x\in\{0,1\}^{N}\right\}.
\]
Each selected item contributes simultaneously to several resource consumptions. Feasibility requires the selected set to satisfy every budget inequality, so the formulation reduces to the ordinary binary knapsack model when \(|R|=1\).

assumptions_latex: \(N\) is partitioned into nonempty finite groups \((N_g)_{g\in G}\).

\[
\max\sum_{i\in N}p_ix_i

\sum_{i\in N}a_ix_i\le b,
\qquad
\sum_{i\in N_g}x_i=1\quad(g\in G),
\qquad
x\in\{0,1\}^{N}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), the canonical mixing set is
\[
M(b)=\{(y,z)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n}:y+z_i\ge b_i\text{ for all }i=1,\ldots,n\}.

children.top_down_role: Activation-cost models independent of a particular application structure.

assumptions_latex: The activity level satisfies \(0\le x\le U\) for a finite constant \(U>0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le x\le Uy\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), with objective contribution \(f y+c x\).

source_refs.locator: 2.10 Modeling Fixed Charges p. 66

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a bounded activity \(x\in[0,U]\), introduce \(y\in\{0,1\}\) and impose
\[
0\le x\le Uy.
\]
If the activity has variable unit cost \(c\) and fixed activation cost \(f\), its objective contribution is \(c x+f y\). When \(y=0\), the linking inequality forces \(x=0\); when \(y=1\), every level in \([0,U]\) is permitted. Consequently, the formulation represents the disjunction \((y,x)=(0,0)\) or \(y=1\) and \(0\le x\le U\).

children.title: Facility Location Formulations
children.top_down_role: Facility-opening decisions coupled to assignment, flow, or service decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Facility Location Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated facility-location formulation; binary assignment is obtained by declaring \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be a finite customer set and \(J\) a finite set of candidate facilities. Given demands \(d_i\ge0\), capacities \(u_j\ge0\), opening costs \(f_j\), and assignment costs \(c_{ij}\), a capacitated facility-location formulation is
\[
\min\ \sum_{j\in J}f_jy_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}
\]
subject to
\[
\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\sum_{i\in I}d_i x_{ij}\le u_jy_j\quad(j\in J),
\]
with \(x_{ij}\ge0\) and \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\). The capacity-linking constraint prevents a closed facility from receiving a positive assignment from any customer with \(d_i>0\). If zero-demand customers are present and their assignments must also be linked to opening, impose \(x_{ij}\le y_j\). Declaring \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) gives unsplittable assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facility-opening binaries are linked to customer assignments through capacity constraints, while each customer receives complete service; a separate assignment-opening link may be needed for zero-demand customers.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets, \(d_i\ge0\) for every \(i\in I\), and \(u_j\ge0\) for every \(j\in J\).
The parameters \(f_j\) and \(c_{ij}\) are respectively facility-opening and assignment costs.
Every customer must be assigned completely, fractionally or integrally according to the declared domain of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(\sum_{i\in I}d_i x_{ij}\le u_jy_j\) for every \(j\in J\), \(x_{ij}\ge0\), and \(y_j\in\{0,1\}\).

notation.meaning: Fraction of customer i assigned to facility j

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite termination of the alternating FCM–FUM algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-termination guarantee under exact subproblem solution, cross-feasibility, boundedness, and finiteness assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every iteration $k$, suppose the FCM and FUM are solved globally; the FCM solution $z_C^k$ is feasible for $\mathrm{FUM}^k$, and the FUM solution $z_U^k$ is feasible for $\mathrm{FCM}^{k+1}$. Then $\operatorname{Min}_U^k\leq\operatorname{Min}_C^k$ and $\operatorname{Min}_C^{k+1}\leq\operatorname{Min}_U^k$. Because the algorithm continues only upon strict improvement, its accepted objective values strictly decrease. If both objective sequences are bounded below and the alternating MIP subproblems have discrete finite feasible regions, the algorithm terminates after finitely many iterations, at either $\operatorname{Min}_U^k=\operatorname{Min}_C^k=F^*$ or $\operatorname{Min}_C^{k+1}=\operatorname{Min}_U^k=F^*$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every capacity and utilization MIP is solved globally and each current solution is feasible for the next coupled model, the utilization optimum cannot exceed the same-iteration capacity optimum, and the next capacity optimum cannot exceed the preceding utilization optimum. Accepted objectives therefore decrease strictly. Boundedness below and finite discrete feasible regions imply finite termination at one of the stated equality stopping conditions.
assumptions_latex: \forall k,\ z_C^k\text{ and }z_U^k\text{ are globally optimal for their respective MIP subproblems}
\text{The alternating MIP subproblems have discrete finite feasible regions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Min}_U^k\leq\operatorname{Min}_C^k,\quad \operatorname{Min}_C^{k+1}\leq\operatorname{Min}_U^k,\quad\text{and the strict-improvement algorithm terminates finitely at a stated equality condition.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Alternating FCM–FUM algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm for the reformulated facility capacity and utilization MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $k=1$, $\operatorname{Min}_U^0$ to a sufficiently large value, and each facility in its highest utilization range. At iteration $k$, use the current utilization indicators to compute facility cost multipliers and product-program costs, then solve the facility-capacity MIP (FCM) globally to obtain $\operatorname{Min}_C^k$ and capacity moves $m_{pj}^k$. Stop unless $\operatorname{Min}_C^k<\operatorname{Min}_U^{k-1}$. Otherwise update process-presence, process-capacity, and facility-utilization parameters from $m_{pj}^k$, solve the facility-utilization MIP (FUM) globally to obtain $\operatorname{Min}_U^k$ and utilization indicators $y_{qj}^k$, and stop unless $\operatorname{Min}_U^k<\operatorname{Min}_C^k$; if both strict inequalities hold, continue to the next alternating solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize all facilities in their highest utilization range. Repeatedly compute costs and solve the facility-capacity MIP, stopping if it does not strictly improve on the preceding utilization-model objective. If it improves, update the capacity and utilization inputs and solve the facility-utilization MIP, stopping if that model does not strictly improve on the capacity-model objective. Continue only while the two solves yield alternating strict objective decreases.
assumptions_latex: \text{The reformulated MINLP is represented by the coupled FCM and FUM MIP models.}
\text{Each FCM and FUM subproblem is solved to global optimality.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure generates alternating FCM and FUM solutions and continues exactly while }\operatorname{Min}_C^k<\operatorname{Min}_U^{k-1}\text{ and }\operatorname{Min}_U^k<\operatorname{Min}_C^k\text{.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), the arc-activation fixed-charge model is
\[
\min\ \sum_{a\in A}(c_a x_a+f_a y_a)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP relaxation of the standard fixed-charge network formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eliminates the relaxed activation variables from the standard fixed-charge network-flow formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(u_{ij}>0\) and \(c_{ij}\ge 0\). In the LP relaxation, \(0\le x_{ij}\le 1\) and \(0\le y_{ij}\le u_{ij}x_{ij}\). For fixed \(y\), an optimal activation choice may be taken as \(x_{ij}=y_{ij}/u_{ij}\). Consequently, the relaxation is
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}\left(h_{ij}+\frac{c_{ij}}{u_{ij}}\right)y_{ij}:\ \sum_{j\in\delta^+(i)}y_{ij}-\sum_{j\in\delta^-(i)}y_{ji}=b_i\ (i\in V),\ 0\le y_{ij}\le u_{ij}\ ((i,j)\in\mathcal A)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LP relaxation of the standard fixed-charge network formulation projects to a capacitated minimum-cost flow problem with arc unit cost equal to the variable cost plus the fixed cost divided by capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{\mathrm{LP}}(FN)=\min\left\{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}\left(h_{ij}+\frac{c_{ij}}{u_{ij}}\right)y_{ij}:\ (4.1a),\ 0\le y_{ij}\le u_{ij}\right\}.

children.top_down_role: Selection among indivisible capacity additions or technology levels.

assumptions_latex: For each asset \(j\), module \(k\) adds capacity \(q_{jk}\ge0\) at cost \(f_{jk}\ge0\).
Required usage \(x_j\) is nonnegative and baseline capacity \(u_j^0\) is given.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_j\le u_j^0+\sum_k q_{jk}y_{jk}\), with binary module choices and any prescribed exclusivity constraints.

notation.meaning: Selection indicator for capacity module k at asset j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary modular expansion, including mutually exclusive technology levels as a special case.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each asset \(j\), let \(y_{jk}\in\{0,1\}\) select indivisible capacity module \(k\). The expanded capacity constraint is
\[
x_j\le u_j^0+\sum_{k\in K_j}q_{jk}y_{jk},
\]
with objective contribution \(\sum_{k\in K_j}f_{jk}y_{jk}\). Independent modules require no additional selection constraint. Alternative technology levels require \(\sum_{k\in K_j}y_{jk}\le1\), or equality when exactly one level, including a zero-capacity level, must be selected. Thus feasible capacity belongs to the finite set or modular sum encoded by the binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary module choices add indivisible capacity; optional exclusivity constraints distinguish cumulative modules from alternative technology levels.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-flow formulation, cut definition, and integer-capacity integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of single-commodity flows and cuts together with the incidence-matrix LP formulation and its integer-capacity consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) and distinct \(s,t\in V\), an \(s,t\)-flow is \(x\in\mathbb R_+^A\) satisfying \(\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e=0\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\), with value \(\operatorname{val}(x)=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(s)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(s)}x_e\). Given \(c\in\mathbb R_+^A\), feasibility additionally requires \(x_e\le c_e\) for every \(e\in A\). The maximum-flow problem maximizes this value and has an LP formulation whose equality matrix is the incidence matrix of the digraph obtained by adding an arc \(t\to s\) for the value variable. Hence this matrix is totally unimodular, and if \(c\in\mathbb Z_+^A\), the linear constraint system describes an integral polyhedron. An \(s,t\)-cut is \(\Gamma=\delta^+(S)\), where \(s\in S\subseteq V\setminus\{t\}\), with capacity \(c(\Gamma)=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S)}c_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative s–t flow satisfies conservation away from s and t, and capacity bounds produce the maximum-flow linear program. Adding a t-to-s arc for the flow-value variable makes the equality matrix a directed incidence matrix, so integer capacities yield an integral feasible polyhedron. An s–t cut consists of the arcs leaving a set containing s but not t, and its capacity is the sum of their capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c\in\mathbb Z_+^A\implies P_{\mathrm{flow}}(D,s,t,c)\text{ is an integral polyhedron, so the maximum integral-flow problem is solvable by the stated LP.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-node variable upper-bound flow region and relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the mixed-integer flow region and its standard continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let N=\{1,\ldots,n\}. The single-node variable upper-bound flow region is
\[
T=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb B^n\times\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{j\in N}y_j\le b,\ y_j\le a_jx_j\quad(j\in N)\right\}.
\]
Its continuous formulation polytope is
\[
P=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{j\in N}y_j\le b,\ y_j\le a_jx_j,\ x_j\le1\quad(j\in N)\right\},
\]
so that \(T=P\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each nonnegative arc flow is at most its capacity when its binary opening variable is one and is zero when that variable is zero; total outflow is at most b. Relaxing the opening variables to the unit interval gives P, and restoring their integrality recovers T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=P\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Flow–cut bound and equality certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak flow–cut duality and the saturation conditions certifying simultaneous flow and cut optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\), let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, let \(c\in\mathbb R_+^A\), let \(x\) be a feasible \(s,t\)-flow, and let \(\Gamma=\delta^+(S)\) be an \(s,t\)-cut. Then \(\operatorname{val}(x)\le c(\Gamma)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{val}(x)=c(\Gamma)\) if and only if \(x_e=c_e\) for every \(e\in\delta^+(S)\) and \(x_e=0\) for every \(e\in\delta^-(S)\). Under these equality conditions, \(x\) is a maximum \(s,t\)-flow and \(\Gamma\) is a minimum-capacity \(s,t\)-cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible flow value is at most every cut capacity. Equality holds exactly when all arcs leaving the cut set are saturated and all arcs entering it carry zero flow, certifying that the flow is maximum and the cut is minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{val}(x)\le c(\Gamma),\quad \operatorname{val}(x)=c(\Gamma)\iff \bigl(x_e=c_e\ \forall e\in\delta^+(S)\bigr)\land\bigl(x_e=0\ \forall e\in\delta^-(S)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A node-throughput formulation augments arc flows \(x_a\ge0\) with a variable \(q_v\ge0\) for each transshipment node \(v\). It imposes
\[
q_v=\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a.
\]
A node capacity is expressed locally as \(q_v\le U_v\), and binary node activation as \(q_v\le U_v y_v\) with \(y_v\in\{0,1\}\). Eliminating \(q_v\) recovers the corresponding arc-flow conservation equation and substitutes the appropriate incident-flow sum into every node-throughput constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node-throughput variables equal both incoming and outgoing flow, enabling local node capacities and activation constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each arc \(a\in A\), define the incidence column by \(B_{t(a),a}=1\), \(B_{h(a),a}=-1\), and \(B_{v,a}=0\) at every other node. Thus every constraint row of \(Bx=b\) involves only arcs incident to its node, and every variable column has exactly two nonzero coefficients of opposite sign. Consequently,
\[
\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}B=0,
\]
so \(Bx=b\) requires \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). For a graph with several weakly connected components, the balance must vanish separately on each component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed incidence column touches only its arc's endpoints with opposite signs, making flow conservation local and imposing componentwise balance.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For commodities \(k\in K\), assign nonnegative arc flows \(x_a^k\). The standard shared-capacity formulation is
\[
Bx^k=b^k\quad(k\in K),\qquad \sum_{k\in K}x_a^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A).
\]
The first constraints conserve each commodity independently; the second couple commodities through common arc capacity. Commodity-specific admissibility is represented by fixing \(x_a^k=0\) on forbidden arcs. Unsplittable variants require additional integer structure, because the continuous formulation permits a commodity's flow to divide among several source-to-sink paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each commodity obeys separate flow conservation, while all commodities compete through shared arc-capacity constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Based Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path decomposition of a capacitated multicommodity flow model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each commodity \(k\in K\), let \(P_k\) be its set of admissible directed source-to-sink paths and let \(\lambda_p^k\ge0\) denote the flow of commodity \(k\) assigned to path \(p\in P_k\). The path formulation imposes
\[
\sum_{p\in P_k}\lambda_p^k=d_k\quad(k\in K),\qquad
\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{\substack{p\in P_k\\a\in p}}\lambda_p^k\le u_a\quad(a\in A).
\]
The corresponding arc flow is \(x_a^k=\sum_{p\in P_k:a\in p}\lambda_p^k\). A feasible nonnegative source-to-sink arc flow decomposes into path flows and circulations; after circulations are discarded, the remaining path flows preserve the commodity balances and do not increase arc-capacity usage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity-indexed path variables meet each demand, and shared arc capacities link all commodity paths traversing an arc; circulations may be discarded when converting a feasible arc flow to this path representation.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a finite commodity set, and \(P_k\) is the set of admissible directed source-to-sink paths for each \(k\in K\).
Commodity demands satisfy \(d_k\ge0\), arc capacities satisfy \(u_a\ge0\), and path-flow variables satisfy \(\lambda_p^k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{p\in P_k}\lambda_p^k=d_k\) for every \(k\in K\), and \(\sum_{k\in K}\sum_{p\in P_k:a\in p}\lambda_p^k\le u_a\) for every arc \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be the set of routes that individually satisfy all sequencing, connectivity, and route-resource restrictions. With route cost \(c_r\), incidence \(a_{ir}\), and integer route variable \(z_r\), the set-partitioning formulation is
\[
\min\ \sum_{r\in R}c_rz_r,
\qquad
\sum_{r\in R}a_{ir}z_r=r_i\quad(i\in I),
\qquad z_r\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
\]
For single-use routes one may impose \(z_r\in\{0,1\}\). Replacing equality by \(\ge r_i\) yields a set-covering route formulation; additional fleet constraints can couple route selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each variable selects an internally feasible route, while master constraints enforce service coverage and any fleet-wide restrictions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For blocks \(j\in J\), let \(C_j\) enumerate all feasible local configurations. Introduce \(\lambda_{jc}\) for \(c\in C_j\) and impose the convexity equations
\[
\sum_{c\in C_j}\lambda_{jc}=1\quad(j\in J).
\]
Global requirements are expressed by
\[
\sum_{j\in J}\sum_{c\in C_j}a_{ijc}\lambda_{jc}\mathrel{\bowtie_i}b_i\quad(i\in I),
\]
where each \(\bowtie_i\) is the required relation. Binary \(\lambda_{jc}\) selects exactly one configuration per block; continuous \(\lambda_{jc}\ge0\) gives the associated convexified master representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Columns encode complete feasible block configurations; convexity constraints choose configurations, and linking rows enforce system-wide requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson formulation of the symmetric TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge-incidence formulation using degree and subtour-elimination cut constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be an undirected graph, let $c_e$ be the cost of edge $e$, and let $\delta(S)$ contain the edges with exactly one endpoint in $S$. The symmetric DFJ formulation is
\[\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\]
subject to
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}x_e=2\quad(i\in V),\]
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge2\quad(\varnothing\subsetneq S\subsetneq V),\qquad x_e\in\{0,1\}\quad(e\in E).\]
Its binary feasible points are exactly the incidence vectors of Hamiltonian cycles in $G$. The subtour-elimination family has exponentially many constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric DFJ model selects two incident edges at every vertex and at least two selected edges across every nontrivial cut. Its binary feasible solutions are exactly the Hamiltonian cycles, and its subtour-elimination family is exponential in size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ satisfies the symmetric DFJ constraints}\iff x\text{ is the incidence vector of a Hamiltonian cycle in }G.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical Traveling Salesman Polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract inconsistently types the aggregated vector as binary before stating that its entries are nonnegative integers; the defining sums and listed properties support the integer-multiplicity interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) partition \(V\) into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, and let \(H=(U,F)\) be obtained from \(G\) by shrinking each \(V_i\) to a node \(u_i\). For a tour-incidence vector \(x\), define \(y=\Phi(x)\) by \(y_{ij}=\sum_{v\in V_i}\sum_{w\in V_j}x_{vw}\) for \(ij\in F\). Then \(y_e\in\mathbb Z_+\) for every \(e\in F\), every degree \(\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}y_e\) is even, and the support graph \((U,\{e\in F:y_e>0\})\) is connected. The convex hull of all nonnegative integer vectors with these even-degree and connected-support properties is the graphical traveling salesman polyhedron, denoted \(GTSP^k\) for a graph on \(k\) nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Contracting the parts of a vertex partition maps a tour to nonnegative integer edge multiplicities with even degree at every contracted node and connected positive support. The convex hull of all vectors with these properties is the graphical traveling salesman polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) partitions \(V\) into pairwise disjoint nonempty sets.
\(H=(U,F)\) is obtained by shrinking each \(V_i\) to \(u_i\).
\(x\) is a tour-incidence vector and \(y_{ij}=\sum_{v\in V_i}\sum_{w\in V_j}x_{vw}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in\mathbb Z_+^F,\quad \sum_{e\in\delta(i)}y_e\in2\mathbb Z\ \forall i\in U,\quad (U,\{e\in F:y_e>0\})\text{ is connected},\quad GTSP^k=\operatorname{conv}\{y\in\mathbb Z_+^F:\text{ these properties hold}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clique tree inequalities for the TSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and known separation boundary of the TSP clique-tree inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H_1,\ldots,H_r\subseteq V be pairwise disjoint handles and let T_1,\ldots,T_s\subsetneq V be pairwise disjoint teeth. Assume T_j\nsubseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}H_i for every j, each H_i intersects an odd number of teeth, and the intersection graph of all handles and teeth is a tree. The associated clique tree inequality is \sum_{i=1}^{r}x(\delta(H_i))+\sum_{j=1}^{s}x(\delta(T_j))\ge2r+3s-1. This facet-inducing family generalizes comb, subtour-elimination, and 2-factor inequalities; no polynomial-time test for the family is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairwise disjoint handles and pairwise disjoint proper teeth define a clique tree inequality when no tooth lies inside the union of the handles, every handle meets an odd number of teeth, and their intersection graph is a tree. The inequality sums the handle and tooth cut values and lower-bounds them by 2r+3s−1. The family generalizes comb, subtour-elimination, and 2-factor inequalities, but no polynomial-time test is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^{r}x(\delta(H_i))+\sum_{j=1}^{s}x(\delta(T_j))\ge2r+3s-1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Equivalence Between Tours and Their Downward Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of an original tour minimization and transformed maximizations over tours and tour-contained edge sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=K_m with m\ge 3, let S be the characteristic vectors of its Hamiltonian tours, and let T=\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x\le x'\text{ for some }x'\in S\}. For c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}, x^0\in S, and \omega>\max_{e\in E}|c_e|, define \bar c_e=\omega-c_e. Then x^0\in\arg\min_{x\in S}c^\top x if and only if x^0\in\arg\max_{x\in S}\bar c^\top x, if and only if x^0\in\arg\max_{x\in T}\bar c^\top x.
