knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Feasible Tour Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-greedy construction maintaining acyclicity and degree bounds, with an explicit failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set E^0=\varnothing. For t<n-1, when (V,E^t) is acyclic and every vertex has degree at most 2, add a minimum-weight e\in E\setminus E^t, if one exists, such that (V,E^t\cup\{e\}) remains acyclic and has maximum degree at most 2. At t=n-1, join the two degree-one vertices if the joining edge exists. The procedure may fail to produce a tour even when G has one, and when it succeeds it need not produce a good tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with no selected edges and repeatedly add a cheapest edge that preserves acyclicity and vertex degree at most two. After selecting a spanning path, join its two degree-one endpoints if possible. The heuristic can fail even on an instance having a tour and has no stated quality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{If all greedy additions and the final endpoint edge exist, the output is a tour; otherwise the method may fail despite tour feasibility.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Traveling Salesman Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the symmetric TSP polytope through the Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson edge formulation and names its degree and subtour-elimination constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be the complete graph on \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The symmetric traveling salesman polytope is
\[
P_{\mathrm{tsp}}:=\operatorname{conv}\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta(i)}x_e=2\ \forall i\in V,\quad \sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge 2\ \forall S\subset V,\ 2\le |S|\le n-2\right\}.
\]
The equalities are degree constraints, and the inequalities are subtour-elimination constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete undirected graph, the symmetric traveling salesman polytope is the convex hull of binary edge vectors satisfying all degree and subtour-elimination constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{tsp}}=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x(\delta(i))=2\ \forall i\in V,\ x(\delta(S))\ge2\ \forall S\subset V,\ 2\le|S|\le n-2\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-Neighbor Tour Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy path construction for the symmetric traveling salesman problem, including failure and quality boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an arbitrary i_1\in V. Given distinct i_1,\ldots,i_j, choose i_{j+1}\in\arg\min\{c_{i_jk}:k\in V\setminus\{i_1,\ldots,i_j\}\}, breaking ties arbitrarily, and continue until all vertices have been selected; then add (i_n,i_1). If G is not complete, a required edge may be absent and the procedure may fail even when G has a tour. Even when G is complete, no good-quality guarantee follows, because late choices may have very large weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any vertex, repeatedly append a cheapest edge from the current endpoint to an unvisited vertex, breaking ties arbitrarily, and finally connect the last vertex to the first. On a noncomplete graph the method can fail despite the existence of a tour; on a complete graph it always closes but can return a very poor tour.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The construction yields a tour when every selected and closing edge exists; completeness ensures existence but not solution quality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dantzig–Fulkerson–Johnson formulation of the ATSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-incidence formulation with directed degree and subtour-elimination constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$, let $x_a\in\{0,1\}$ indicate whether arc $a$ belongs to the tour, and define $\delta^+(S)=\{ij\in A:i\in S,\ j\notin S\}$ and $\delta^-(S)=\{ij\in A:i\notin S,\ j\in S\}$. The DFJ formulation is
\[\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\]
subject to
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(i)}x_a=1,\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^-(i)}x_a=1\quad(i\in V),\]
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}x_a\ge 1\quad(\varnothing\subsetneq S\subsetneq V),\qquad x_a\in\{0,1\}\quad(a\in A).\]
Its binary feasible points are exactly the incidence vectors of directed Hamiltonian tours. The subtour-elimination family is exponential in number but admits efficient separation, so its inequalities may be generated as needed from the degree-constrained LP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directed DFJ model minimizes arc cost subject to one entering and one leaving arc at every vertex and at least one selected arc leaving every nonempty proper vertex subset. Its binary solutions are exactly Hamiltonian tours. Although the subtour constraints are exponential, they can be separated efficiently and added on demand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ satisfies the DFJ constraints}\iff x\text{ is the incidence vector of a directed Hamiltonian tour of }D.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-tree/perfect-matching tour construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic construction; the shortcutting step presumes that deleting repeated vertices yields edges of the original graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a weighted graph $G=(V,E)$, find a minimum-weight spanning tree $G'=(V,E')$. Let $U$ be the vertices having odd degree in $G'$, find a minimum-weight perfect matching $M$ in $G(U)$, and find an Eulerian cycle $Q$ in the multigraph $(V,E'\cup M)$. Obtain a tour $T$ by shortcutting repeated vertices of $Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a minimum-weight spanning tree, add a minimum-weight perfect matching on its odd-degree vertices, traverse the resulting Eulerian multigraph, and delete repeated vertex visits to obtain a tour.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a weighted graph for which the stated spanning tree, matching, and shortcutting operations are well-defined}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is the tour extracted from an Eulerian cycle of }(V,E'\cup M).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-tree Lagrangian bound and branch-and-bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compound exact-search method using minimum one-trees as Lagrangian subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^{|V|}$ with $\lambda_1=0$, define $z_{1T}(\lambda)=2\sum_{i\in V}\lambda_i+\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{|E|}}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(c_{ij}-\lambda_i-\lambda_j)x_{ij}$ over characteristic vectors of $1$-trees, and let $z_{LD}=\max_{\lambda:\lambda_1=0}z_{1T}(\lambda)$. Then $z_{LD}=z_{MIT}$. For fixed $\lambda$, a minimum-weight $1$-tree is obtained by a minimum spanning tree on $V\setminus\{1\}$ plus the two least-weight edges incident to vertex $1$, using reduced weights $c_{ij}-\lambda_i-\lambda_j$. If this $1$-tree is a tour, then $z_{1T}(\lambda)=z_{LD}=z_{TS}$. Otherwise, $\delta_i(\lambda)=2-\deg_i(x)$ is a subgradient for multiplier optimization. One may stop when $|z_{1T}(\lambda^*)-\bar z_{TS}|<\varepsilon$ and, if optimality is not established, continue by branching on a subtour of the incumbent $1$-tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize the Lagrangian one-tree bound by repeatedly solving reduced-cost minimum one-tree problems and using degree deficits as subgradients; a one-tree that is a tour proves optimality, while a remaining gap may be handled by tolerance-based stopping and branch-and-bound on subtours.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ ranges over characteristic vectors of }1\text{-trees}
\bar z_{TS}\text{ is the cost of a feasible tour}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{LD}=z_{MIT};\quad x\text{ a tour}\Rightarrow z_{1T}(\lambda)=z_{LD}=z_{TS},\quad\text{otherwise }\delta_i=2-\deg_i(x)\text{ supplies a subgradient and the bound supports branch-and-bound.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tour Set and Its Downward-Closed Independence System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the symmetric TSP tour set and the full-dimensional downward closure used for polyhedral analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be a complete undirected graph on m\ge 3 vertices, with n=|E|=m(m-1)/2. A set E'\subseteq E induces a tour exactly when (V,E') is connected and every vertex has degree two. Let S\subseteq\{0,1\}^n be the characteristic vectors of tours and define T=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n: x\le x'\text{ for some }x'\in S\}. Then T is an independence system whose maximal members are S, S\subseteq T, every inequality valid for T is valid for S, and \dim(\operatorname{conv}T)=n. Moreover, objectives can be transformed so that optimization over S is represented by optimization over T while preserving a specified optimal tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a complete undirected graph, tours are connected spanning subgraphs of degree two at every vertex. Their characteristic vectors form S, while T consists of every binary edge set contained in a tour. The set T is downward closed with maximal members S; its valid inequalities remain valid for S, and its convex hull is full-dimensional. A suitable objective transformation can preserve optimal tours when passing from S to T.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\exists x'\in S,\ x\le x'\},\quad S\subseteq T,\quad \dim(\operatorname{conv}T)=n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hamiltonian tours and the asymmetric traveling salesperson problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-graph definition of a Hamiltonian tour and the minimum-cost ATSP, including possible infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph $D=(V,A)$, a directed Hamiltonian tour is a directed circuit that traverses every vertex exactly once. Given arc costs $(c_a)_{a\in A}$, the asymmetric traveling salesperson problem is
\[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in T}c_a:T\text{ is a directed Hamiltonian tour in }D\right\}.\]
The feasible set may be empty because $D$ need not contain a Hamiltonian tour. In the city-pair formulation, the problem is symmetric when $c_{ij}=c_{ji}$ for every pair and asymmetric when direction-dependent costs are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed Hamiltonian tour is a circuit traversing every vertex exactly once. The ATSP seeks a minimum-cost such tour and may be infeasible if the digraph has none. Equal costs in opposite directions define the symmetric case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ATSP}(D,c)=\min\left\{\sum_{a\in T}c_a:T\text{ is a directed Hamiltonian tour in }D\right\},\quad\text{with a possibly empty feasible set.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: STSP formulation and initial cutting-plane relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the binary tour formulation and the initial relaxation used because the subtour family is exponential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, STSP is $\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e$ subject to $\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e=2$ for every $v\in V$, $\sum_{e\in E(U)}x_e\leq |U|-1$ for every $U\subset V$ with $3\leq |U|\leq\lfloor |V|/2\rfloor$, and $x\in\{0,1\}^{|E|}$. Because the subtour family is exponential, a cutting-plane/branch-and-bound method may begin with $S_R^1=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^{|E|}:x\text{ satisfies the degree equations and the edge upper bounds}\}$ and add violated subtour or other facet inequalities through separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model a symmetric TSP tour by binary edge variables, degree-two equations, and subtour-elimination inequalities. Since the subtour family is exponential, begin with degree constraints, nonnegativity, and edge upper bounds, then separate violated inequalities during cutting-plane branch-and-bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-Insertion Tour Heuristic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Insertion-based tour construction on complete weighted graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume G is complete and let T be a subtour. Define d(i,T)=\min_{j\in T}c_{ij} for i\in V\setminus T. Choose i^*\in\arg\min_{i\in V\setminus T}d(i,T) and j^*\in\arg\min_{j\in T}c_{i^*j}. Of the two neighbors j_1,j_2 of j^* in T, choose j_r minimizing c_{i^*j_r}, replace (j_r,j^*) by (j_r,i^*) and (i^*,j^*), and repeat. The process terminates with a tour, but no good-quality guarantee is provided.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a complete graph, repeatedly select the unvisited vertex closest to the current subtour, identify its closest subtour vertex, and insert it beside that vertex through the cheaper of its two neighboring positions. Repetition terminates with a tour, although the resulting tour can be poor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Repeated nearest insertion terminates with a tour, without a guaranteed quality bound.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: k-Interchange Tour Local Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tour improvement by equal-cardinality edge exchanges, including the 2-interchange specialization and locality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a tour, a k-interchange replaces k tour edges by k nontour edges whenever the replacement is again a tour and has lower total weight. For k=2, the removed edges cannot be adjacent; when replacement edges exist, the reconnection is unique. For k small relative to |V|, a k-interchange-local optimum can nevertheless have poor objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The k-interchange heuristic improves a tour by replacing k selected edges with k unselected edges when the exchange yields a lower-weight tour. In a 2-interchange the removed edges must be nonadjacent and have a unique feasible reconnection when it exists. Local optimality for a neighborhood whose k is small relative to the number of vertices does not ensure a good tour.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Accept any feasible }k\text{-edge exchange that lowers tour weight; for small }k/|V|,\ k\text{-local optimality need not imply good global quality.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: TSP 2-factor relaxation: constraints, tractability, and limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A 2-factor-based strengthening of the symmetric TSP relaxation, including its optimization complexity, nonexactness, and facet property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For G=(V,E), impose (i)\ 0\le x_e\le1\ (e\in E),\quad (ii)\ x(\delta(v))=2\ (v\in V),\quad (iii)\ x(\delta(U))\ge2\ (\varnothing\ne U\ne V),\quad (iv)\ x(\delta(U)\setminus F)-x(F)\ge1-|F|, where U\subseteq V and F\subseteq\delta(U) is an odd-cardinality matching. This strengthens relaxation (58.4), and \min l^{\top}x over this system is computable in strongly polynomial time. The system does not generally equal the traveling-salesman polytope: for the Petersen graph, x_e=2/3 for every e satisfies it but is not a tour-polytope point. For complete graphs, every inequality (iv) with |F|\ge3 defines a facet of the traveling-salesman polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The 2-factor relaxation consists of edge bounds, degree-two equations, subtour cuts, and odd matching cut inequalities. It strengthens the earlier TSP relaxation and permits strongly polynomial optimization, but it is not generally an exact description: the all-two-thirds vector on the Petersen graph is a counterexample. On complete graphs, each odd matching cut inequality with at least three matching edges is facet-defining.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{l^{\top}x:x\text{ satisfies (i)--(iv)}\}\text{ is strongly polynomially computable; the system is generally nonexact, and (iv) is facet-defining on complete graphs when }|F|\ge3

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Traveling Salesman Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tours and the minimum-weight symmetric traveling-salesman problem on a weighted undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be an undirected graph and c\in\mathbb{R}^{|E|}. A tour is a spanning subgraph T=(V,E_T) that is a cycle on V; equivalently, T is connected, every vertex has degree 2, and |E_T|=|V|. If G contains at least one tour, then z_{\mathrm{TS}}=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E_T}c_e:T=(V,E_T)\text{ is a tour of }G\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tour is a spanning cycle: it is connected, every vertex has degree two, and it has as many edges as vertices. If the weighted undirected graph has a tour, the symmetric traveling-salesman problem minimizes total selected-edge weight over all tours.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z_{\mathrm{TS}}=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in E_T}c_e:T=(V,E_T)\text{ is a tour of }G\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Miller–Tucker–Zemlin formulation of the ATSP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-variable formulation, its exact integer projection, and its weaker relaxation relative to DFJ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, designate vertex $1$ as the start, and let binary arc variables $x$ satisfy the directed in-degree and out-degree equations. Introduce real position variables $u_i$ for $i\ne1$ and impose
\[u_i-u_j+1\le n(1-x_{ij})\qquad(ij\in A,\ i,j\ne1).\]
The projection of the resulting integer feasible set onto $x$ is exactly the set of directed Hamiltonian-tour incidence vectors. A tour admits its visit positions as $u$, while any subtour not containing vertex $1$ would yield a contradiction after summing its MTZ inequalities. The resulting relaxation gives weaker branch-and-cut bounds than the DFJ formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The MTZ formulation adds position variables and big-M precedence inequalities to binary arc variables satisfying the degree equations. These inequalities eliminate subtours not containing the fixed start vertex, so the integer model represents exactly the Hamiltonian tours, although its relaxation gives weaker bounds than DFJ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists u:\ u_i-u_j+1\le n(1-x_{ij})\ \forall ij\in A\text{ with }i,j\ne1\iff x\text{ is a directed Hamiltonian-tour incidence vector.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Leg-indexed formulation of the traveling salesperson problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended binary formulation that indexes each selected arc by its position in the tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $D=(V,A)$ with $V=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, let $x_{ak}=1$ exactly when arc $a$ is the $k$th leg. Minimize
\[\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{k=1}^n c_ax_{ak}\]
subject to each vertex being entered once and left once, exactly one arc being selected for each leg, the continuity equations
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^-(i)}x_{ak}=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(i)}x_{a,k+1}\quad(i\in V,\ k=1,\ldots,n-1),\]
and
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^-(1)}x_{an}=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(1)}x_{a1}=1,\qquad x_{ak}\in\{0,1\}.\]
Its integer feasible solutions encode exactly the Hamiltonian tours whose first leg leaves vertex $1$ and whose last leg returns to it. The formulation has $n|A|$ binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The leg-indexed model chooses one arc at each tour position, enters and leaves every vertex once, links each arrival to the next departure, and anchors the first and last legs at vertex 1. It represents Hamiltonian tours but uses one binary variable for every arc-position pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ satisfies the leg-indexed constraints}\iff x\text{ encodes a Hamiltonian tour whose first leg leaves vertex }1\text{ and whose last leg returns to vertex }1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated vehicle routing by route selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_r\) be the cost of route \(r\in\mathcal R\). A route-selection formulation for at most \(K\) vehicles is \[\min\left\{\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}c_r\lambda_r:\ \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}a_{ir}\lambda_r=1\ \text{for every }i\in N,\ \sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\lambda_r\le K,\ \lambda_r\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Capacity is enforced in the column definition: every \(r\in\mathcal R\) satisfies \(\sum_{i\in N}d_i a_{ir}\le Q\). If multiple identical vehicles may traverse the same route, the domain can instead be \(\lambda_r\in\mathbb Z_+\), with the same coverage and fleet-size rows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edge and q2-route formulations of the capacitated vehicle-routing problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CVRP formulations and their LP-relaxation relationship, including a scaling inconsistency in the extracted intersected formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), where \(V=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\) and 0 is the depot. The edge formulation imposes \(x(\delta(0))=2K\), \(x(\delta(i))=2\) for every client, and \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2\lceil d(S)/Q\rceil\) for \(S\subset V\) with \(0\notin S\). A second formulation selects capacity-feasible q2-routes \(t\in\mathcal R\) using variables \(\lambda_t\), with \(\sum_t a_{0t}\lambda_t=2K\) and \(\sum_t a_{it}\lambda_t=2\). The two LP relaxations are incomparable. Linking them by \(x_e=\sum_t\rho_{et}\lambda_t\) permits their intersection. Under the extract's definition of \(A_{S,t}\) as the number of route-edge occurrences in \(\delta(S)\), direct substitution into the edge capacity inequality gives \(\sum_t A_{S,t}\lambda_t\ge 2\lceil d(S)/Q\rceil\); the displayed third formulation instead omits the factor 2 and therefore requires an unstated normalization or correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The CVRP has both an edge formulation with degree and capacitated-cut constraints and a route formulation whose columns are capacity-feasible q2-routes. Their LP relaxations are incomparable, and linking route and edge variables permits an intersected relaxation. The extracted third formulation has an unresolved factor-of-two inconsistency in its translated capacity cut.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is complete, with }V=\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\text{ and depot }0.
d_i\text{ is client }i\text{'s demand and }d(S)=\sum_{i\in S}d_i.
\mathcal R\text{ is the set of capacity-feasible q2-routes, which exclude two-cycles}.
\rho_{et}\text{ counts occurrences of edge }e\text{ in route }t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_1\nsubseteq P_2,\qquad P_2\nsubseteq P_1,\qquad x_e=\sum_t\rho_{et}\lambda_t\text{ links the formulations, subject to the stated scaling caveat.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Capacitated vehicle-routing formulation with time windows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded arc-flow formulation for heterogeneous vehicle capacities, unsplit deliveries, and customer time windows. Several displayed expressions are typographically corrupted; the customer-assignment, capacity, and upper-window indices are recoverable from the accompanying prose, but the printed vehicle-activation condition is not safely interpretable and is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let customer $0$ be the depot and let $k=1,\ldots,m$ index vehicles with capacities $Q_k$. Each nondepot customer $i$ has demand $q_i$ and time window $[a_i,b_i]$. Define $\delta_{ijk}=1$ iff vehicle $k$ travels directly from $i$ to $j$, $\gamma_{ik}=1$ iff vehicle $k$ visits $i$, and let $\tau_i$ be the visit time. The recoverable formulation minimizes $\sum_{i,j,k}c_{ij}\delta_{ijk}$ subject to $\sum_j\delta_{ijk}=\sum_j\delta_{jik}=\gamma_{ik}$, $\sum_k\gamma_{ik}=1$ for every nondepot customer $i$, $\sum_iq_i\gamma_{ik}\le Q_k$ for every vehicle $k$, $\tau_i-\tau_j\le M(1-\delta_{ijk})-d_{ij}$ on applicable arcs, and $a_i\le\tau_i\le b_i$. Additional subtour-elimination constraints are generally required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary arc and visit variables require a vehicle visiting a customer to enter and leave it once, assign each nondepot customer to exactly one vehicle without split deliveries, respect vehicle capacities, and enforce travel-time implications and customer time windows. Total arc cost is minimized, and additional subtour-elimination constraints are generally needed. The extract's vehicle-activation condition is internally inconsistent and cannot be included reliably.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every nondepot customer receives an unsplit delivery from exactly one vehicle.}
M\text{ is sufficiently large to deactivate the time constraint when }\delta_{ijk}=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arc-load formulation of the capacitated vehicle-routing problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A pseudo-polynomial load-indexed CVRP formulation for integral demands and vehicle capacity, allowing directed travel costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(d_i\) and \(Q\) are integral. Introduce binary variables \(x_{ij}^q\) indicating that a vehicle travels from i to j while carrying load q. Minimize \(\sum_{q=0}^Q\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}^q\), subject to \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(0)}x_a^0=K\), \(\sum_{q=0}^Q\sum_{a\in\delta^+(i)}x_a^q=1\) for every client i, and \(\sum_{a\in\delta^-(i)}x_a^{q-d_i}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(i)}x_a^q=0\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\) and \(d_i\le q\le Q\). These constraints send K empty vehicles from the depot, visit each client once, and increase the indexed load by \(d_i\) at client i. Because load levels range through \(0,\ldots,Q\), the formulation size is pseudo-polynomial in Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arc-load formulation indexes each routing arc by the vehicle's load. Its depot, visit, and load-flow constraints ensure that K empty vehicles depart, every client is visited once, and load increases by the visited client's demand. Its size is pseudo-polynomial in the numerical capacity Q.
assumptions_latex: Q\in\mathbb Z_+\text{ is the vehicle capacity}.
x_{ij}^q\in\{0,1\}\text{ for every admissible load-indexed arc}.
c_{ij}\text{ may depend on travel direction}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The load-indexed flow constraints encode client service and load evolution, and the formulation has pseudo-polynomial size in }Q.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branch-cut-and-price scheme for q2-route CVRP formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternates pricing and capacitated-subtour separation, then branches using constraints compatible with the pricing subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start with a restricted master containing a subset of q2-route columns and capacitated-subtour constraints. After solving it, price a q2-route by \(\zeta=\min\{\sum_{e\in E}\bar c_e x_e:x\text{ is the incidence vector of a q2-route}\}\), using reduced edge costs determined by the master dual variables. As stated in the extract, add columns while \(\zeta>0\), and regard \(\zeta=0\) as completion of column generation. For \(x_e^*=\sum_t\rho(e,t)\lambda_t^*\), solve \(\phi=\min_{S\subset V,\,0\notin S}\{\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e^*-\lceil d(S)/Q\rceil\}\). If \(\phi<0\), add a violated capacitated-subtour constraint and repeat; if \(\phi=0\) and \(x^*\) is integral, terminate, otherwise branch. Compatible branches have the form \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\le 2s\) or \(\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge 2s+2\), leaving the pricing subproblem essentially unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve a restricted route master, generate q2-route columns through reduced-cost pricing, separate violated capacitated-subtour inequalities, and repeat. If separation finds no violation, accept an integral solution or branch using even cut-set disjunctions that preserve the structure of the pricing problem.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal R\text{ initially contains only a subset of q2-route columns}.
S_1,\ldots,S_p\text{ is the current subset of capacitated-subtour constraints}.
\bar c_e\text{ is computed from the restricted-master dual solution}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi<0\Rightarrow\text{add a violated cut};\qquad \phi=0\land x^*\in\mathbb Z_+^E\Rightarrow\text{optimal termination};\qquad \phi=0\land x^*\notin\mathbb Z_+^E\Rightarrow\text{branch}.

e k}\min_{d_k\le q\le Q}\{H(j,k,q-d_k)+ ar c_{0k}\}.\] For ng-routes, choose neighborhoods \(N(i)
i i\). A node i may be revisited only if some node visited since its preceding visit lies outside \(N(i)\). If \(G(i,q,S)\) is the minimum cost of an ng-walk reaching i after delivering q, with S forbidden as immediate successors, then \[G igl(j,q,(S\cap N(j))\cup\{j\} igr)=\min_{i\in V}\{G(i,q-d_j,S)+ ar c_{ij}\}.\]

The stronger ng-route relaxation uses a state recording the current node, delivered load, and a neighborhood-based forbidden-successor set; its transition updates that set by intersecting it with the next node's neighborhood and adding the next node.

children.title: Spanning-Tree Formulations
children.top_down_role: Connectivity models selecting a tree spanning required vertices.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a connected undirected graph with \(|V|\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary feasible vectors are exactly the incidence vectors of spanning trees of \(G\).

notation.meaning: binary variable indicating whether edge e is selected
edges with both endpoints in S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: spanning-tree cardinality and forest inequalities
exact authoritative spanning-tree polytope locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected edge formulation using forest inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A spanning tree is represented by a vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in E}x_e=|V|-1,\qquad \sum_{e\in E(S)}x_e\le |S|-1\quad\text{for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V.\] The subset inequalities ensure that the selected edges contain no cycle. Together with the cardinality equation and connectedness of the ambient graph, they force the selected subgraph to be connected and to span every vertex. For edge costs \(c_e\), minimizing \(\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\) over this system gives a minimum-cost spanning tree formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select exactly one fewer edge than vertices and impose forest inequalities; the resulting binary subgraph is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cardinality equation and forest inequalities give a standard exact binary spanning-tree representation and fit this container. The record nevertheless lacks an inspectable authoritative source and specific locator supporting the formulation and exactness claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning trees and the spanning-tree polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines spanning trees and their incidence-vector polytope and records the connectivity criterion and elementary edge-count consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), an edge set \(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree if \((V,T)\) is connected and acyclic. The spanning-tree polytope is \(P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\). Moreover, \(G\) has a spanning tree if and only if \(G\) is connected, and every spanning tree \(T\) satisfies \(|T|=|V|-1\) and \(|T\cap E[S]|\le |S|-1\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is an edge set whose spanning subgraph is connected and acyclic, and the spanning-tree polytope is the convex hull of all spanning-tree incidence vectors. A graph has a spanning tree exactly when it is connected. Every spanning tree has |V|-1 edges and at most |S|-1 edges induced by each nonempty proper vertex subset S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a spanning tree}\iff (V,T)\text{ is connected and acyclic};\quad P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\};\quad G\text{ has a spanning tree}\iff G\text{ is connected};\quad T\text{ spanning tree}\Rightarrow\left(|T|=|V|-1\ \land\ |T\cap E[S]|\le |S|-1\ \forall\,\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear description of the spanning-tree polytope

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph. Then
\[
P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:\sum_{e\in E[S]}x_e\le |S|-1\ \forall\,\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\quad \sum_{e\in E}x_e=|V|-1,\quad x_e\ge 0\ \forall e\in E\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spanning-tree polytope consists exactly of the nonnegative edge vectors whose total value is |V|-1 and whose value on the edges induced by every nonempty proper vertex subset S is at most |S|-1.

children.title: Steiner-Tree Formulations
children.top_down_role: Connectivity models permitting auxiliary vertices within a selected tree.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph, \(R\subseteq V\) is a nonempty terminal set, and \(r\in R\) is a root.
Selected edges have nonnegative costs when a tree-shaped optimum is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cut system selects a connected subgraph containing \(R\); under nonnegative costs, an optimal solution has a Steiner-tree representative.

notation.meaning: edges crossing the cut defined by S

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rooted cut formulation for undirected Steiner connectivity
exact authoritative Steiner-tree formulation locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted undirected cut formulation for Steiner connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cut formulation for a Steiner subgraph uses \(x_e\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge1\quad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ such that }r\in S\text{ and }R\setminus S\ne\varnothing.\] These inequalities prevent any terminal from being separated from the root by an unselected cut. Thus the selected subgraph contains a connected component spanning all terminals, while vertices in \(V\setminus R\) may be used as Steiner vertices. With objective \(\min\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\) and \(c_e\ge0\), cycles and selected components containing no terminal can be removed without increasing cost, yielding a Steiner tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root-separating cut constraints connect all required terminals while permitting optional Steiner vertices; nonnegative costs allow redundant cycles to be removed.
knowledge_statements.title: Steiner-Tree Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted cut formulation is a plausible exact representation of terminal connectivity, and the nonnegative-cost qualification appropriately limits the tree-representative conclusion. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required to support the precise cut family and optimal-representative claim.

children.title: Capacitated Infrastructure Design
children.top_down_role: Network-design models coupling selected infrastructure to capacity choices.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a directed network with commodities \(K\).
Commodity \(k\) has origin \(o_k\), destination \(t_k\), and demand \(d_k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation couples routable commodity flows to installed arc capacity.

notation.meaning: flow of commodity k on arc a
integer number of capacity units installed on arc a
capacity supplied by one installed unit on arc a

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical multicommodity capacitated network-design formulation
exact authoritative infrastructure-design locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-capacity installation with splittable multicommodity flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each commodity \(k\), define \(b_{o_k}^k=d_k\), \(b_{t_k}^k=-d_k\), and \(b_v^k=0\) otherwise. A capacitated infrastructure formulation imposes \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a^k-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a^k=b_v^k\quad\text{for every }v\in V,\ k\in K,\] together with \[\sum_{k\in K}f_a^k\le u_a y_a\quad\text{for every }a\in A,\qquad f_a^k\ge0,\quad y_a\in\mathbb Z_+.\] An objective such as \(\min\sum_{a\in A}c_ay_a+\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{k\in K}q_a^kf_a^k\) trades installation against routing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Commodity-balance equations route demand, while linking inequalities require installed integer capacity to support the aggregate arc flow.

children.title: Connectivity-Enforcement Families

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is an undirected graph, \(R\subseteq V\) is nonempty, and \(r\in R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rooted cut constraints and feasible root-to-terminal flows are alternative exact ways to enforce connectivity of the required vertices.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equivalence of cut and flow connectivity enforcement
exact authoritative connectivity-formulation locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cut and flow families for rooted terminal connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Connectivity of \(R\) within the selected subgraph is enforced by the rooted cut family \[\sum_{e\in\delta(S)}x_e\ge1\quad\text{for every }S\subset V\text{ with }r\in S\text{ and }R\setminus S\ne\varnothing.\] An extended alternative sends one unit from \(r\) to each \(t\in R\setminus\{r\}\) using directed flows \(f_{ij}^t\ge0\), standard flow-balance equations, and linking bounds \(f_{ij}^t\le x_{\{i,j\}}\). For binary \(x\), either family is feasible exactly when every terminal lies in the selected component containing \(r\). Cut constraints may be separated dynamically; flow constraints give a polynomial-size extension with one commodity per terminal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Connectivity can be imposed directly by root-separating cuts or through linked root-to-terminal flows in an extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Connectivity-Enforcement Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-versus-flow comparison belongs in Connectivity-Enforcement Families, but the flow alternative refers to directed flows and standard balance equations without defining the directed arc construction or stating those equations. Because no source is supplied and connectivity extensions vary in their linking bounds and arc conventions, the exact version requires sourcing.

children.title: Discrete-Time Indexed Formulations
children.top_down_role: Representations indexed over a predefined discrete time grid.

assumptions_latex: Time is partitioned into integer periods \(T=\{0,\ldots,H\}\).
Each activity \(j\) has integer duration \(p_j\ge1\), demand \(q_{jr}\), and one nonpreemptive start.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every integer feasible solution assigns one grid-aligned start to each activity and respects precedence and period capacities.

notation.meaning: one when activity j starts at period t
capacity of resource r in period tau

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical time-indexed nonpreemptive scheduling formulation
exact authoritative scheduling locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Grid-based nonpreemptive scheduling with precedence and renewable resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_j\subseteq T\) be the feasible start periods for activity \(j\). A discrete-time formulation imposes \[\sum_{t\in T_j}x_{jt}=1\quad\text{for every }j,\qquad x_{jt}\in\{0,1\}.\] For each precedence arc \((i,j)\in P\), it requires \[\sum_{t\in T_i}(t+p_i)x_{it}\le\sum_{t\in T_j}t x_{jt}.\] Renewable-resource feasibility is expressed for every resource \(r\) and period \(\tau\) by \[\sum_j q_{jr}\sum_{t\in T_j:\ t\le\tau<t+p_j}x_{jt}\le Q_{r\tau}.\] Completion times and objectives are derived from the selected starts, for example by minimizing a makespan variable dominating every selected completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary start variables place each activity on a time grid; convolution-style rows enforce precedence and capacity in every period.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-indexed representation fits the container and its principal equations are standard. No authoritative citation is supplied, and the activity and resource index sets and the conditions defining feasible start sets T_j are not stated explicitly enough to certify the claimed scheduling semantics.

children.title: Continuous-Time Event Formulations
children.top_down_role: Representations organized around decision-dependent event times.

assumptions_latex: A finite ordered set of event points \(E=\{0,\ldots,m\}\) is available.
Each activity \(j\) has duration \(p_j>0\) and is assigned to one admissible start event.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selected event assignments place activities at ordered continuous times without discretizing the time horizon.

notation.meaning: one when activity j starts at event e

review_flags: event semantics vary across scheduling models; a dedicated source is required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic event-point encoding with continuous event times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous-time event formulation introduces ordered event times \[0\le\tau_0\le\tau_1\le\cdots\le\tau_m\] and binary assignments satisfying \(\sum_{e\in E}u_{je}=1\) for every activity \(j\). With continuous start variables \(s_j\), the implications \(u_{je}=1\Rightarrow s_j=\tau_e\) are linearized by \[-M(1-u_{je})\le s_j-\tau_e\le M(1-u_{je}).\] If precedence requires activity \(i\) to finish before activity \(j\), impose \(s_i+p_i\le s_j\). Resource-specific assignment or sequencing constraints must additionally exclude simultaneous incompatible activities. Unlike time-indexed models, the event times are decision variables rather than fixed grid points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activities are assigned to an ordered finite set of events whose times remain continuous decision variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Time Event Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record describes a plausible continuous-time event-point encoding and uses the correct representation kind, but event-point semantics and valid implication bounds depend on the scheduling variant. The supplied assumptions do not identify that variant, and no inspectable source is provided.

children.title: Event-Position Formulations
children.top_down_role: Representations assigning activities or changes to ordered event positions.

assumptions_latex: Activities \(J\) are assigned to ordered positions \(K=\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
Each activity occupies exactly one position and each position accepts at most one activity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment variables encode a partial permutation, and the cumulative inequalities translate activity precedence into position precedence.

notation.meaning: one when activity j occupies event position k
continuous time attached to position k

review_flags: event-position terminology is model-dependent; a dedicated source is required
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-style assignment to ordered event positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An event-position formulation uses \(u_{jk}\in\{0,1\}\) with \[\sum_{k\in K}u_{jk}=1\quad\text{for every }j\in J,\qquad \sum_{j\in J}u_{jk}\le1\quad\text{for every }k\in K.\] For each precedence arc \((i,j)\in P\), the cumulative inequalities \[\sum_{h=1}^{k}u_{jh}\le\sum_{h=1}^{k-1}u_{ih}\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,m\] force \(i\) into an earlier position than \(j\). If positions carry continuous times, impose \(\tau_k\le\tau_{k+1}\) and link an activity assigned to \(k\) to \(\tau_k\) by valid implication constraints. Additional rows encode resource compatibility or permitted idle positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary assignment variables place activities in ordered event slots, while cumulative inequalities enforce precedence between their positions.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-Position Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partial-permutation and cumulative-precedence constraints are internally plausible and fit an ordered event-position interpretation. Because event-position terminology is model-dependent and no authoritative locator is supplied, the intended formulation and its additional timing semantics cannot be established reliably.

children.title: Stage-Position Formulations
children.top_down_role: Representations assigning decisions to ordered process or sequence stages.

assumptions_latex: A process has ordered stages \(K=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), state space \(X\), and action set \(A\).
Admissible transitions are described by relations \(\mathcal T_k\subseteq X\times A\times X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation represents a feasible operation sequence as one admissible state transition at each ordered stage.

notation.meaning: state at the beginning of stage k
admissible transition relation at stage k

review_flags: stage-position terminology and intended application require source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered-stage state-transition formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stage-position formulation introduces a state \(z_k\in X\) and an action \(a_k\in A\) for each stage \(k\). Feasibility is defined by \[(z_k,a_k,z_{k+1})\in\mathcal T_k\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,m,\] together with prescribed initial and terminal conditions \(z_1\in X_0\) and \(z_{m+1}\in X_F\). When actions are chosen from a finite set, binary variables \(x_{ak}\) satisfy \(\sum_{a\in A}x_{ak}=1\) at every occupied stage, and linear linking constraints encode the corresponding transition. Optional occupancy variables permit unused stages while preserving the order of occupied positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stage-indexed variables encode an ordered sequence of actions and states, with transition constraints linking each stage to the next.
knowledge_statements.title: Stage-Position Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This record gives a generic stage-indexed state-transition model rather than a stage-position formulation in the local Temporal Representation Family. Its states, actions, and transition relations describe dynamic-system staging, while no positional assignment or temporal scheduling structure identifies the intended leaf sense. The candidate should not be retained in this immutable container.

children.title: Conflict-Based Scheduling Formulation Family
children.top_down_role: Resource conflicts represented through ordering and alternative temporal regimes.

children.title: Precedence-Based Scheduling Formulations
children.top_down_role: Scheduling representations centered on required activity order.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible start times realize every precedence arc, and minimizing \(C_{\max}\) yields a minimum-makespan precedence-feasible schedule absent other restrictions.
review_flags: exact authoritative scheduling locator not supplied
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Start-time formulation for an acyclic precedence network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A precedence-based scheduling formulation uses continuous start times \(s_j\ge0\) and imposes \[s_i+p_i\le s_j\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in P.\] For makespan minimization, introduce \(C_{\max}\) with \(C_{\max}\ge s_j+p_j\) for every terminal activity, or for every \(j\in J\), and minimize \(C_{\max}\). Because \((J,P)\) is acyclic, the precedence system is feasible and its earliest-start solution is obtained from longest-path distances in the precedence digraph. Machine conflicts, release dates, deadlines, and renewable-resource limits are separate constraint families and are not implied by precedence inequalities alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start-time inequalities require each predecessor to finish before its successor; a makespan variable measures the latest completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Precedence-Based Scheduling Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The start-time precedence representation is standard, explicitly separates precedence from resource and machine restrictions, and fits the leaf container. No inspectable authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied for the formulation or longest-path characterization.

children.title: Disjunctive Scheduling Formulations

assumptions_latex: Jobs form a finite set \(J\), with processing times \(p_i>0\) and start times \(s_i\ge 0\).
Each conflict edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\) requires jobs \(i\) and \(j\) to use an exclusive resource without preemption.
Valid bounds imply constants \(M_{ij}\ge \sup(s_i+p_i-s_j)\) over the remaining bounded scheduling domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed mixed-integer constraints represent the pairwise scheduling disjunction exactly on the bounded domain.

notation.meaning: Start time and processing time of job \(i\).
Binary variable equal to one when \(i\) precedes \(j\).
Set of unordered conflicting job pairs.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\{i,j\}\in E\), non-overlap is the disjunction \(s_i+p_i\le s_j\) or \(s_j+p_j\le s_i\). Introduce \(y_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), where \(y_{ij}=1\) selects the first ordering. A mixed-integer representation is
\[
s_i+p_i\le s_j+M_{ij}(1-y_{ij}),\qquad s_j+p_j\le s_i+M_{ji}y_{ij}.
\]
If both constants are valid over the bounded scheduling domain, projection onto the start-time variables gives exactly the union of the two ordering alternatives for each conflict edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each conflicting job pair chooses one of two temporal orders; valid big-M inequalities encode that disjunction exactly over a bounded scheduling domain.

children.title: Pairwise Order Representations
children.top_down_role: Representations selecting the relative order of competing activities.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Order Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary orientation representation for pairwise conflicts; temporal feasibility and any required global consistency are imposed separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\) be a finite job set, let \(E\subseteq\{\{i,j\}:i,j\in J,\ i\ne j\}\) be the set of unordered conflict edges, and define \(\overrightarrow E=\{(i,j):\{i,j\}\in E\}\). For every \(\{i,j\}\in E\), introduce \(y_{ij},y_{ji}\in\{0,1\}\) and impose
\[
y_{ij}+y_{ji}=1.
\]
The selected directed relation is
\[
A_y=\{(i,j)\in\overrightarrow E:y_{ij}=1\}.
\]
Thus every conflict edge receives exactly one orientation. If job \(i\) has start time \(s_i\) and processing time \(p_i>0\), the selected arc \((i,j)\in A_y\) may activate \(s_i+p_i\le s_j\). Additional constraints may be required when global consistency is modeled independently of the start-time inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each conflicting pair, two directed binary variables constrained to sum to one select exactly one precedence orientation; separate temporal or consistency constraints enforce the consequences of that selection.
assumptions_latex: Jobs form a finite set \(J\), and \(E\) is a set of unordered pairs of distinct jobs that cannot overlap.
For each job \(i\in J\), \(s_i\) denotes its start time and \(p_i>0\) its processing time.
Every conflict edge must receive exactly one orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\{i,j\}\in E\), the equation \(y_{ij}+y_{ji}=1\) selects exactly one of the arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\).

notation.meaning: Set of unordered conflicting job pairs.
Directed arcs induced by the unordered conflict edges.

children.title: No-Overlap Regimes

Their occupied half-open intervals are \([s_i,s_i+p_i)\) and \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\), with \(p_i,p_j>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The jobs do not overlap if and only if \(s_i+p_i\le s_j\) or \(s_j+p_j\le s_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two jobs with occupied intervals \(I_i=[s_i,s_i+p_i)\) and \(I_j=[s_j,s_j+p_j)\), the no-overlap requirement is
\[
I_i\cap I_j=\varnothing
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(s_i+p_i\le s_j)\ \lor\ (s_j+p_j\le s_i).
\]
Endpoint equality is permitted because the intervals are half-open: one job may start exactly when the other finishes. For a conflict set \(E\), a feasible schedule satisfies this predicate for every \(\{i,j\}\in E\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonpreemptive jobs do not overlap exactly when either the first finishes before the second starts or conversely.

children.title: Lot-Sizing Formulations
children.top_down_role: Intertemporal production models with setup, lot, demand, or inventory structure.

assumptions_latex: Periods are \(t=1,\ldots,T\), demands satisfy \(d_t\ge0\), and initial inventory \(I_0\ge0\) is given.
Production capacities \(U_t\ge0\) are valid finite bounds; unmet demand is forbidden.
Setup, production, and holding costs are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is defined by inventory balance, nonnegativity, binary setups, and the coupling inequalities \(0\le x_t\le U_ty_t\).

notation.meaning: Production quantity and end-of-period inventory in period \(t\).
Unit production, holding, and fixed setup costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon capacitated single-item lot sizing without backlogging.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Uncapacitated Lot-Sizing p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-horizon single-item lot-sizing formulation is
\[
\min\ \sum_{t=1}^{T}(c_tx_t+h_tI_t+f_ty_t)
\]
subject to
\[
I_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+I_t\quad(t=1,\ldots,T),
\qquad 0\le x_t\le U_ty_t,
\qquad I_t\ge0,
\qquad y_t\in\{0,1\}.
\]
The balance equations couple consecutive periods, while \(x_t\le U_ty_t\) forbids production without a setup. The uncapacitated convention is recovered by choosing any valid demand-derived bound, such as \(U_t=\sum_{k=t}^{T}d_k\) when excess terminal inventory is unnecessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lot sizing balances production, demand, and inventory over time while binary setups activate bounded production in each period.
knowledge_statements.title: Lot-Sizing Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 5.2 Uncapacitated Lot-Sizing p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MIP and Fixed-Charge Network Representation of ULS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-horizon uncapacitated single-item lot-sizing model without backlogging and with zero initial and terminal inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For periods \(t=1,\ldots,n\), let demands satisfy \(d_t\ge 0\), setup costs satisfy \(f_t\ge 0\), and let \(y_t\ge 0\), \(s_t\ge 0\), and \(x_t\in\{0,1\}\) denote production, end-of-period inventory, and setup activation. The ULS problem is represented by
\[\min \sum_{t=1}^n p_ty_t+\sum_{t=1}^n h_ts_t+\sum_{t=1}^n f_tx_t\]
subject to \(s_{t-1}+y_t=d_t+s_t\), \(y_t\le Mx_t\), and \(s_0=s_n=0\). Every feasible solution corresponds to a flow in a network having production arcs \((0,t)\), inventory arcs \((t,t+1)\), and fixed charges on production arcs; hence ULS is a fixed-charge network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard uncapacitated lot-sizing problem minimizes production, inventory, and setup costs subject to period-by-period inventory balance, setup-linked production, nonnegativity, binary setup decisions, and zero initial and final inventory. It has a fixed-charge network-flow representation whose opened production arcs identify production periods.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a valid upper bound for production}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{ULS}\text{ admits the stated MIP representation and is a fixed\text{-}charge network\text{-}flow problem.}

X^{\mathrm{CLS}}=\left\{(x,s,y)\in\{0,1\}^n\times\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^n: s_{t-1}+y_t=d_t+s_t,\quad y_t\leq C_tx_t,\quad t=1,\ldots,n\right\}.

children.title: Unit-Commitment Formulations
children.top_down_role: Intertemporal operating-state models for discrete generation or equipment commitment.

assumptions_latex: Periods are \(t=1,\ldots,T\), and the initial commitment state \(u_0\in\{0,1\}\) is given.
Startup and shutdown variables record changes in binary commitment state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation links commitment transitions to startup and shutdown decisions and permits generation only within the committed operating range.

notation.meaning: Binary on/off commitment state in period \(t\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core single-unit commitment logic; network, ramping, and minimum-time constraints are outside this record.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For one generating unit, the core unit-commitment formulation imposes, for \(t=1,
\ldots,T\),
\[
u_t-u_{t-1}=v_t-w_t,
\qquad v_t+w_t\le1,
\qquad P_t^{\min}u_t\le p_t\le P_t^{\max}u_t,
\]
with \(u_t,v_t,w_t\in\{0,1\}\) and \(p_t\ge0\). The transition equation records each off-to-on change as a startup and each on-to-off change as a shutdown. The generation bounds force \(p_t=0\) when off and restrict output to the admissible operating interval when on.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary commitment transitions determine startups and shutdowns, while output bounds force zero generation when off and admissible generation when on.
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Commitment Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated core transition and generation constraints are standard and appropriately scoped, but no inspectable source is supplied for this unit-commitment formulation.

children.title: Setup-Production Coupling
children.top_down_role: Links between setup states and permitted production activity.

assumptions_latex: For each period \(t\), activity \(x_t\ge0\) has a valid finite upper bound \(U_t\).
The binary variable \(y_t\) indicates whether the corresponding setup is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(0\le x_t\le U_ty_t\) enforces \(y_t=0\Rightarrow x_t=0\) and permits every bounded activity level when \(y_t=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard fixed-charge activation link for a bounded nonnegative production variable.

source_refs.locator: 5.2 Uncapacitated Lot-Sizing p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_t\in[0,U_t]\) denote production and \(y_t\in\{0,1\}\) denote setup selection. The setup-production coupling condition is
\[
0\le x_t\le U_ty_t.
\]
Consequently, \(y_t=0\) forces \(x_t=0\), whereas \(y_t=1\) retains the entire admissible interval \([0,U_t]\). If setup incurs fixed cost \(f_t\ge0\), the objective term \(f_ty_t\) charges that cost whenever positive production requires activation. Validity requires \(U_t\) to dominate every feasible value of \(x_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded production variable is linked to a binary setup so production is zero unless the setup is selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Setup-Production Coupling

children.title: Intertemporal Inventory Coupling
children.top_down_role: Inventory relationships connecting production decisions across periods.

knowledge_statements.title: Intertemporal Inventory Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-item inventory conservation without backlogging, loss, disposal, or production lead time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let periods be \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(I_0\ge0\) be given initial inventory, and let \(x_t\ge0\), \(d_t\ge0\), and \(I_t\ge0\) denote production, demand, and end-of-period inventory. Intertemporal conservation requires
\[
I_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+I_t\qquad(t=1,\ldots,T).
\]
Thus inventory carried from period \(t-1\), together with current production, supplies current demand and the inventory carried into the next period. Any required terminal inventory is imposed through an additional boundary condition on \(I_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In every period, prior inventory plus current production equals current demand plus end-of-period inventory.
assumptions_latex: Periods are \(t=1,\ldots,T\), with given demand \(d_t\ge0\) and initial inventory \(I_0\ge0\).
Production \(x_t\ge0\) and end-of-period inventory \(I_t\ge0\) are measured consistently.
Backlogging, loss, disposal, and production lead time are absent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(t=1,\ldots,T\), inventory feasibility requires \(I_{t-1}+x_t=d_t+I_t\).

children.title: Cutting-Stock Formulations
children.top_down_role: Material-cutting models selecting feasible cutting configurations.

assumptions_latex: Item types are \(i=1,\ldots,m\), with integer demands \(d_i\ge0\), widths \(w_i>0\), and stock width \(W>0\).
The pattern set \(P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\sum_iw_ia_i\le W\}\) is finite.
Each used stock roll has unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The integer covering model minimizes the number of stock rolls while producing at least the required quantity of every item type.

notation.meaning: Number of pieces of item \(i\) in pattern \(p\).
Number of stock rolls cut according to pattern \(p\).
Finite set of width-feasible cutting patterns.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional cutting stock with integer demands and unit-cost stock rolls.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48
5.5 The Cutting Stock Problem* p. 89

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m w_i a_i\le W\}\), and write \(a_{ip}\) for component \(i\) of pattern \(p\). The Gilmore--Gomory integer formulation is
\[
\min\ \sum_{p\in P}x_p
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\ \ (p\in P).
\]
Each variable counts stock rolls assigned to one feasible pattern, and each covering inequality ensures that aggregate output meets the demand for its item type.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose integer numbers of feasible cutting patterns to meet every item demand while minimizing the number of stock rolls used.
knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Stock Formulations

children.title: Pattern-Selection Formulations
children.top_down_role: Models selecting complete patterns from an explicit or implicit family.

knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Selection Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic integer covering formulation over an explicitly enumerated finite pattern family with nonnegative pattern costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be a finite requirement set and \(P\) a finite pattern family. For each \(p\in P\), let \(a_{ip}\ge0\) be its contribution to requirement \(i\in I\), let \(c_p\ge0\) be its finite cost, and let \(x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\) be its selected multiplicity. The pattern-selection formulation is
\[
\min\ \sum_{p\in P}c_px_p
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\quad(i\in I),
\qquad x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\quad(p\in P).
\]
Each column \(a_p=(a_{ip})_{i\in I}\) describes the output or coverage supplied by one copy of pattern \(p\). Equality may replace a covering inequality only when overproduction is forbidden and exact fulfillment is attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select nonnegative integer pattern multiplicities whose aggregate contributions cover every requirement at minimum nonnegative pattern cost.
assumptions_latex: The requirement set \(I\) and pattern set \(P\) are finite.
Pattern \(p\) contributes \(a_{ip}\ge0\) units to requirement \(i\), whose demand is \(d_i\ge0\).
Each pattern has a finite nonnegative cost \(c_p\ge0\), and its multiplicity is a nonnegative integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation minimizes \(\sum_{p\in P}c_px_p\) subject to \(\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(x_p\in\mathbb Z_+\) for every \(p\in P\).

notation.meaning: Finite nonnegative cost of selecting one copy of pattern \(p\).

children.title: Implicit Pattern Families
children.top_down_role: Large pattern spaces represented without full initial enumeration.

knowledge_statements.title: Implicit Pattern Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite but nonenumerated integer pattern sets represented by compact feasibility systems and accessed through LP column pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:Aa\le b\}
\]
be a finite pattern family represented by a compact feasibility system rather than explicit enumeration. Consider the master LP
\[
\min\ \sum_{a\in P}c(a)x_a
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\sum_{a\in P}a_i x_a\ge d_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),
\qquad x_a\ge0\quad(a\in P).
\]
Let \(P'\subseteq P\) be the current restricted family, and let \(\pi_i\ge0\) be optimal dual prices for the restricted master coverage constraints. The pricing problem is
\[
\min_{a\in P}\left(c(a)-\sum_{i=1}^m\pi_i a_i\right).
\]
A negative optimum identifies a pattern outside \(P'\) with negative reduced cost; if the optimum is nonnegative, no omitted pattern has negative reduced cost with respect to \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite but very large pattern family is specified by compact integer feasibility constraints, while an LP pricing problem searches it for omitted columns having negative reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: The pattern family \(P=\{a\in\mathbb Z_+^m:Aa\le b\}\) is finite but potentially too large to enumerate.
The master is a minimization LP with covering constraints and nonnegative pattern variables.
The restricted family satisfies \(P'\subseteq P\), and \(\pi\ge0\) is an optimal dual solution of the restricted master LP.
The pricing problem is solved globally over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compact system represents the implicit family \(P\), and minimizing \(c(a)-\pi^\mathsf{T}a\) over \(P\) either finds an omitted negative-reduced-cost column or certifies that none exists relative to \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Current restricted subset of generated patterns.
Nonnegative master-LP variable associated with pattern \(a\).
Optimal dual-price vector for the restricted master coverage constraints.

children.title: Pattern-Coverage Structure
children.top_down_role: Relationships linking selected patterns to item, demand, or coverage requirements.

assumptions_latex: Requirements are indexed by a finite set \(I\), and patterns by a finite set \(P\).
Each coefficient \(a_{ip}\ge0\) is the amount of requirement \(i\) supplied by one copy of pattern \(p\).
Demands satisfy \(d_i\ge0\), and pattern multiplicities satisfy \(x_p\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pattern coverage holds exactly when \(\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise covering structure induced by nonnegative pattern columns.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Cutting Stock: Formulations with Many Variables p. 48

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given pattern columns \(a_{p}=(a_{ip})_{i\in I}\in\mathbb R_+^{I}\), selection vector \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{P}\), and requirements \(d\in\mathbb R_+^{I}\), the pattern-coverage condition is
\[
Ax\ge d,
\quad\text{equivalently}\quad
\sum_{p\in P}a_{ip}x_p\ge d_i\qquad(i\in I).
\]
If patterns must be used in indivisible copies, impose \(x\in\mathbb Z_+^{P}\); its linear relaxation uses \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{P}\). Each row aggregates the contribution of all selected patterns to one requirement, while each column records one feasible operational pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage is achieved when the summed contributions of selected patterns meet or exceed every componentwise requirement.
knowledge_statements.title: Pattern-Coverage Structure

children.title: Indicator-Constraint Formulations
children.top_down_role: Native conditional constraints controlled by binary states.

assumptions_latex: The binary variable \(z\in\{0,1\}\) controls a constraint \(g(x)\le0\) on an ambient domain \(X\).
The intended implication is enforced natively by the modeling or solution system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The indicator constraint \(z=1\Rightarrow g(x)\le0\) restricts \(x\) only in the active binary state and imposes no condition from this indicator when \(z=0\).

notation.meaning: Continuous or mixed decision vector in ambient domain \(X\).
Constraint function activated by the indicator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Native binary implication semantics, independent of any particular big-M reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and a function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\), an indicator constraint with active value one is the implication
\[
z=1\ \Longrightarrow\ g(x)\le0.
\]
Its feasible set is
\[
\bigl(\{0\}\times X\bigr)\ \cup\ \bigl(\{1\}\times\{x\in X:g(x)\le0\}\bigr).
\]
Thus the indicated inequality is mandatory when \(z=1\) and contributes no restriction when \(z=0\). An active-on-zero indicator is obtained by replacing \(z=1\) with \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator constraint makes an inequality compulsory in one binary state and inactive in the other state.
knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Constraint Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The native implication and its feasible-set description are mathematically precise and fit the definition leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the claimed indicator-constraint semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single linear implication over a bounded base set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(y\in\{0,1\}\), and consider the implication \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq b\). If \(M\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a^\top x-b)\) is finite, then, relative to \(x\in X\), the implication is represented exactly by \[a^\top x\leq b+M(1-y).\] When \(y=1\), this inequality enforces \(a^\top x\leq b\); when \(y=0\), it imposes no restriction beyond those already defining \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid finite bound converts a binary-triggered linear inequality into one linear big-M constraint without changing its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=1\Rightarrow a^\top x\leq b\) is equivalent on \(X\) to \(a^\top x\leq b+M(1-y)\).

notation.meaning: Base feasible set for the continuous variables.
Valid upper bound on the inactive constraint violation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically precise and fits the Big-M container, but no inspectable source reference is supplied. Candidate-review acceptance requires a section, theorem, definition, or page locator supporting the bound-dependent equivalence.

children.title: Disaggregated Conditional Formulations
children.top_down_role: Alternative-specific variable copies used to strengthen conditional models.

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Conditional Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact disaggregation of a finite union of bounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bounded nonempty polyhedra \(P_k=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:A^ku\leq b^k\}\), \(k=1,\ldots,K\), introduce copies \(x^k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and selectors \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\). Then \(x\in\bigcup_{k=1}^K P_k\) is represented exactly by \[x=\sum_{k=1}^Kx^k,\qquad A^kx^k\leq b^kz_k\ \ (k=1,\ldots,K),\qquad \sum_{k=1}^Kz_k=1.\] Boundedness ensures that \(z_k=0\) forces \(x^k=0\), while the unique active copy belongs to its selected polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copying variables by alternative and selecting exactly one copy gives an exact mixed-integer representation of a finite union of bounded polyhedra.
assumptions_latex: \(P_k=\{u:A^ku\leq b^k\}\) is nonempty and bounded for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\bigcup_{k=1}^KP_k\) holds exactly when the displayed disaggregated system is feasible.

notation.meaning: Variable copy assigned to alternative k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-polyhedron disaggregation is mathematically sound and correctly classified as a representation, but it has no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Product Linearization Families
children.top_down_role: Representations for products involving binary, integer, and continuous variables.

children.title: Binary–Binary Product Linearization
children.top_down_role: Representations of Boolean interactions and quadratic binary terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Binary Product Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear graph of one binary product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), introduce \(w\in\mathbb{R}\). The nonlinear equality \(w=xy\) is represented exactly by \[w\leq x,\qquad w\leq y,\qquad w\geq x+y-1,\qquad w\geq0.\] Every feasible binary pair determines \(w\) uniquely: \(w=1\) precisely when \(x=y=1\), and \(w=0\) otherwise. The continuous relaxation of these inequalities is the convex hull of \(\{(x,y,w)\in\{0,1\}^2\times\mathbb{R}:w=xy\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four linear inequalities exactly represent the product of two binary variables and describe the convex hull of its graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are equivalent to \(w=xy\) for binary \(x,y\), and their relaxation is the graph's convex hull.

children.title: Binary–Continuous Product Linearization
children.top_down_role: Bound-dependent representations of on–off continuous terms.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Continuous Product Linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact bounded on–off product formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(L\leq x\leq U\), and introduce \(w\in\mathbb{R}\). The equality \(w=zx\) is represented exactly by \[Lz\leq w\leq Uz,\qquad x-U(1-z)\leq w\leq x-L(1-z).\] If \(z=0\), the first pair forces \(w=0\); if \(z=1\), the second pair forces \(w=x\). Thus the inequalities describe the convex hull of the bounded on–off graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four bound-dependent inequalities exactly linearize a binary variable multiplied by a bounded continuous variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system is equivalent to \(w=zx\) and gives the convex hull of the bounded product graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bound-dependent binary-continuous product formulation and convex-hull claim are correct, but no inspectable source reference is provided.

children.title: Bounded-Integer Product Encodings
children.top_down_role: Expansion and disaggregation routes for products involving bounded integers.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer Product Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary expansion of a bounded nonnegative integer factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\in\mathbb{Z}\) satisfy \(0\leq p\leq U\), let \(L\leq y\leq H\), and set \(K=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\). Introduce \(z_k\in\{0,1\}\) and \(w_k\in\mathbb{R}\) with \(p=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}2^kz_k\) and \(p\leq U\). For every \(k\), impose the exact binary–continuous product inequalities for \(w_k=z_ky\). Then \[w=\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}2^kw_k\] represents \(w=py\) exactly. The encoding uses \(K\) binary digits and \(K\) auxiliary product variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary expansion reduces a bounded-integer product to logarithmically many exact binary–continuous product linearizations.
assumptions_latex: Each \(w_k=z_ky\) uses the bounded product formulation.

notation.meaning: Binary digit of the bounded integer p.
Linearized product of digit z_k and y.

children.title: Assignment-Interaction Linearization Family

children.title: Fortet Linearizations

knowledge_statements.title: Fortet Linearizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fortet inequalities for pairwise binary interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary variables \(x_i,x_j\), an interaction variable \(y_{ij}\) represents \(x_ix_j\) exactly when \[y_{ij}\leq x_i,\qquad y_{ij}\leq x_j,\qquad y_{ij}\geq x_i+x_j-1,\qquad y_{ij}\geq0.\] Applying these Fortet inequalities to every quadratic monomial replaces a binary quadratic expression \(\sum_{(i,j)}q_{ij}x_ix_j\) by the linear expression \(\sum_{(i,j)}q_{ij}y_{ij}\) without changing its value at integer-feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fortet inequalities replace each pairwise binary product by an auxiliary variable that is exact at every binary solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities force \(y_{ij}=x_ix_j\), so quadratic binary terms may be replaced linearly.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linearizability of 0-1 polynomial programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended linear reformulation when all original variables are binary and the objective and constraints are polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\) be polynomials. Every program \[\min\{f(x):g_i(x)=0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\}\] can be formulated equivalently as a pure \(0\)-\(1\) linear program by introducing additional variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every polynomial program over binary variables, with polynomial equality constraints, has an equivalent pure binary linear formulation in an extended variable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ an equivalent pure }0\text{-}1\text{ linear formulation obtained by introducing additional variables}.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite index sets of equal cardinality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearization of a specified set of pairwise interactions in a finite assignment matrix.

source_refs.locator: 2.12 The Quadratic Assignment Problem and Fortet's Linearization p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets of equal cardinality, and let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\), \((i,j)\in I\times J\), satisfy \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(i\in I\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\) for every \(j\in J\). Let \(E\subseteq(I\times J)\times(I\times J)\) be a specified interaction set. For each \(((i,j),(k,\ell))\in E\), introduce \(y_{ijk\ell}\in\mathbb{R}\) and impose \[0\leq y_{ijk\ell}\leq x_{ij},\qquad y_{ijk\ell}\leq x_{k\ell},\qquad y_{ijk\ell}\geq x_{ij}+x_{k\ell}-1.\] At every integer assignment, these inequalities give \(y_{ijk\ell}=x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\). Therefore an objective \(\sum_{((i,j),(k,\ell))\in E}c_{ijk\ell}x_{ij}x_{k\ell}\), with \(c_{ijk\ell}\in\mathbb{R}\), is replaced exactly by \(\sum_{((i,j),(k,\ell))\in E}c_{ijk\ell}y_{ijk\ell}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finite assignment index sets and a specified interaction set, Fortet variables replace every retained quadratic assignment product exactly at integer assignments.

children.title: Interaction-Symmetry Variants

assumptions_latex: \(V=I\times J\) is a finite assignment-index set.
\(E\subseteq V\times V\) is closed under reversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing each reversed pair of off-diagonal terms by one variable with coefficient \(c_{ab}+c_{ba}\), and replacing each diagonal product by \(x_a\), preserves every integer objective value.

notation.meaning: Binary assignment variable indexed by a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry reduction for a finite reversal-closed set of assignment interactions.

source_refs.locator: 2.12 The Quadratic Assignment Problem and Fortet's Linearization p. 72

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=I\times J\) be a finite assignment-index set, let \(x_a\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(a\in V\), and let \(E\subseteq V\times V\) be closed under reversal. Consider the ordered interaction expression \(\sum_{(a,b)\in E}c_{ab}x_ax_b\). For every distinct pair \(a,b\in V\), commutativity gives \(x_ax_b=x_bx_a\), so the two reversed terms may use one product variable \(y_{\{a,b\}}\) with combined coefficient \(c_{ab}+c_{ba}\). For a diagonal interaction, \(x_a^2=x_a\). Consequently, retaining one exact product variable for each unordered off-diagonal pair and simplifying diagonal terms preserves the objective value at every integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reversal-closed assignment objective needs only one exact interaction variable per unordered off-diagonal pair; reversed coefficients are combined and diagonal binary products are simplified.
