children.title: Incumbent Validation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Hooks for validating, rejecting, or completing candidate integer solutions.

assumptions_latex: A candidate \(\bar x\) satisfies the solver's explicit constraints and declared integrality requirements.
The validator tests every external condition required for membership in the intended feasible set \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validator's acceptance is a verifiable feasibility certificate for \(\bar x\in F\); rejection must prevent \(\bar x\) from becoming an incumbent.

notation.meaning: intended feasible set including externally checked conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility validation and optional completion of candidate integer solutions before incumbent acceptance.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\bar x\), the interface returns exactly one of three outcomes: accept, reject with a violated globally valid condition, or complete. Acceptance is permitted only after certifying \(\bar x\in F\). Rejection supplies a condition valid for every point of \(F\) that excludes \(\bar x\), or otherwise marks the candidate unusable without incorrectly pruning other feasible points. Completion returns \(\widehat x\in F\) whose fixed components agree with the prescribed components of \(\bar x\); the solver evaluates and stores \(\widehat x\), not the uncompleted vector. Any objective value reported for acceptance must be computed from the same feasible vector that is installed as the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validation hook accepts only fully feasible candidates, rejects invalid ones without excluding other feasible solutions, or completes partial candidates into feasible vectors whose actual objective values are recorded.
knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Validation Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role is defensible for the acceptance result, and the feasibility-validation portion is plausible. However, the cited generic branch-and-cut section does not specifically support the asserted three-outcome interface, partial-solution completion semantics, component agreement, or incumbent installation behavior. Those details require an inspectable solver-interface or algorithm source.

children.title: Solver-Recognizable Structure Family
children.top_down_role: Modeling structures revealing reductions, implications, aggregation, and interchangeable objects.

children.title: Presolve Inference Exposure Interface
children.top_down_role: Representations exposing finite bounds, implications, eliminable variables, and aggregations.

children.title: Bound-Propagation Exposure
children.top_down_role: Model structures that make variable-bound implications visible.

assumptions_latex: Variable bounds satisfy \(l_j\le x_j\le u_j\), and a row \(a^\top x\le b\) is present.
All quantities used in the update are finite, and \(a_k\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed update is valid and never removes a point satisfying the row and the original bounds.

notation.meaning: minimum contribution of variable \(j\) to the row

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-row interval propagation for a linear inequality with finite variable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k=\sum_{j\ne k}m_j\). If \(a_k>0\), every feasible point satisfies \(x_k\le (b-s_k)/a_k\), so the exposed propagation is \(u_k\leftarrow\min\{u_k,(b-s_k)/a_k\}\). If \(a_k<0\), every feasible point satisfies \(x_k\ge (b-s_k)/a_k\), so use \(l_k\leftarrow\max\{l_k,(b-s_k)/a_k\}\). For an integer variable, round a derived upper bound downward and a derived lower bound upward. Applying these updates repeatedly until no bound changes computes a propagation fixed point for the chosen collection of row inference rules; it need not yield all bounds implied by the complete formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear row and the other variables' bounds imply a tighter bound on each variable. Integer bounds are rounded inward, and repeated propagation stops at a rule-dependent fixed point.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Propagation Exposure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role and single-row bound formulas fit the terminal container and are mathematically plausible under the stated finite-bound assumptions. No source is supplied, however, and the integer-rounding and repeated-closure claims require an authoritative presolve or propagation locator.

children.title: Substitution Exposure
children.top_down_role: Model structures that reveal eliminable variables or expressions.

assumptions_latex: The formulation contains an equality \(a_kx_k+\sum_{j\ne k}a_jx_j=b\) with \(a_k\ne0\).
Substitution preserves the declared domains of all remaining variables or adds the necessary induced restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating \(x_k\) by the displayed identity preserves a bijection between feasible assignments before and after elimination.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of a variable exposed by a linear equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The equality gives the exact representation \[x_k=\frac{b-
obreak\sum_{j\ne k}a_jx_j}{a_k}.\] Replace every occurrence of \(x_k\) in the objective and remaining constraints by this affine expression, then remove \(x_k\) and its defining equality. Bounds or integrality on \(x_k\) become induced conditions on \(x_{-k}\); for example, \(l_k\le x_k\le u_k\) must be retained after substitution. If \(x_k\) is integer, the affine expression must be integral for every retained feasible assignment, or an equivalent divisibility condition must be imposed. Omitting such induced conditions can enlarge the feasible set and makes the substitution inexact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality can eliminate one variable by affine substitution, provided all induced bounds, integrality, and divisibility restrictions are retained. Then feasible solutions correspond exactly before and after elimination.
knowledge_statements.title: Substitution Exposure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits exact equality-based elimination, and the record correctly notes induced bounds and divisibility restrictions. Because no source is supplied, the exact mixed-integer substitution conditions and bijection claim cannot be admitted at candidate-review status.

children.title: Aggregation Exposure
children.top_down_role: Model structures that reveal combinable rows, columns, or relations.

assumptions_latex: Two valid rows are \(a^\top x\le b\) and \(c^\top x\le d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The aggregate row \((\lambda a+\mu c)^\top x\le\lambda b+\mu d\) is valid for every point satisfying both original rows.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and elimination role of nonnegative linear-row aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Multiplying the two inequalities by \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\) and adding yields \[(\lambda a+\mu c)^\top x\le
otag\lambda b+
obreak\mu d.\] Thus the aggregate may be exposed as an additional valid row. If \(\lambda a_k+
obreak\mu c_k=0\), the variable \(x_k\) is absent from the aggregate, which can reveal a constraint on the remaining variables. Replacing the original rows by the aggregate alone is generally not equivalent because their conjunction implies the aggregate but the converse can fail. Exact presolve deletion therefore requires a separate redundancy or reconstruction certificate; mere validity of the aggregate is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative combination of valid inequalities is valid and may cancel a variable. The aggregate may be added safely, but it cannot generally replace its source rows without an equivalence certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation Exposure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits aggregation exposure and the validity claim is standard, but no source supports the presolve replacement and reconstruction boundary. The display also uses \(\notag\) within an ordinary display expression, where it is unnecessary and potentially invalid for the renderer.

children.title: Propagation–Substitution Interaction
children.top_down_role: Structural effects linking bound inference with variable elimination.

assumptions_latex: Every propagation update is valid for the current formulation.
Every substitution is an exact feasible-set-preserving elimination including induced domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interleaving the operations preserves the original feasible set under reconstruction, but a propagation fixed point before substitution need not remain a fixed point afterward.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order dependence of valid presolve inference under alternating bound propagation and exact substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a formulation state \(M\), both compositions \(P(S(M))\) and \(S(P(M))\) are exact with respect to reconstructed feasible solutions when their component operations satisfy the assumptions. They need not expose identical intermediate bounds or rows: substitution can combine coefficients and remove variables, thereby enabling propagation unavailable in \(M\), while propagated bounds can make a defining equality or fixed variable eligible for substitution. Consequently \(P\circ S\) and \(S\circ P\) need not commute. A presolve interface seeking closure under these rules should alternate them until neither operation changes the represented formulation, while retaining a reconstruction map for every eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid propagation and exact substitution preserve feasible solutions, but their order can change which further inferences become visible. Alternating them to a fixed point requires reconstruction data for eliminated variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation–Substitution Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits the interaction leaf, but no source is supplied for the noncommutativity and closure claims. Moreover, an instruction to alternate until neither operation changes the formulation needs termination or convergence conditions if it is intended as an algorithmic guarantee.

children.title: Redundant-Structure Strengthening Interface
children.top_down_role: Additional valid structure included to improve inference or relaxation quality.

children.title: Redundant Valid Structure
children.top_down_role: Additional valid relations retained to expose useful model structure.

assumptions_latex: A base formulation has feasible set \(F=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\le 0\text{ for every }i\in I\}\).
An additional relation \(h(x)\le 0\) holds for every \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Adding \(h(x)\le 0\) leaves the feasible set unchanged and is therefore redundant in the exact formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy relative to the exact feasible set, independent of relaxation or computational usefulness.

source_refs.locator: 7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relation \(h(x)\le 0\) is redundant and valid for the formulation precisely when \[F=\{x\in D:g_i(x)\le 0\text{ for every }i\in I,\ h(x)\le 0\}.\] Equivalently, the original constraints and domain imply \(h(x)\le 0\). Redundancy is relative to the declared domain: a relation implied only after enforcing integrality can be redundant for the mixed-integer feasible set while cutting points from its continuous relaxation. Adding a redundant valid relation therefore cannot remove any intended feasible solution, although it may change the relaxation, presolve deductions, numerical behavior, or representation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relation is redundant and valid when every feasible point already satisfies it, so adding it leaves the exact feasible set unchanged even though the relaxation or solver behavior may improve.
knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Valid Structure

source_witnesses.locator: 7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

children.title: Relaxation Strengthening
children.top_down_role: Additional structure intended to improve continuous relaxation quality.

assumptions_latex: The exact feasible set is \(F\), and the original continuous relaxation is \(P\supseteq F\).
The added inequalities define a set \(H\) satisfying \(F\subseteq H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strengthened relaxation \(P'=P\cap H\) is valid, and its minimization lower bound is at least that of \(P\).

notation.meaning: set imposed by added valid inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set inclusion and objective-bound effect of redundant valid inequalities in a minimization model.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Cut Strengthening p. 86
7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(F\subseteq P'\subseteq P\), the added inequalities preserve every integer-feasible solution while possibly deleting relaxation points. For a minimization objective \(c^\top x\), \[\inf_{x\in P}c^\top x\le \inf_{x\in P'}c^\top x\le \inf_{x\in F}c^\top x.\] Thus the relaxation bound cannot weaken. The strengthening is strict as a set exactly when some point of \(P\) violates an added inequality. Strict set inclusion does not guarantee a strictly improved bound for a particular objective, because all removed points may be nonoptimal for that objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting a relaxation with inequalities valid for every integer-feasible point preserves validity and cannot worsen a minimization lower bound. A strictly smaller relaxation need not improve every objective bound strictly.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strengthening

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Cut Strengthening p. 86
7.5 Using a Branch-and-Bound/Cut System p. 123

children.title: Inference Enhancement
children.top_down_role: Additional structure intended to improve propagation or presolve deductions.

assumptions_latex: A redundant relation \(r\) is valid for the exact feasible set.
A specified inference operator \(Q\) maps a formulation to its derived bounds, fixings, or domain reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Adding \(r\) enhances inference under \(Q\) exactly when \(Q(M
otag\cup
otag\{r
otag\})\) yields a strictly stronger valid domain reduction than \(Q(M)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-relative enhancement of presolve or propagation caused by an exact-feasible-set redundant relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_Q(M)\) denote the variable domain remaining after applying \(Q\) to closure on \(M\). Since \(r\) is valid, both \(D_Q(M)\) and \(D_Q(M
otag\cup
otag\{r
otag\})\) must contain every feasible assignment. The relation provides inference enhancement for \(Q\) when \[D_Q(M
otag\cup
otag\{r
otag\})
otag\subsetneq D_Q(M).\] This is a property of the pair consisting of the representation and the inference operator, not of the feasible set alone. A mathematically redundant row may expose coefficient patterns, implications, or short propagation paths recognized by \(Q\), yet provide no enhancement to a stronger operator that already derives the same closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant relation enhances inference when a specified solver inference procedure derives strictly tighter valid domains after the relation is added. The effect depends on both representation and inference procedure.
knowledge_statements.title: Inference Enhancement

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle role fits this solver-relative inference leaf, and the record appropriately conditions enhancement on a specified operator. No source is supplied for the closure construction or strict-domain criterion, and the statement uses unnecessary \(\notag\) commands in set and display expressions. An authoritative presolve or constraint-propagation source is required before the mathematical formulation can be settled.

children.title: Redundancy Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Size, degeneracy, or processing costs associated with extra valid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Cost Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates representation-size costs from possible search benefits of redundant valid structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an optimization formulation have relaxation \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), and append the redundant system \(Dx\le d\), where \(P\subseteq\{x:Dx\le d\}\). The feasible region and every relaxation optimum are unchanged. If \(A\) and \(D\) contain respectively \(s_A\) and \(s_D\) stored nonzeros, the explicit constraint representation grows from \(s_A\) to \(s_A+s_D\). Consequently redundancy has an unavoidable positive storage and input-processing cost whenever \(s_D>0\); any overall computational gain must arise from solver-dependent inference, propagation, cutting, or search-tree reduction and is not implied by validity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant constraints preserve feasibility but enlarge the explicit representation; they are worthwhile only when solver inference or search savings offset that cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Dx\le d\}\) and the stored-nonzero increase is \(s_D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasible-set identity and stored-nonzero increase are mathematically clear, but the claimed unavoidable positive input-processing cost and the solver-dependent benefit boundary have no cited source. A solver-facing cost reference with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Model Symmetry Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Interchangeability arising from variables, labels, resources, or modeled objects.

children.title: Variable Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Interchangeability among variables with equivalent modeled roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-permutation symmetry of an optimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an optimization problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\) with \(X\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), a variable symmetry is a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that the coordinate action \((\sigma x)_i=x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}\) is well-defined and satisfies \(x\in X\iff \sigma x\in X\) and \(f(\sigma x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). A variable-symmetry group is a subgroup of all such permutations under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variable symmetry permutes coordinates while preserving the feasible set and objective value.
assumptions_latex: The coordinate permutation maps the ambient product into itself.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X\iff \sigma x\in X\) and \(f(\sigma x)=f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate-permutation definition is precise and fits the Variable Symmetry leaf, but no inspectable authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Value Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Interchangeability among labels or values assigned within a model.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry acting on variable values rather than only coordinate positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), let \(\tau_i:D_i\to D_i\) be bijections and define \((\tau x)_i=\tau_i(x_i)\). The tuple \(\tau=(\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_n)\) is a value symmetry of \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\) when \(x\in X\iff \tau x\in X\) and \(f(\tau x)=f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus transformed assignments occur in feasibility- and objective-equivalent orbits even though variable indices remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value symmetry bijectively relabels admissible values at fixed coordinates while preserving feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in X\iff \tau x\in X\) and \(f(\tau x)=f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Bijection of the i-th value domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The componentwise value-relabeling definition is internally consistent and fits the Value Symmetry leaf, but it lacks an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Object Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Interchangeability among modeled resources, entities, or structural objects.

assumptions_latex: A finite object set \(O\) is represented in the formulation.
A group \(G\) acts on \(O\) by permutations and induces an action on the assignment space containing \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For an object-symmetry action, \(x\in X\iff gx\in X\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Assignment induced by relabeling objects with g

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relabeling symmetry induced by interchangeable modeled objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a formulation encode a finite object set \(O\), and let a group \(G\) act on \(O\) by permutations. Suppose these relabelings induce an action \(x\mapsto gx\) on the assignment space. The induced action is an object-symmetry action for \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\) if \(x\in X\iff gx\in X\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\). An individual \(g\in G\) satisfying these conditions is an object symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An object-symmetry action relabels modeled entities while preserving the feasible set and objective value for every group element.
knowledge_statements.title: Object Symmetry

children.title: Mixed Symmetry Actions
children.top_down_role: Symmetry actions simultaneously affecting multiple modeled entity types.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts on the assignment space \(D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\).
For every \(g\in G\) and index \(i\), the map \(\tau_{g,i}:D_{\sigma_g^{-1}(i)}\to D_i\) is a bijection compatible with the group action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(gX=X\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Bijection from the source coordinate domain to the target coordinate domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Group actions combining coordinate and value transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\), let \(G\) act on the assignment space. Suppose each \(g\in G\) acts by \((gx)_i=\tau_{g,i}(x_{\sigma_g^{-1}(i)})\), where \(\sigma_g\) is a permutation of the indices and \(\tau_{g,i}:D_{\sigma_g^{-1}(i)}\to D_i\) is a bijection, with these maps satisfying the group-action law. This is a mixed symmetry action for \(\min\{f(x):x\in X\}\) when \(gX=X\) and \(f(gx)=f(x)\) for every \(g\in G\) and \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed symmetry combines coordinate permutations with compatible value bijections and acts as a group while preserving the feasible set and objective value.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Symmetry Actions

children.title: Symmetry-Breaking Formulations
children.top_down_role: Ordering, canonicalization, and representative-selection structures.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible subset selected by symmetry-breaking constraints

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative-selection formulation for a finite symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite group \(G\) act on a feasible set \(X\) and preserve an objective function \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\). A symmetry-breaking formulation adds constraints defining \(S\subseteq X\) such that \(S\cap(Gx)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in X\), where \(Gx=\{gx:g\in G\}\). Then \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). If additionally \(|S\cap(Gx)|=1\) for every orbit, the formulation selects a unique representative from each orbit; otherwise it provides partial symmetry breaking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetry-breaking constraints retain at least one point from every orbit and preserve the objective infimum; exact breaking retains one representative per orbit.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Breaking Formulations

children.title: Polyhedral Geometry
children.top_down_role: Foundational geometric structure of linear feasible regions.

assumptions_latex: The ambient space is finite-dimensional and \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\iff P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R)\) for suitable finite data.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Minkowski-Weyl representation of nonempty polyhedra.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8. The structure of polyhedra p. 99
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty. The set \(P\) is a polyhedron if and only if there exist finite sets \(V,R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[P=\operatorname{conv}(V)+\operatorname{cone}(R).\] Equivalently, there exist a matrix \(A\) and vector \(b\) such that \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\). For such a representation, \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\operatorname{cone}(R)=\{r\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ar\le0\}\). The polyhedron \(P\) is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional polyhedron is equivalently a finite intersection of halfspaces or the sum of a finite convex hull and a finitely generated cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8. The structure of polyhedra p. 99

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal Complement of a Subspace
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Context-dependent notation whose antecedent is the orthogonal subspace constructed in the immediately preceding proposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a subspace $H\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, the orthogonal subspace $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x^\top y=0\text{ for every }y\in H\}$ is denoted by $H^\perp$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subspace consisting of all vectors orthogonal to every vector in H is called the orthogonal subspace of H and is denoted H⊥.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H^\perp:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\forall y\in H)\ x^\top y=0\}.

children.title: Face Structure
children.top_down_role: Facial organization relevant to formulation strength and dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Face Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed-face definition and the induced face lattice of a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. A nonempty set \(F\subseteq P\) is a face of \(P\) if there exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) for all \(x\in P\) and \(F=\{x\in P:a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\}\). Including \(\varnothing\) and \(P\), the faces ordered by inclusion form the face lattice. Zero-dimensional faces are vertices, and codimension-one proper faces are facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the subset where a valid linear inequality is tight; faces ordered by inclusion form the polyhedron’s face lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a nonempty face exactly when \(F=P\cap\{x:a^{\mathsf T}x=\beta\}\) for a valid inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum Face Dimension from Constraint-Matrix Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General polyhedral geometry; faces are understood to be nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing. If \operatorname{rank}(A)=n-k, then P has a face of dimension k, and no proper nonempty face of P has dimension less than k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a nonempty polyhedron has a constraint matrix of rank n−k, it has a k-dimensional face and no proper nonempty face of smaller dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists F\unlhd P:\dim F=k,\qquad \nexists G\lhd P:\ G\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \dim G<k

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces of a polyhedron: equivalent characterizations and basic properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polyhedral face theory, stated for a nonempty inequality-form polyhedron; extraction-grounded evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) be nonempty and let \(F\subseteq P\). Then \(F\) is a face of \(P\) if and only if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\max_{x\in P}c^\top x\) is finite and \(F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^\top x\); allowing \(c=0\) includes \(F=P\). Equivalently, \(F\ne\varnothing\) and \(F=\{x\in P:A'x=b'\}\) for some subsystem \(A'x\le b'\) of \(Ax\le b\). Consequently, \(P\) has finitely many faces, every face is a nonempty polyhedron, and whenever \(F\) is a face of \(P\) and \(F'\subseteq F\), \(F'\) is a face of \(P\) if and only if \(F'\) is a face of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polyhedron, the faces are exactly the maximizer sets of finite linear objectives, with the zero objective yielding the whole polyhedron. Equivalently, a face is a nonempty subset obtained by making a subsystem of the defining inequalities tight. A polyhedron has finitely many faces; each face is a nonempty polyhedron; and a subset of a face is a face of the original polyhedron exactly when it is a face of that face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a face of }P\iff \exists c\in\mathbb R^n:\ \max_{x\in P}c^\top x<\infty\ \land\ F=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^\top x\iff \exists\text{ a subsystem }A'x\le b':\ F\ne\varnothing\ \land\ F=\{x\in P:A'x=b'\};\quad |\mathcal F(P)|<\infty,\ \forall G\in\mathcal F(P),\ G\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron},\ \text{and }F'\subseteq F\in\mathcal F(P)\Rightarrow\bigl(F'\in\mathcal F(P)\iff F'\in\mathcal F(F)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal faces of a polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimal faces and states their affine-subspace characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron and let \(F\) be a nonempty face of \(P\). Then \(F\) is a minimal face if it contains no distinct face of \(P\) properly contained in \(F\). Moreover, \[F\text{ is a minimal face of }P\iff F\text{ is an affine subspace}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty face is minimal when it contains no distinct proper face of the polyhedron. A face is minimal exactly when it is an affine subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is minimal}\iff F\text{ is an affine subspace}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural properties of the faces of a polyhedron
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects finiteness, lineality, face-lattice, affine-hull, dimension, and hereditary-face properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every polyhedron \(P\): (i) \(P\) has finitely many faces; (ii) every nonempty face \(F\) satisfies \(\operatorname{lin}(F)=\operatorname{lin}(P)\); (iii) for faces \(F,F'\), \(F\cap F'\) is a face and there is a unique minimal face containing \(F\cup F'\); (iv) \(F\neq F'\) if and only if \(\operatorname{aff}(F)\neq\operatorname{aff}(F')\); (v) if \(F\subsetneq F'\), then \(\dim F\leq\dim F'-1\); and (vi) the faces of a face \(F\) are exactly the faces of \(P\) contained in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedron has finitely many faces. Its nonempty faces share its lineality space; face intersections and unique minimal common containing faces exist; distinct faces have distinct affine hulls; strict face inclusion lowers dimension; and the faces of a face are exactly the ambient faces contained in it.
assumptions_latex: F,F'\text{ are faces of }P\text{ where applicable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
|\mathcal F(P)|<\infty;\ F
eq\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{lin}(F)=\operatorname{lin}(P);\ F\cap F'\in\mathcal F(P);\ F
eq F'\iff\operatorname{aff}(F)
eq\operatorname{aff}(F');\ F\subsetneq F'\Rightarrow\dim F\leq\dim F'-1;\ \mathcal F(F)=\{G\in\mathcal F(P):G\subseteq F\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposition of a Nonempty Polyhedron by Minimal Faces, Recession Directions, and Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded general polyhedral decomposition theorem whose canonical ownership belongs with continuous polyhedral geometry in convex analysis; the packet supplies no precise A02 parent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{x\mid Ax\le b\}\neq\varnothing\). For every minimal face \(F\) of \(P\), choose an arbitrary \(x_F\in F\). For every minimal proper face \(F\) of \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\), choose an arbitrary \(y_F\in F\setminus\operatorname{lin}(P)\). Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) generate \(\operatorname{lin}(P)\). Then
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}\{x_F:F\text{ is a minimal face of }P\}+\operatorname{cone}\{y_F:F\text{ is a minimal proper face of }\operatorname{rec}(P)\}+\operatorname{span}\{z_1,\ldots,z_t\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty polyhedron equals the Minkowski sum of the convex hull of one arbitrary point from each minimal face, the cone generated by one nonlineality direction from each minimal proper face of its recession cone, and its lineality space.
assumptions_latex: x_F\in F\quad\text{for every minimal face }F\text{ of }P
y_F\in F\setminus\operatorname{lin}(P)\quad\text{for every minimal proper face }F\text{ of }\operatorname{rec}(P)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}\{x_F:F\text{ minimal in }P\}+\operatorname{cone}\{y_F:F\text{ minimal proper in }\operatorname{rec}(P)\}+\operatorname{span}\{z_1,\ldots,z_t\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face and Proper Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a face exposed by equality in a valid inequality, including the proper-face condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\pi^{\top}x\leq\pi_0\) is valid for \(P\), then \(F=\{x\in P:\pi^{\top}x=\pi_0\}\) is a face of \(P\), represented by \((\pi,\pi_0)\). It is proper if \(F\neq\varnothing\) and \(F\neq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The points of P attaining equality in a valid inequality form a face represented by that inequality. The face is proper when it is nonempty and is not all of P.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F:=\{x\in P:\pi^{\top}x=\pi_0\}\text{ is a face of }P,\qquad F\text{ is proper}\iff F\neq\varnothing\ \land\ F\neq P

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertices and pointed polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a vertex and the vertex-existence criterion for a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron. A face of \(P\) having dimension \(0\) is a vertex of \(P\). Furthermore, \(P\) has a vertex if and only if \(\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\), equivalently, if and only if \(P\) is pointed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex is a zero-dimensional face. A nonempty polyhedron has a vertex exactly when its lineality space is trivial, equivalently when it is pointed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a vertex of }P\iff F\text{ is a face of }P\text{ and }\dim(F)=0;\qquad P\text{ has a vertex}\iff\operatorname{lin}(P)=\{0\}\iff P\text{ is pointed}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal Proper Faces of a Polyhedral Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines minimal proper faces through the lineality dimension and identifies them with extremal rays in the pointed case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{x\mid Ax\leq 0\}\) be a polyhedral cone, and let \(t=\dim(\operatorname{lin}(C))\). The unique minimal face of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{lin}(C)\). A face of \(C\) of dimension \(t+1\) is called a minimal proper face. If \(t=0\), the minimal proper faces of \(C\) are precisely its extremal rays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral cone C, the lineality space is its unique minimal face. If that space has dimension t, a face of dimension t+1 is called a minimal proper face. When t is zero, these faces are precisely the extremal rays of C.
assumptions_latex: C=\{x\mid Ax\leq 0\}\text{ is a polyhedral cone}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lin}(C)\text{ is the unique minimal face of }C;\quad \dim(F)=t+1\Rightarrow F\text{ is a minimal proper face};\quad t=0\Rightarrow \{\text{minimal proper faces of }C\}=\{\text{extremal rays of }C\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine witnesses for a face of a convex hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the dimension of a face of a convex hull through affinely independent generating points on its defining hyperplane.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\pi x\leq \pi_0\) defines a face of dimension \(k-1\) of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), then there exist \(k\) affinely independent points \(x^1,\ldots,x^k\in S\) such that \(\pi x^i=\pi_0\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an inequality defines a face of dimension k−1 of the convex hull of S, its defining hyperplane contains k affinely independent points of S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x^1,\ldots,x^k\in S\) affinely independent such that \(\pi x^i=\pi_0\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimal faces are translates of the lineality space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the direction space of a minimal face and the rank of a subsystem equality representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\), and let \(F\) be a minimal face of \(P\). For every \(x_0\in F\), \[F=x_0+\operatorname{lin}(P),\qquad \operatorname{lin}(P)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ad=0\}.\] If \(F=\{x:A'x=b'\}\) for a subsystem \(A'x\le b'\) of \(Ax\le b\), then \[\ker A'=\operatorname{lin}(P)\quad\text{and}\quad \operatorname{rank}(A')=\operatorname{rank}(A).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimal face is a translate of the polyhedron's lineality space. If it is represented by making a subsystem tight, that subsystem has the same kernel as the lineality space and the same rank as the full constraint matrix.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a minimal face of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=x_0+\operatorname{lin}(P),\quad \ker A'=\operatorname{lin}(P),\quad \operatorname{rank}(A')=\operatorname{rank}(A)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, supporting hyperplanes, proper faces, and facets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for arbitrary polyhedra, including the empty face and the whole polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron. A face of \(P\) is a set \(F=P\cap\{x:cx=\delta\}\), where \(cx\leq\delta\) is valid for \(P\); the inequality defines \(F\). If \(c\neq0\) and \(F\neq\varnothing\), then \(\{x:cx=\delta\}\) is a supporting hyperplane of \(P\). Every face is a polyhedron, and both \(\varnothing\) and \(P\) are faces. A proper face is nonempty and properly contained in \(P\). A facet is an inclusionwise maximal proper face, and a valid inequality defining a facet is facet-defining. Every proper face is contained in a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the equality set of a valid inequality within a polyhedron. A nonzero valid inequality attaining equality on a nonempty face gives a supporting hyperplane. The empty set and the whole polyhedron are faces. Facets are maximal nonempty strict faces, and inequalities defining them are facet-defining.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F=P\cap\{x:cx=\delta\}\text{ is a face of }P;\quad \varnothing,P\text{ are faces; facets are maximal proper faces}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, supporting hyperplanes, facets, vertices, and edges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General facial terminology for a full-dimensional convex polytope, following the source's supporting-halfspace formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a convex polytope with \(\dim P=d\). Let \(HS\) be a closed halfspace bounded by a hyperplane \(H\). If \(f=P\cap HS\subseteq H\), then \(f\) is a face of \(P\), and \(H\) is a supporting hyperplane defining \(f\). A face of dimension \(d-1\) is a facet, a face of dimension \(0\) is a vertex, and a face of dimension \(1\) is an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a closed halfspace intersects a full-dimensional convex polytope only in the halfspace's boundary hyperplane, that intersection is a face and the hyperplane is supporting. Faces of dimensions d−1, 0, and 1 are called facets, vertices, and edges, respectively.
assumptions_latex: HS\text{ is a closed halfspace bounded by the hyperplane }H
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a face of }P\text{ supported by }H;\quad \dim f=d-1,0,1\text{ yields a facet, vertex, or edge, respectively.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterization of faces by active defining inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes all nonempty faces of a nonempty finitely described polyhedron; an arbitrary activated subset may produce the empty face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^ix\leq b_i,\ i\in M\}\neq\varnothing\). For every \(I\subseteq M\), the set \(F_I=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^ix=b_i\ (i\in I),\ a^ix\leq b_i\ (i\in M\setminus I)\}\) is a face of \(P\). Conversely, every nonempty face \(F\) of \(P\) equals \(F_I\) for some \(I\subseteq M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Activating any subset of the inequalities describing a nonempty polyhedron produces a face, possibly the empty face. Conversely, every nonempty face is obtained by activating some subset of the defining inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_I\text{ is a face of }P,\qquad \forall F\neq\varnothing\text{ face of }P\;\exists I\subseteq M:\ F=F_I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Face lattice and dimensions in maximal chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-lattice and rank structure of a polyhedron, including nonpointed polyhedra with lineality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $P$ be a polyhedron. The faces of $P$, together with $\varnothing$, form a lattice under inclusion. If $\dim P=k$ and the lineality space of $P$ has dimension $t$, then every maximal chain in the face lattice contains $\varnothing$ and exactly one face of each dimension $t,t+1,\ldots,k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The faces of a polyhedron, together with the empty set, form a lattice under inclusion. If the polyhedron has dimension k and its lineality space has dimension t, every maximal chain contains the empty set and exactly one face of each dimension from t through k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal F(P)\cup\{\varnothing\}\text{ is a lattice under inclusion, and every maximal chain contains }\varnothing\text{ and exactly one face of each dimension }t,t+1,\ldots,k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faces, facets, and face-defining inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions of faces and facets of a polyhedron and of inequalities representing faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron. A set \(F\) defines a face of \(P\) if there exist \(\pi\) and \(\pi_0\) such that \(\pi x\leq\pi_0\) is valid for \(P\) and \(F=\{x\in P:\pi x=\pi_0\}\). A face \(F\) is a facet of \(P\) if \(\dim(F)=\dim(P)-1\). Whenever a face has the displayed representation, the valid inequality \(\pi x\leq\pi_0\) represents or defines that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is the equality set in a polyhedron of some valid inequality. A face is a facet when its dimension is one less than the polyhedron's dimension. The corresponding valid inequality represents or defines the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a face of }P\iff \exists(\pi,\pi_0)\;[\pi x\leq\pi_0\text{ is valid for }P\ \land\ F=\{x\in P:\pi x=\pi_0\}],\quad F\text{ is a facet of }P\iff [F\text{ is a face of }P\ \land\ \dim(F)=\dim(P)-1].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+m}:Ax+By\le b\}\) be a polyhedron. Its coordinate projection onto the \(x\)-space is \[\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ Ax+By\le b\}.\] This projection is a polyhedron, so there exist a finite matrix \(C\) and vector \(d\) such that \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Cx\le d\}\). More generally, the image of a polyhedron under a linear map between finite-dimensional real vector spaces is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existentially eliminating variables from a finite-dimensional polyhedron, or applying a linear map to it, yields another polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate projection and auxiliary-variable elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projection, objective equivalence, elimination descriptions, and possible exponential growth after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\), define \(\operatorname{proj}_x(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists z\in\mathbb R^p\text{ with }(x,z)\in S\}\). For any \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), the projected and lifted problems have the same attainable objective values and the same optimal \(x\)-vectors. If \(P=\{(x,z):Ax+Gz\le b\}\), Fourier elimination of all components of \(z\) produces a system \(A^*x\le b^*\) satisfying \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)=\{x:A^*x\le b^*\}\). There exist families for which an irredundant description of \(\operatorname{proj}_x(P)\) has exponentially more inequalities than the lifted description of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The x-projection contains precisely the x-vectors admitting an auxiliary vector z. An objective depending only on x has the same attainable values and optimal x-vectors in the projected and lifted models. Fourier elimination describes a polyhedral projection, but an irredundant projected description can be exponentially larger than its lifted description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f(x):x\in\operatorname{proj}_x(S)\}=\{f(x)+0z:(x,z)\in S\},\qquad \operatorname{proj}_x(P)=\{x:A^*x\le b^*\},

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-ray description of a polyhedral projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite projection description obtained from the extreme rays of the projection cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:Ax+Bz\le b\}\), let \(C_P=\{u\in\mathbb R^m:uB=0,\ u\ge0\}\ne\{0\}\), and let \(r^1,\ldots,r^q\) be the extreme rays of \(C_P\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(P)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:r^tAx\le r^tb\text{ for }t=1,\ldots,q\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polar duality for full-dimensional polytopes containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-dimensional polytope with \(0\in\operatorname{int}(P)\). Its polar is \[P^\circ=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^n:y^{\mathsf T}x\le1\text{ for every }x\in P\}.\] Then \(P^\circ\) is also a full-dimensional polytope containing the origin in its interior, and \((P^\circ)^\circ=P\). For each nonempty proper face \(F\) of \(P\), the set \(F^*=\{y\in P^\circ:y^{\mathsf T}x=1\text{ for all }x\in F\}\) is a face of \(P^\circ\), inclusion is reversed, and \(\dim F+\dim F^*=n-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity is involutive and reverses the face lattice, pairing each proper face with a complementary-dimensional face of the polar polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((P^\circ)^\circ=P\), with an inclusion-reversing correspondence satisfying \(\dim F+\dim F^*=n-1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-Point and Facet Correspondence under Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polarity for full-dimensional bounded polyhedra containing the origin in their interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be full-dimensional and bounded with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and define \(\Pi^1=\{\pi\in\mathbb R^n:\pi^\top x\le 1\ \forall x\in P\}\). If \(\{\pi^t\}_{t\in T}=\operatorname{ext}(\Pi^1)\) and \(\{x^k\}_{k\in K}=\operatorname{ext}(P)\), then \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:(\pi^t)^\top x\le1\ \forall t\in T\},\qquad \Pi^1=\{\pi\in\mathbb R^n:\pi^\top x^k\le1\ \forall k\in K\}.\] Every inequality in each displayed description defines a facet of the polyhedron being described.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-dimensional bounded polyhedron containing the origin in its interior, the extreme points of its polar yield a facet description of the original polyhedron, and the extreme points of the original yield a facet description of its polar.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is full-dimensional and bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:(\pi^t)^\top x\le1\ \forall t\in T\},\quad \Pi^1=\{\pi\in\mathbb R^n:\pi^\top x^k\le1\ \forall k\in K\},\quad\text{with every listed inequality facet-defining.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension, pointedness, and boundedness under polyhedral polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric equivalences between a polyhedron containing the origin and its polar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron with \(0\in P\). Then: (i) \(P\) is full-dimensional if and only if \(P^*\) is pointed; (ii) \[\dim\!\left(\operatorname{lin}(P^*)\right)=n-\dim P,\] where \(\operatorname{lin}(P^*)\) is the lineality space of \(P^*\); and (iii) \(0\) is an interior point of \(P\) if and only if \(P^*\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron containing the origin, full dimensionality is equivalent to pointedness of the polar, the dimension of the polar's lineality space is the ambient dimension minus the dimension of the original polyhedron, and the origin is an interior point exactly when the polar is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is full-dimensional}\iff P^*\text{ is pointed};\quad \dim\operatorname{lin}(P^*)=n-\dim P;\quad 0\in\operatorname{int}P\iff P^*\text{ is bounded}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Antiblocker of a Nonnegative Packing Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the antiblocker and the associated extreme-point matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times n}\) have no zero columns and let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:Ax\le\mathbf1\}\). The antiblocker of \(P\) is \[P^C:=\{\pi\in\mathbb R_+^n:\pi^\top x\le1\ \text{for all }x\in P\}.\] If the extreme points of \(P\) are \(x^1,\ldots,x^r\), let \(C\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) denote the matrix whose rows are \((x^k)^\top\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blocking and antiblocking matrix pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract states the blocking-pair definition explicitly and defines antiblocking pairs only by analogy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A and B be nonnegative matrices. The pair (A,B) is a blocking pair if \{\pi\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:B\pi\geq\mathbf 1\} is the blocker of \{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:Ax\geq\mathbf 1\}. Antiblocking pairs are defined similarly using the corresponding antiblocker relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonnegative matrices form a blocking pair when the polyhedron defined by the second is the blocker of the polyhedron defined by the first. Antiblocking pairs are defined analogously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\pi\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:B\pi\geq\mathbf 1\}=\operatorname{blocker}\!\left(\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:Ax\geq\mathbf 1\}\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar correspondence for inequality and generator descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutual polarity between normalized inequality and convex-conic generator descriptions of polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a^1,\ldots,a^m\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(0\le k\le m\). Define \[P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(a^i)^\top x\le1\ (i=1,\ldots,k),\ (a^i)^\top x\le0\ (i=k+1,\ldots,m)\}\] and \[Q:=\operatorname{conv}(0,a^1,\ldots,a^k)+\operatorname{cone}(a^{k+1},\ldots,a^m).\] Then \(P^*=Q\) and \(Q^*=P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The polar of the polyhedron defined by the given unit and zero right-hand-side inequalities is the sum of the convex hull generated by the unit-inequality normals and the cone generated by the homogeneous-inequality normals. Polarizing that generator description recovers the original polyhedron.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(a^i)^\top x\le1\ (1\le i\le k),\ (a^i)^\top x\le0\ (k+1\le i\le m)\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^*=Q\quad\text{and}\quad Q^*=P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Membership Tests via Polar Support Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent membership characterizations under the assumptions of the preceding polarity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be full-dimensional and bounded with \(0\in\operatorname{int}P\), and let \(\Pi^1=\{\pi\in\mathbb R^n:\pi^\top x\le1\ \forall x\in P\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Involution, boundedness, and dimension properties of polyhedral polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental polarity properties of polyhedra containing the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron with \(0\in P\). Then: (i) \(P^{**}=P\); (ii) \(P^*\) is bounded if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{int}(P)\); and (iii) \[\operatorname{aff}(P^*)=\operatorname{lin}(P)^\perp,\qquad \dim(P^*)=n-\dim(\operatorname{lin}(P)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron containing the origin, taking the polar twice recovers the polyhedron. Its polar is bounded exactly when the origin is an interior point. The affine hull of the polar is the orthogonal complement of the lineality space, giving the stated dimension formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{**}=P;\qquad P^*\text{ is bounded}\iff 0\in\operatorname{int}(P);\qquad \operatorname{aff}(P^*)=\operatorname{lin}(P)^\perp;\qquad \dim(P^*)=n-\dim(\operatorname{lin}(P)).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and vertex representation of normalized polarity for a full-dimensional polytope after placing the origin in its interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a full-dimensional polytope translated so that \(0\in\operatorname{int}(P)\). knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi^1=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}^n:(\pi,1)\in\Pi\}=\{\pi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\pi x^k\le1\ \forall k\in K\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polarity theorem for polyhedra containing the origin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedrality, bipolarity, membership characterization, and the correspondence between generator and inequality representations under polarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron with \(0\in P\). Then (i) \(P^*\) is a polyhedron; (ii) \(P^{**}=P\); and (iii) \[x\in P\iff (\forall z\in P^*)\ z^\top x\leq 1.\] Moreover, for \(x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_t\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[P=\operatorname{conv}\{0,x_1,\ldots,x_m\}+\operatorname{cone}\{y_1,\ldots,y_t\}\] if and only if \[P^*=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:z^\top x_i\leq1\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\ z^\top y_j\leq0\ (j=1,\ldots,t)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedron containing the origin, the polar is polyhedral, taking the polar twice recovers the original polyhedron, and membership is characterized by all polar inequalities. A convex-hull-plus-cone representation of the polyhedron corresponds conversely to the displayed inequality representation of its polar.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^*\text{ is polyhedral},\quad P^{**}=P,\quad x\in P\iff\forall z\in P^*:\ z^\top x\leq1,\quad\text{and the stated generator--inequality representation equivalence holds}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Max–min and min–max inequalities for nonnegative matrix pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The two conditions are universal identities over w in the nonnegative orthant; b^j and c^j denote rows of B and C.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times n} and B\in\mathbb{R}_+^{r\times n}. The max\text{-}min inequality holds for (A,B) if, for every w\in\mathbb{R}_+^n, \max\{\mathbf 1y:yA\leq w,\ y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\}=\min_{1\leq j\leq r}b^jw. Let C\in\mathbb{R}_+^{r\times n}. The min\text{-}max inequality holds for (A,C) if, for every w\in\mathbb{R}_+^n, \min\{\mathbf 1y:yA\geq w,\ y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\}=\max_{1\leq j\leq r}c^jw.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The max–min condition requires every nonnegative right-hand side to give a packing optimum equal to the minimum row evaluation of the second matrix. The min–max condition analogously equates a covering optimum with the maximum row evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall w\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:\quad \max\{\mathbf 1y:yA\leq w,\ y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\}=\min_{1\leq j\leq r}b^jw,\qquad \min\{\mathbf 1y:yA\geq w,\ y\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\}=\max_{1\leq j\leq r}c^jw.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex hull of the integer points contained in a polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer hull is the convex hull of a polyhedron’s integer points and gives their exact convex relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedra equal to the convex hull of their integer points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is integral if \[P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).\] Equivalently, \(P\) equals its integer hull. For every vector \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), whenever \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is finite and attained, at least one optimal solution is integral. For a polytope, integrality is equivalent to every vertex belonging to \(\mathbb{Z}^n\); the vertex criterion alone does not describe nonpointed unbounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral polyhedron equals its integer hull; for polytopes, this is equivalent to all vertices being integer.
assumptions_latex: The vertex equivalence additionally assumes that \(P\) is a polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is integral exactly when \(P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimization Characterizations of Integral Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterizations by integral optimizers and integral optimal values, under the section's standing extreme-point assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron having an extreme point, and define \(\mathrm{LP}(c)=\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) with optimal value \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(P\) is integral; (ii) for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\) for which \(\mathrm{LP}(c)\) has an optimal solution, it has an integral optimal solution; (iii) the same holds for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\); and (iv) for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) for which \(\mathrm{LP}(c)\) has an optimal solution, \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(c)\in\mathbb{Z}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: DFNP and FNP Algorithm for Chordal Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-phase procedure in the source's DFNP/FNP notation; \(\widetilde{k}^i\) is inherited from that formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given the perfect elimination ordering \((1,\ldots,n)\), initialize \(c^1=c\) and \(J_0=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,n\), set \(u_i=\max\{0,c_i^i\}\). If \(u_i>0\), set \(J_i=J_{i-1}\cup\{i\}\) and \(c^{i+1}=c^i-u_i\widetilde{k}^i\); otherwise set \(J_i=J_{i-1}\) and \(c^{i+1}=c^i\). Then initialize \(J=J_n\) and \(x_j=0\) for \(j\notin J\). While \(J\ne\varnothing\), let \(l\) be its last element, set \(x_l=1\), and replace \(J\) by \(J\setminus\{i:\widetilde{k}_{il}=1\}\). The resulting \(u\) and \(x\) are optimal for DFNP and FNP, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual phase processes vertices in perfect-elimination order and builds a selected set. The primal phase processes that set backward, selects its last vertex, and removes all indices identified by the corresponding clique vector. The phases return optimal DFNP and FNP solutions.
assumptions_latex: (1,\ldots,n)\text{ is a perfect elimination scheme for }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)\text{ is optimal for DFNP and }x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\text{ is optimal for FNP}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Polyhedra and Equivalent Characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and equivalent face and optimization characterizations of rational integral polyhedra, including the pointed case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(P_I=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n)\). Then the following are equivalent: (i) \(P=P_I\); (ii) every face of \(P\) contains an integral vector; (iii) every minimal face of \(P\) contains an integral vector; and (iv) for every \(c\) for which \(\max\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) is finite, the maximum is attained by an integral vector. A rational polyhedron satisfying these conditions is integral. If \(P\) is pointed, it is integral if and only if every vertex of \(P\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational polyhedron is integral when it equals the convex hull of its integer points. Equivalently, every face, or only every minimal face, contains an integer point, and every finite linear-objective maximum is attained at an integer point. For a pointed rational polyhedron, integrality is equivalent to integrality of every vertex.

P=P_I\iff( orall F	ext{ face of }P,\ F\cap\mathbb{Z}^n
eq\varnothing)\iff( orall F	ext{ minimal face of }P,\ F\cap\mathbb{Z}^n
eq\varnothing)\iff( orall c:\max_{x\in P}c^Tx	ext{ is finite},\ \operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^Tx\cap\mathbb{Z}^n
eq\varnothing);\quad P	ext{ pointed}\Rightarrow(P	ext{ integral}\iff\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Submatrix Characterization of Clique Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence for incidence matrices of clutters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the \(m\times n\) incidence matrix of a clutter. Then \(A\) is a clique matrix if and only if, whenever \(A\) contains a \(p\times p\) submatrix \(A'\), with \(p\geq3\), whose row sums and column sums all equal \(p-1\), the submatrix \(A'\) is contained in a \((p+1)\times p\) submatrix of \(A\) that contains a row of all ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A clutter incidence matrix is a clique matrix exactly when every square submatrix of order at least three having all row and column sums one below its order can be extended by one row to a submatrix containing an all-one row.
assumptions_latex: A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}\text{ is the incidence matrix of a clutter}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\text{ is a clique matrix}\iff \forall p\geq3,\ \forall A'\subseteq A,\ \bigl[A'\in\{0,1\}^{p\times p},\ A'\mathbf1=(p-1)\mathbf1,\ \mathbf1^TA'=(p-1)\mathbf1^T\bigr]\Rightarrow \bigl[A'\text{ is contained in a }(p+1)\times p\text{ submatrix of }A\text{ containing an all-one row}\bigr]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of recession-cone preservation without rationality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an irrational number \(\alpha\) and consider the closed convex ray \[P=\{t(1,\alpha):t\ge0\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2.\] If \(t(1,\alpha)\in\mathbb Z^2\), then either \(t=0\) or \(\alpha=(t\alpha)/t\in\mathbb Q\), which is impossible. Hence \(P\cap\mathbb Z^2=\{(0,0)\}\) and \(P_I=\{(0,0)\}\). Therefore \[\operatorname{rec}(P_I)=\{0\}\ne P=\operatorname{rec}(P).\] Thus rationality is essential to the usual recession theorem for integer hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irrational ray contains only the origin as an integer point, so its integer hull loses the ray's nonzero recession direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual lattice and dual-basis identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a full-dimensional lattice in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a full-dimensional lattice \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), define \(L^*=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x^Ty\in\mathbb Z\text{ for every }y\in L\}\). If \((b_1,\ldots,b_n)\) is a basis of \(L\), the vectors \((c_1,\ldots,c_n)\) satisfying \(c_i^Tb_j=\delta_{ij}\) form a basis of \(L^*\). Consequently, \(L^{**}=L\) and \(\det(L)\det(L^*)=1\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with the ordered basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\) and its Gram-Schmidt data. For \(i=2,\ldots,k\), size-reduce by replacing \(b_i\leftarrow b_i-\lfloor\mu_{ij}\rceil b_j\) for \(j=i-1,i-2,\ldots,1\). If \[\delta\|b_{i-1}^*\|^2>\|b_i^*+\mu_{i,i-1}b_{i-1}^*\|^2,\] swap \(b_i\) and \(b_{i-1}\), update the Gram-Schmidt data, and resume at \(\max\{2,i-1\}\); otherwise increment \(i\). Stop when \(i>k\). The returned basis generates the original lattice and is \(\delta\)-LLL-reduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LLL repeatedly size-reduces basis vectors and swaps adjacent vectors violating the Lovasz condition, terminating with a reduced basis of the same lattice.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequality \(x+y/f\ge\lceil b\rceil\) is valid, and \(\operatorname{conv}(S_b)=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_+:x+y\ge b,\ x+y/f\ge\lceil b\rceil\}\).

notation.meaning: Fractional part of the right-hand side

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-row mixed-integer rounding inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\notin\mathbb Z\), set \(f=b-\lfloor b\rfloor\in(0,1)\), and define \[S_b=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z\times\mathbb R_+:x+y\ge b\}.\] The mixed-integer rounding inequality is \[x+\frac{y}{f}\ge\lceil b\rceil.\] It is valid for \(S_b\), and the convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S_b)=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R_+:x+y\ge b,\ x+\frac{y}{f}\ge\lceil b\rceil\right\}.\] More general MIR cuts are obtained by aggregating and scaling a valid mixed-integer row into this canonical form before applying the rounding inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the canonical mixed-integer row, the MIR inequality is valid; together with nonnegativity and the original row inequality, it describes the convex hull.

children.title: Classical Cut Relationships

assumptions_latex: The cut is derived from one tableau row whose basic variable is required to be integral.
The associated split is \(x_B\le\lfloor\bar b\rfloor\) or \(x_B\ge\lceil\bar b\rceil\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a tableau row with fractional basic value \(\bar b\), where the basic variable \(x_B\) is integral and all nonbasic variables are nonnegative. Applying the split disjunction \[x_B\le\lfloor\bar b\rfloor\quad\lor\quad x_B\ge\lceil\bar b\rceil\] and convexifying the two branches yields the mixed-integer Gomory inequality. After the standard one-row normalization, the same inequality is the corresponding mixed-integer rounding cut; viewed geometrically from the tableau cone, it is the intersection cut generated by the split set. Thus these constructions coincide in the single-row setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For one fractional tableau row, the GMI cut is equivalently obtained as a split cut, an MIR cut, or an intersection cut.

children.title: Intersection Cut Families

assumptions_latex: \(P=\{\bar x+\sum_{j=1}^q r^js_j:s\in\mathbb R_+^q\}\) is a pointed polyhedral cone.
\(S\) is closed, convex, lattice-free, and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{j=1}^q s_j/\alpha_j\ge1\) is valid for every point of \(P\setminus\operatorname{int}(S)\), with \(1/\infty=0\).

notation.meaning: Distance along ray j to the boundary of S

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection cuts from a lattice-free convex set and a polyhedral cone.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{\bar x+\sum_{j=1}^q r^js_j:s\ge0\}\), and let \(S\) be a closed convex lattice-free set with \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}(S)\). For each ray define \[\alpha_j=\sup\{t\ge0:\bar x+tr^j\in S\}.\] Then the intersection cut is \[\sum_{j=1}^q\frac{s_j}{\alpha_j}\ge1,\] where \(1/\infty=0\). It is valid for every point of \(P\setminus\operatorname{int}(S)\), hence for every integer point of \(P\) whenever \(\operatorname{int}(S)\cap\mathbb Z^n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ray-boundary intersection distances define an inequality excluding the cone apex while preserving all points outside a lattice-free set's interior.

The associated disjunctive hull is \[P_D=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^k(P\cap D_i)\right).\] A linear inequality is a disjunctive cut for \(P\) relative to \(D\) if it is valid for \(P_D\) but not necessarily for \(P\). Its validity follows solely from validity on every branch \(P\cap D_i\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(P)=\bigcap_{j=1}^p Q_j\subseteq P\), and every inequality valid for some \(Q_j\) is valid for all binary-feasible points of \(P\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull obtained from the elementary split on coordinate j.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary binary-variable lift-and-project closure and its associated cut family.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Lift-and-Project Cuts for Mixed 0-1 Programs p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(j\), define \[Q_j=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap\{x:x_j=0\})\cup(P\cap\{x:x_j=1\})\bigr).\] A lift-and-project cut for the split on \(x_j\) is any linear inequality valid for \(Q_j\). The corresponding one-round closure is \[L(P)=\bigcap_{j=1}^p Q_j.\] Since every point of \(P\) satisfying all binary restrictions belongs to each disjunctive union, every lift-and-project cut is valid for the mixed-binary feasible set, and \(L(P)\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift-and-project cuts describe convex hulls of elementary binary disjunctions; intersecting those hulls yields a relaxation tighter than the original linear relaxation.

children.title: Lattice-Free Geometric Links
children.top_down_role: Shared lattice-free geometry connecting intersection and disjunctive cut families.

assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed, convex, full-dimensional, and lattice-free, with \(f\in\operatorname{int}(B)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), then \(\sum_{j=1}^k \psi_B(r^j)s_j\ge 1\).

notation.meaning: Gauge of the translated lattice-free set B-f.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure-integer intersection inequality induced by a lattice-free convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the gauge \[\psi_B(r)=\inf\{\lambda>0:f+r/\lambda\in B\}.\] Equivalently, when the ray from \(f\) in direction \(r\) meets \(\partial B\) at \(f+r/\psi_B(r)\), the gauge records the reciprocal boundary distance. Because \(\operatorname{int}(B)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=\varnothing\), every representation \(x=f+\sum_{j=1}^k r^j s_j\) with \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) and \(s\ge0\) satisfies \[\sum_{j=1}^k\psi_B(r^j)s_j\ge1.\] Thus lattice-free geometry supplies valid intersection cuts for the associated corner relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lattice-free convex set containing the fractional apex induces a gauge inequality that every integer point represented by the relaxation's rays must satisfy.
knowledge_statements.title: Lattice-Free Geometric Links

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i\in C}x_i\le |C|-1\) is valid, and any valid lifting of this inequality remains valid for the full model.

notation.meaning: A cover for the binary knapsack constraint.
Coefficients for variables outside the cover in a lifted inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representative cover inequality illustrating model-structured valid-inequality families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is a cover because selecting every member violates the knapsack constraint. Hence every feasible binary vector satisfies \[\sum_{i\in C}x_i\le |C|-1.\] A lifted cover inequality has the form \[\sum_{i\in C}x_i+[0m\sum_{j\notin C}\alpha_jx_j\le |C|-1,\] where the coefficients \(\alpha_j\) are chosen so that the inequality is valid for every feasible vector. Cover, flow-cover, routing, and analogous families are structured because their validity exploits a distinguished combinatorial subsystem rather than only the ambient linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A knapsack cover cannot be selected completely, giving a cover inequality; valid lifting and analogous subsystem-specific constructions produce structured inequality families.

children.title: Separation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational difficulty of identifying violated inequalities within a specified family.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a rational point \(\bar x\), and an encoded inequality family \(\mathcal F\) are given.
Arithmetic cost is measured in the Turing bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separation complexity is the worst-case bit-operation count required to solve the stated search-or-certification problem.

auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit complexity of exact separation over an encoded cut family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The separation problem for \(\mathcal F\) takes \(\bar x\) as input and must either return an encoded inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) in \(\mathcal F\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}\bar x>b\), or certify that no inequality in \(\mathcal F\) is violated. Its separation complexity is the worst-case number of bit operations as a function of the binary encoding lengths of \(P\), \(\bar x\), and any parameters defining \(\mathcal F\). assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational relaxation and \(C_{\mathcal F}(P)\) is its closure under cut family \(\mathcal F\).
\(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is valid for the intended integer feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(\mathcal F\)-rank is the least \(t\in\mathbb{Z}_+\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is valid for \(C_{\mathcal F}^{t}(P)\), or \(+\infty\) if none exists.

notation.meaning: Closure obtained by imposing all cuts from family F valid for the relevant integer set.
t-fold iteration of the closure operator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank relative to a fixed cutting-plane closure operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(C_{\mathcal F}^{0}(P)=P\) and recursively define \(C_{\mathcal F}^{t+1}(P)=C_{\mathcal F}(C_{\mathcal F}^{t}(P))\). The \(\mathcal F\)-rank of the valid inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) with respect to \(P\) is \[\operatorname{rank}_{\mathcal F,P}(a,b)=\min\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_+:a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\text{ is valid for }C_{\mathcal F}^{t}(P)\}.\] If the set is empty, the rank is \(+\infty\). assumptions_latex: A fixed cutting-plane proof system specifies admissible premises and inference rules.
The target is either a valid inequality or an infeasibility conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proof length is the minimum number of derived inequalities among all admissible derivations of the target.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cutting-plane derivation is a finite sequence \((I_1,[0m\ldots,I_m)\) in which every \(I_k\) is an initial inequality or follows from earlier lines by an admissible rule. The sequence proves \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) when its final line is that inequality, and proves infeasibility when its final line is an explicit contradiction such as \(0\le-1\). Its length is the number \(m\) of derived lines under the chosen convention concerning initial premises. The proof length of a target is the minimum such \(m\) over all admissible derivations.

children.title: Branching Enumeration Search

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finiteness of fractional-variable dichotomy trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to enumeration over a bounded nonnegative polyhedron when every divided node branches on a nonintegral variable value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:Ax\le b\}\) be bounded. Suppose that whenever a node \(i\) requires division, some index \(j\) with \(x_j^i\notin\mathbb{Z}\) is selected and the node is split by \(x_j\le\lfloor x_j^i\rfloor\) or \(x_j\ge\lfloor x_j^i\rfloor+1\). Then the resulting enumeration tree is finite. Moreover, with \(\omega_j=\left\lceil\max\{x_j:x\in P\}\right\rceil\), no path contains more than \(\sum_{j\in N}\omega_j\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded nonnegative polyhedron, an enumeration tree that branches at every divided node on a fractional variable using the adjacent floor-based dichotomy is finite. If omega_j is the ceiling of the largest feasible value of variable j, no path has more than the sum of the omega_j edges.
assumptions_latex: \forall i\text{ requiring division},\ \exists j:\ x_j^i\notin\mathbb{Z}\text{ and the dichotomy is }x_j\le\lfloor x_j^i\rfloor\ \lor\ x_j\ge\lfloor x_j^i\rfloor+1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The enumeration tree is finite, and no path contains more than }\sum_{j\in N}\left\lceil\max_{x\in P}x_j\right\rceil\text{ edges.}

knowledge_statements.title: Branching Disjunction Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustiveness requirement for branching disjunctions in exact enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A branching disjunction is exact at node \(N\) when \[F_N\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^k D_i.\] The child feasible sets are \(F_N\cap D_i\); they may overlap, although a partition avoids duplicate enumeration. For an integer variable \(x_j\) and any \(t\in\mathbb{Z}\), the split \[x_j\le t\quad\vee\quad x_j\ge t+1\] is exhaustive. Consequently, replacing the parent by all its children cannot remove an integer-feasible solution. For finite binary enumeration, the branching rule should additionally resolve at least one previously unresolved binary choice on every nonterminal path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching disjunction must cover every feasible point at its node; variable splits are exhaustive examples, while finite binary enumeration also requires progress along each nonterminal path.
assumptions_latex: \(F_N\) is the integer-feasible set represented by search node \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(N\) by children with feasible sets \(F_N\cap D_i\) preserves every feasible solution represented by \(N\).
