children.title: Model-Semantics Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between intended decisions and the feasible region represented by logical or linking structure.

children.title: One-Way Implication Errors
children.top_down_role: Representations encoding only one direction of an intended equivalence.

assumptions_latex: The intended feasible set uses a binary indicator and a predicate with a well-defined truth value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The incomplete encoding may admit points outside the intended set; adding the reverse implication restores logical equivalence.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encodings of an intended if-and-only-if relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(x,z)\in X\times\{0,1\}:z=1\Longleftrightarrow P(x)\}\). If a formulation enforces only \(z=1\Longrightarrow P(x)\), its feasible set is \(\widehat S=\{(x,z):z=0\text{ or }P(x)\}\). Whenever some \(\bar x\in X\) satisfies \(P(\bar x)\), the point \((\bar x,0)\in\widehat S\setminus S\). Thus the encoding is exact only if the reverse implication \(P(x)\Longrightarrow z=1\) follows from other constraints or is imposed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Encoding only one direction of an intended equivalence admits incorrect indicator assignments unless the reverse implication is separately implied or enforced.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Way Implication Errors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement is mathematically precise and fits the terminal container, but it has no inspectable citation beyond a standard-field rationale.

children.title: Missing Exclusivity or Exhaustiveness
children.top_down_role: Alternative-regime models allowing unintended combinations or omitting valid choices.

assumptions_latex: Exactly one of finitely many regimes is intended to hold for each feasible decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality \(\sum_{k=1}^m z_k=1\) enforces both exclusivity and exhaustiveness; either one-sided inequality omits one property.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-hot selection among finitely many alternative regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For selectors \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\in\{0,1\}\), exact selection of one regime requires \(\sum_{k=1}^m z_k=1\). Replacing this equality by \(\sum_{k=1}^m z_k\le 1\) preserves exclusivity but permits the unintended all-zero assignment, so exhaustiveness is lost. Replacing it by \(\sum_{k=1}^m z_k\ge 1\) preserves exhaustiveness but permits simultaneous activation of several regimes, so exclusivity is lost. Omitting both bounds permits both failure modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-hot equality is required when exactly one regime must hold; either one-sided inequality permits unintended or missing selections.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Exclusivity or Exhaustiveness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-hot characterization is correct and appropriately classified, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Inactive-Branch Leakage
children.top_down_role: Supposedly inactive variables or constraints retaining unintended influence.

knowledge_statements.title: Inactive-Branch Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic leakage from a branch whose indicator equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq X\) be the intended domain of the shared variables when the branch is inactive, and let \(F\subseteq X\times\mathbb R^p\times\{0,1\}\) be the encoded feasible set. If inactivity is intended to impose \(u=0\) and no branch-specific restriction beyond \(x\in D\), leakage occurs when either \((x,u,0)\in F\) for some \(u\ne0\), or \(\{x\in X:(x,0,0)\in F\}\subsetneq D\). The first condition witnesses residual variable activity, and the second witnesses residual branch restrictions on shared variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inactive branch leaks when branch-specific variables can remain nonzero or when deactivated branch constraints exclude some shared decisions from the intended inactive domain.
assumptions_latex: An inactive branch is intended to fix its branch-specific variables at zero and otherwise permit every shared-variable decision in a specified inactive domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible point with \(z=0\) and \(u\ne0\), or a strict reduction of the intended inactive domain, is a leakage witness.

notation.meaning: intended domain of shared variables when the branch is inactive

children.title: Unintended or Excluded Solutions
children.top_down_role: Incomplete or overly restrictive structure admitting or removing real-world decisions.

assumptions_latex: The intended and encoded models are expressed in a common decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonempty \(\widehat S\setminus S\) certifies unintended solutions, while nonempty \(S\setminus\widehat S\) certifies excluded valid solutions.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic criterion for model-semantic correctness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An encoding is semantically exact precisely when \(S=\widehat S\), equivalently when \(S\mathbin\triangle\widehat S=\varnothing\). Every point in \(\widehat S\setminus S\) is an unintended encoded solution, and every point in \(S\setminus\widehat S\) is an intended decision excluded by the encoding. Consequently, checking only \(S\subseteq\widehat S\) detects no exclusions but cannot rule out unintended solutions, whereas checking only \(\widehat S\subseteq S\) has the opposite limitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semantic correctness is equality of intended and encoded feasible sets; the two directed set differences identify admitted and excluded decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Unintended or Excluded Solutions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The directed set differences correctly characterize admitted and excluded decisions, and the condition kind fits the criterion-oriented statement, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: False Model-Status Failures
children.top_down_role: Missing or inconsistent structure creating false global model status.

children.title: Spurious Unboundedness
children.top_down_role: False unbounded status caused by missing links, bounds, or intended restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem and the intended feasible set is nonempty.
The encoded objective agrees with the intended objective on intended feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An encoded feasible sequence with objective tending to \(-\infty\), absent from the intended model, produces spurious unboundedness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:optimization status follows feasible-set and objective behavior
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False unbounded status caused by unintended encoded directions or missing bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)>-\infty\). Spurious unboundedness occurs if the encoding has a sequence \((x^k)_{k\ge1}\subseteq\widehat S\) satisfying \(f(x^k)\to-\infty\), while no such sequence lies in \(S\). In particular, if \(S\subsetneq\widehat S\), every sufficiently improving term must eventually belong to \(\widehat S\setminus S\). Missing variable bounds, activation links, or constraints can therefore make the encoded problem unbounded although the intended problem has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is spuriously unbounded when unintended encoded solutions support unlimited improvement although the intended objective is bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Unboundedness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimization-specific failure boundary is coherent and properly scoped, but the causal examples and status characterization lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Artificial Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: False infeasible status caused by inconsistent or overly restrictive modeled structure.

assumptions_latex: The intended and encoded formulations use a common decision space or a specified projection into one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(S\ne\varnothing\) and \(\widehat S=\varnothing\) characterizes artificial infeasibility of the encoding.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:infeasibility is emptiness of the feasible set
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: False infeasible status introduced by the mathematical encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Artificial infeasibility occurs exactly when \(S\ne\varnothing\) but \(\widehat S=\varnothing\). More locally, a family of added encoding constraints \(C\) causes the failure when \(S\cap C=\varnothing\) although \(S\ne\varnothing\). An intended feasible point \(\bar x\in S\) together with identification of a violated constraint in \(C\) witnesses exclusion, while an infeasibility certificate for \(\widehat S\) confirms that the encoded model admits no point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Artificial infeasibility means the intended model has a feasible decision but the implemented encoding has none.
knowledge_statements.title: Artificial Infeasibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly distinguishes intended feasibility from encoded infeasibility, but it has no citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Status-Diagnosis Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural routes for distinguishing genuine global status from formulation artifacts.

assumptions_latex: The solver can separately test feasibility and objective boundedness and can expose constraint or bound diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface outputs a status together with a checkable witness or a localized set of suspect model components.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:status diagnosis separates feasibility, boundedness, and evidence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract diagnostic contract independent of a particular solver API.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an encoded problem \(\min\{f(x):x\in\widehat S\}\). First solve a feasibility-only problem over \(\widehat S\). If infeasible, request an irreducible inconsistent subsystem or another infeasibility certificate and report the implicated constraints and bounds. If feasible, test whether \(f\) is bounded below on \(\widehat S\); when unbounded, return an improving ray or sequence. Otherwise return a feasible incumbent, a valid bound, and the termination gap. Status is reported as unresolved when the required certificate is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A diagnosis interface separates feasibility, boundedness, and termination checks and pairs each status with available certificates or suspect constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Status-Diagnosis Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the diagnostic-interface leaf, but availability and interpretation of IISs, rays, bounds, and gaps are solver-dependent and require authoritative sourcing.

children.title: Global-Status Root Causes
children.top_down_role: Modeling omissions and contradictions capable of corrupting global solver status.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Status Root Causes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of mathematical model-status discrepancies from solver-reported status failures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(v=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\) and \(\widehat v=\inf_{x\in\widehat S}\widehat f(x)\). If \(S=\widehat S\) and \(f(x)=\widehat f(x)\) for every \(x\in S\), then \(v=\widehat v\), including the infeasible and unbounded-below cases under the stated extended-real conventions. Therefore a discrepancy between the mathematical statuses of the intended and encoded problems requires a feasible-set or objective discrepancy. A discrepancy between a solver-reported status and the encoded problem's mathematical status may instead result from tolerances, premature termination, unsupported problem structure, invalid algorithmic assumptions, or implementation failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching feasible sets and objectives give matching mathematical statuses. Differences between intended and encoded mathematical statuses come from model or objective discrepancies, while an incorrect solver-reported status can also arise from numerical, algorithmic, termination, or implementation failures.
assumptions_latex: The intended and encoded problems are minimization problems represented in a common decision space.
Objective values use the conventions \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\) and value \(-\infty\) for a problem unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Mathematical status disagreement requires a feasible-set or objective discrepancy; solver-reported status disagreement can additionally arise at the numerical, algorithmic, termination, or implementation layer.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:mathematical status is determined by feasibility and extended-real optimal value

children.title: Structural Relaxation Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Correct formulations whose representation choices obscure or weakly approximate discrete structure.

children.title: Coupling Convexification Gaps
children.top_down_role: Weakness caused by loose activation links or independent treatment of coupled structures.

children.title: Weak Activation Linking
children.top_down_role: Relaxation weakness caused by loose links between activation decisions and dependent variables.

assumptions_latex: The intended activation relation is \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\) with a valid finite bound \(0\le x\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Using \(M>U\) is integer-valid but strictly weakens the continuous relaxation relative to the tight link \(x\le Uz\).

notation.meaning: valid bound and chosen linking constant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Big-M activation links with an available tight upper bound.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Convexification of sets and functions p. 21
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tight linear activation link is \(0\le x\le Uz\). Replacing it by \(0\le x\le Mz\) with \(M>U\), while retaining \(x\le U\), preserves all points with \(z\in\{0,1\}\). After relaxing \(z\in[0,1]\), however, any \(z\in(0,U/M)\) permits \(x=Mz>Uz\). Thus the larger constant creates fractional points excluded by the tight formulation and strictly weakens the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oversized valid big-M preserves integer semantics but admits extra fractional activation, weakening the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Activation Linking

children.title: Lost Joint Convexification
children.top_down_role: Strength lost when coupled structures are convexified independently.

assumptions_latex: The component sets share variables, so their convexifications need not preserve their joint dependence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate convexification can strictly contain the convex hull of the jointly constrained set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictness of convexifying coupled components separately.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Convexification of sets and functions p. 21
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary sets \(S_1,S_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\operatorname{conv}(S_1\cap S_2)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(S_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2)\), and equality need not hold. For example, let \(S_1=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R\times\{0,1\}:x=z\}\) and \(S_2=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R\times\{0,1\}:x=1-z\}\). Then \(S_1\cap S_2=\varnothing\), but \((1/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{conv}(S_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2)\). Separate convexification therefore loses the shared discrete coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying coupled components separately may retain fractional points that no convex combination of jointly feasible integer points can produce.
knowledge_statements.title: Lost Joint Convexification

children.title: Coupling-Gap Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Indicators of relaxation gaps attributable to missing cross-structure coupling.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation and the convex hull of the intended feasible set are represented in the same space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A relaxation point violating a jointly valid inequality is a verifiable certificate of a coupling gap.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Point-and-separating-inequality certificate for relaxation coupling loss.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Convexification of sets and functions p. 21
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coupling-gap certificate is a pair consisting of \(\bar x\in R\) and an inequality \(a^Tx\le\beta\) valid for every \(x\in S\), such that \(a^T\bar x>\beta\). Validity implies \(a^Tx\le\beta\) throughout \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), so the strict violation proves \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Therefore \(R\supsetneq\operatorname{conv}(S)\), and the excess point is attributable to a missing jointly valid coupling restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation point and a violated inequality valid for all intended solutions certify that the relaxation has lost joint coupling strength.
knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Gap Diagnostics

children.title: Strength-Recovery Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural routes for restoring tighter linking or joint representations.

assumptions_latex: An extended formulation maps linearly into the original decision space.
All added inequalities or conic constraints are valid for the intended feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strength is fully recovered exactly when the strengthened formulation projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal-formulation criterion for complete recovery of relaxation strength.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Convexification of sets and functions p. 21
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

source_refs.locator: 3.5 Reducing the duality gap p. 28

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strengthened extended formulation \(Q\) is ideal for \(S\) when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\). If only \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\) holds, some coupling gap remains. Strength-recovery interfaces include tightening valid activation bounds, adding jointly valid inequalities that separate points in \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\), or replacing separate component relaxations by an extended convex-hull formulation. Complete recovery is certified by projection equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strengthening fully recovers coupling strength precisely when its continuous extended formulation projects onto the convex hull of intended solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Strength-Recovery Interfaces

children.title: Compact but Weak Encodings
children.top_down_role: Small representations whose coding choices yield poor relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact but Weak Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A big-M family showing that a small formulation can have an arbitrarily weak continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(M\ge 1\), consider \(x\ge 1\), \(x\le My\), \(0\le x\le M\), \(y\in\{0,1\}\), with objective \(\min y\). The formulation has two variables and four linear bounds or inequalities. Every integer-feasible solution has \(y=1\), so its optimal value is \(1\). After replacing \(y\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\le y\le1\), the point \((x,y)=(1,1/M)\) is feasible and optimal, with value \(1/M\). Thus the additive relaxation gap tends to \(1\), and the integer-to-relaxation objective ratio equals \(M\), despite constant formulation size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-size big-M formulation can become arbitrarily weak: its integer optimum is 1 while its relaxation optimum is 1/M.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}=1\), \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=1/M\), and \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}/z_{\mathrm{LP}}=M\).
review_flags: Exact big-M gap family is self-contained but lacks a supplied supporting locator.

children.title: Unmodeled Valid Structure
children.top_down_role: Omitted implied bounds, conservation relations, or strengthening structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Unmodeled Valid Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of omitted valid inequalities on a minimization formulation's continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) be the intended feasible set, let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{p+q}\) satisfy \(X\subseteq P\), and let \(I\) be an index set with \(a_i\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) for every \(i\in I\). If \(V=\{z\in\mathbb R^{p+q}:a_i^\top z\le b_i\text{ for all }i\in I\}\) satisfies \(X\subseteq V\), then \(P'=P\cap V\) satisfies \(X\subseteq P'\subseteq P\). Consequently, for every \(c\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\), \(\inf_{z\in P}c^\top z\le\inf_{z\in P'}c^\top z\le\inf_{z\in X}c^\top z\), with the infima interpreted in the extended real sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding valid implied bounds or conservation inequalities preserves every intended feasible point and can only improve a minimization relaxation bound.
assumptions_latex: All displayed infima are interpreted in the extended real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\subseteq P\cap V\subseteq P\) and \(\inf_{z\in P}c^\top z\le\inf_{z\in P\cap V}c^\top z\le\inf_{z\in X}c^\top z\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^{p+q}\).

notation.meaning: set defined by omitted valid inequalities
index set for the valid inequalities

children.title: Unnecessary Variable Expansion
children.top_down_role: Replication across time, scenarios, states, or alternatives without compensating structural value.

knowledge_statements.title: Unnecessary Variable Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for an exact extension that adds variables without strengthening the projected relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a relaxation and let \(Q=\{(x,u)\in\mathbb R^{n+r}:A x+B u\le d\}\) be an extended relaxation, with projection \(\pi_x(Q)=\{x:\exists u,(x,u)\in Q\}\). The expansion is unnecessary relative to \(P\) when \(r>0\), \(\pi_x(Q)=P\), and the auxiliary coordinates are not required by the objective, requested output, or a decomposition interface. Under these conditions every objective depending only on \(x\) has the same relaxation bound over \(P\) and \(Q\), while \(Q\) introduces additional variables and constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expansion is unnecessary when its projection equals the original relaxation and its auxiliary variables serve no objective, output, or algorithmic interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(Q)=P\) and \(\inf_{(x,u)\in Q}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in P}c^\top x\).

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Bloat
children.top_down_role: Excess lifted-variable growth relative to formulation strength or clarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Bloat
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A size criterion for auxiliary variables growing disproportionately to the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family indexed by \(n\), let \(p(n)\) be the number of original variables and \(a(n)\) the number of introduced auxiliary variables. The family exhibits auxiliary-variable bloat when \(a(n)/p(n)\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\), while projection onto the original variables supplies neither a strictly stronger relaxation nor an interface required by the selected algorithm. In particular, if each of \(p(n)\) original variables is coupled to \(q(n)\) interchangeable auxiliaries with \(q(n)\to\infty\), then \(a(n)=p(n)q(n)\) and the bloat criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary-variable bloat occurs when auxiliary counts dominate original-variable counts without improving projected strength or supporting a required algorithmic interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(n)/p(n)\to\infty\); in the replicated construction, \(a(n)=p(n)q(n)\).

children.title: Index-Set Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation growth driven by products of indexing dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Index-Set Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation-size growth generated by variables or constraints indexed over Cartesian products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a formulation family contain one variable or constraint for every tuple in \(I_1(n)\times\cdots\times I_k(n)\). If \(|I_j(n)|=\Theta(n^{\alpha_j})\) for fixed \(k\) and nonnegative constants \(\alpha_j\), then the indexed block contains \(\Theta(n^{\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_k})\) objects. If instead \(k=k(n)\) and every factor has at least two elements, the block size is at least \(2^{k(n)}\); hence \(k(n)=\Theta(n)\) causes exponential growth. These counts measure explicit formulation storage before presolve or implicit generation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-dimensional Cartesian indices give polynomial size; a linearly growing number of nontrivial indices gives exponential explicit size.
assumptions_latex: Index tuples generate distinct explicit variables or constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left|\prod_{j=1}^k I_j(n)\right|=\Theta(n^{\sum_j\alpha_j})\), while \(\left|\prod_{j=1}^{k(n)}I_j(n)\right|\ge2^{k(n)}\).
review_flags: Elementary counting claim is unambiguous, but no supplied source locator addresses formulation index growth.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cartesian-product counts and complexity-bound classification are correct, but the record supplies no source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Size-Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Comparisons between formulation size and resulting relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Size-Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of exact formulations by explicit size and projected continuous-relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1,Q_2\) be exact extended formulations of the same mixed-integer set in original variables \(x\), and let \(R_i=\pi_x(Q_i^{\mathrm{cont}})\) be their projected continuous relaxations. Formulation \(Q_1\) is at least as strong as \(Q_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), and it is no larger when its total number \(s_1\) of explicit variables and constraints satisfies \(s_1\le s_2\). A genuine size-strength tradeoff occurs when \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\) but \(s_1>s_2\): the stronger bound is purchased with a larger explicit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A size-strength tradeoff occurs when one exact formulation has a strictly tighter projected relaxation but more explicit variables and constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) represent the same mixed-integer set after projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\) and \(s_1>s_2\) characterize the stated tradeoff.

notation.meaning: projected continuous relaxation of formulation i

children.title: Formulation-Induced Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Redundant symmetry created by auxiliaries, duplicated alternatives, or interchangeable codes.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation-Induced Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry created by interchangeable formulation variables rather than by distinct original decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+r}\) be a formulation in original variables \(x\) and auxiliary variables \(u\). A nonidentity permutation group \(G\) induces formulation symmetry when, for every \(g\in G\), \((x,u)\in Q\) if and only if \((x,g u)\in Q\), the objective satisfies \(f(x,u)=f(x,g u)\), and \(\pi_x(x,u)=\pi_x(x,g u)=x\). Each auxiliary orbit therefore represents the same original solution and objective value. If an orbit has size greater than one, the formulation contains distinct symmetric representatives invisible after projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interchangeable auxiliaries create symmetry when their permutations preserve feasibility and objective value while projecting to the same original decision.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts by permutations of auxiliary coordinates.
The objective and feasible set are invariant under this action.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,g u):g\in G\}\) is an orbit of equivalent formulation representatives of \(x\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports formulation-induced symmetry.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The group-action characterization is coherent and fits formulation-induced symmetry, but no supporting source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Numerical Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision weaknesses caused by scaling, conditioning, and interacting tolerances.

children.title: Scaling-Unit Consistency Failures
children.top_down_role: Poorly scaled coefficients and inconsistent units across model components.

children.title: Coefficient-Scale Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Large coefficient-magnitude disparities across rows, columns, or model blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient-Scale Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A row- and column-aware diagnostic for widely separated nonzero coefficient magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a linear constraint matrix \(A\), define the global scale ratio \(\rho(A)=\max_{A_{ij}\ne0}|A_{ij}|/\min_{A_{ij}\ne0}|A_{ij}|\). For each nonzero row and column, define analogous ratios \(\rho_i^{\mathrm{row}}\) and \(\rho_j^{\mathrm{col}}\). A formulation has coefficient-scale imbalance at threshold \(\Gamma>1\) when at least one of these ratios exceeds \(\Gamma\). The predicate is diagnostic rather than invariant: multiplying rows or substituting scaled variables can change the ratios without changing the exact feasible set under the corresponding inverse transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale imbalance means that nonzero coefficients within the matrix, a row, or a column differ by more than a specified ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has at least one nonzero entry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{\rho(A),\max_i\rho_i^{\mathrm{row}},\max_j\rho_j^{\mathrm{col}}\}>\Gamma\).

notation.meaning: ratio of largest to smallest nonzero magnitude

review_flags: The diagnostic threshold is user-selected and no numerical-optimization source was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagnostic is internally defined, but its global, row, and column criterion and threshold are uncited conventions rather than a source-supported standard.

children.title: Unit Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Incompatible measurement units across linked variables, coefficients, or constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional-homogeneity test for algebraic constraints and objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign each variable and parameter a dimension vector \(d(\cdot)\) over fixed base units, with \(d(ab)=d(a)+d(b)\) and \(d(a/b)=d(a)-d(b)\). An equality \(\sum_k t_k=0\) is unit-consistent only if all nonzero terms \(t_k\) have the same dimension vector. An inequality \(g(x)\le h(x)\) is unit-consistent only if \(d(g)=d(h)\); arguments of exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions must be dimensionless. A model has unit inconsistency when any constraint or additive objective violates these predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is unit-inconsistent when it adds or compares quantities with different physical dimensions or applies dimensionless functions to dimensional arguments.
assumptions_latex: Every modeled quantity has an assigned dimension vector.
Base units are fixed consistently across the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\) an addition, comparison, or dimensionless-function argument violating dimensional homogeneity.
review_flags: No supplied source locator addresses dimensional analysis in optimization models.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimensional-homogeneity conditions are precise and fit the container, but no inspectable source locator supports their application to optimization models.

children.title: Rescaling Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Model-level routes for improving numerical scale while preserving intended semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Rescaling Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact variable and row scaling with explicit forward and inverse solution maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x_j\in\mathbb Z\ (j\in J)\}\). Let \(D_r\) and \(D_x\) be nonsingular diagonal matrices, set \(x=D_x\hat x\), and multiply inequalities by \(D_r\) with positive diagonal entries. The scaled representation is \(\min\{(D_x^\top c)^\top\hat x:(D_r A D_x)\hat x\le D_r b\}\). The interface maps solutions by \(x=D_x\hat x\) and residuals by \(r=D_r^{-1}\hat r\). If integer coordinates are scaled, their transformed domains must be \(\hat x_j\in D_{x,jj}^{-1}\mathbb Z\), unless the scaling preserves \(\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal row and variable scaling preserves the model through explicit inverse maps, provided transformed integer lattices are represented correctly.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) is diagonal with strictly positive entries.
Transformed integer domains are enforced exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=D_x\hat x\) gives a feasibility- and objective-preserving bijection between the two representations.
review_flags: Exact scaling representation is standard, but no supplied numerical linear-programming locator supports it.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling maps, objective transformation, residual map, and transformed integer lattice are coherent, but the nontrivial representation claim lacks a cited source.

children.title: Numerical Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes where scaling or unit choices materially affect solver reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local sensitivity classified by amplification of admissible data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(d)\) denote a selected solution or solution statistic for model data \(d\), and fix compatible norms. At a datum \(d_0\ne0\), define the local relative sensitivity modulus \(\kappa(d_0)=\limsup_{d\to d_0,\ d\ne d_0}\frac{\|S(d)-S(d_0)\|/\max\{1,\|S(d_0)\|\}}{\|d-d_0\|/\|d_0\|}\). For a prescribed threshold \(K>0\), the model is in a numerically sensitive regime when \(\kappa(d_0)>K\) or when \(S\) is discontinuous at \(d_0\). The definition requires a fixed solution selection when optima are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is numerically sensitive when small relative data perturbations can cause disproportionately large changes in a specified solution statistic.
assumptions_latex: A single-valued solution statistic \(S\) and compatible norms are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(d_0)>K\) or \(S\) is discontinuous at \(d_0\).
review_flags: Sensitivity conventions vary by solution mapping and norm; a dedicated source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed modulus depends on a nonstandard output normalization, a selected solution statistic, norms, and an arbitrary threshold. A dedicated source is required to establish the intended sensitivity convention.

children.title: Integrality-Tolerance Leakage
children.top_down_role: Near-integral values causing unintended conditional or logical behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Tolerance Leakage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A big-M family where an accepted near-zero binary value transmits a positive continuous activity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a solver accepts a nominally binary value \(y\) as zero whenever \(0\le y\le\tau_I\), where \(\tau_I>0\) is the integrality tolerance. In the big-M implication encoding \(0\le x\le My\), choose a required activity \(x=d>0\). If \(M\ge d/\tau_I\), then \((x,y)=(d,d/M)\) satisfies the linear constraint and \(y\le\tau_I\). Thus the reported near-zero binary state can coexist with positive activity \(x=d\), contrary to the intended semantic interpretation that the off state \(y=0\) forces \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If M is large enough, a binary value accepted as zero can still permit positive activity through a big-M constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)=(d,d/M)\) satisfies \(x\le My\) and \(y\le\tau_I\) while \(x>0\).
review_flags: Solver acceptance rules vary, and no supplied locator documents integrality-tolerance semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic big-M construction is valid, but the assertion that a solver accepts or reports the near-zero binary as zero is implementation-dependent and requires a solver-specific tolerance source.

children.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Interacting inequalities whose numerical tolerances admit or reject unintended points.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Tolerance Conflicts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive row tolerances can make jointly enforced inequalities accept unintended points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the intended constraints be \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), while a numerical checker accepts row \(i\) whenever \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i+\tau_i\), where \(\tau_i\ge0\). The numerically accepted set is \[F_{\tau}=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\{x:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i+\tau_i\}.\] A feasibility-tolerance conflict occurs when \(F_{\tau}\setminus F\ne\varnothing\), where \(F\) is the intended feasible set. In particular, intended bounds \(x\le u\) and \(x\ge \ell\) with \(\ell>u\) are numerically compatible whenever \(\ell-u\le\tau_{+}+\tau_{-}\), despite being exactly infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row tolerances enlarge each inequality. Their combined enlargement can admit unintended points or make contradictory bounds appear compatible when their inconsistency is no larger than the summed tolerances.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is tested using additive row tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\tau}\setminus F\ne\varnothing\) precisely identifies unintended tolerance-feasible points.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports solver feasibility-tolerance semantics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the set-enlargement claim is mathematically plausible. However, no source with an inspectable locator supports the stated feasibility-checker semantics. In addition, the contradictory-bounds example uses \(\tau_{+}\) and \(\tau_{-}\) without defining which bound each tolerance applies to, so the exact mathematical version requires sourced clarification.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent representations with unstable linear algebra or fragile coefficient patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent exact formulations may have sharply different sensitivity to coefficient perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two exact linear representations \(P=\{x:A x\le b\}\) and \(P=\{x:\widetilde A x\le\widetilde b\}\). For a nonsingular square basis matrix \(B\) extracted from either representation, the basic solution satisfies \(x_B=B^{-1}b_B\). Under perturbations \(\Delta B\) and \(\Delta b_B\), first-order sensitivity obeys \[\frac{\|\Delta x_B\|}{\|x_B\|}\lesssim \kappa(B)\left(\frac{\|\Delta B\|}{\|B\|}+\frac{\|\Delta b_B\|}{\|b_B\|}\right),\] when the relative perturbations are small. Thus exact feasible-set equivalence does not ensure numerical equivalence: a reformulation admitting bases with large \(\kappa(B)\) can amplify data and rounding errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations can describe the same exact set yet behave differently numerically because poorly conditioned basis matrices amplify coefficient, right-hand-side, and rounding errors.
assumptions_latex: The compared formulations define the same set in exact arithmetic.
\(B\) is nonsingular and the relative perturbations are sufficiently small.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Large \(\kappa(B)\) permits large relative solution error despite small relative data error.

notation.meaning: condition number in the chosen induced norm

children.title: Model Quality Assurance Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural routes for checking correctness, diagnoses, and alternative representations.

children.title: Small-Instance Feasible-Set Checks
children.top_down_role: Comparison of represented and intended feasible decisions on tractable instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Instance Feasible-Set Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhaustive comparison validates a formulation on finite, tractable test domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite decision domain \(D\), an intended feasibility predicate \(I:D\to\{0,1\}\), and a formulation predicate \(M:D\to\{0,1\}\), initialize \(E^{+}=E^{-}=\varnothing\). For every \(x\in D\), evaluate both predicates; add \(x\) to \(E^{+}\) when \(M(x)=1\) and \(I(x)=0\), and add \(x\) to \(E^{-}\) when \(I(x)=1\) and \(M(x)=0\). Stop after enumerating \(D\). Output \((E^{+},E^{-})\); the formulation matches the intended feasible decisions on \(D\) if and only if \(E^{+}=E^{-}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate every decision in a small finite domain and compare intended with modeled feasibility. Empty false-positive and false-negative sets certify equality on that test domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite and can be exhaustively enumerated.
Both feasibility predicates are decidable on every \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E^{+}=E^{-}=\varnothing\iff\{x\in D:M(x)=1\}=\{x\in D:I(x)=1\}\).
review_flags: Standard-field algorithmic rationale; no supplied locator directly documents exhaustive feasible-set validation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the exact terminal container, and exhaustive comparison of two decidable predicates over a finite domain correctly characterizes equality on that domain. No source with a specific locator is supplied for this validation procedure, so it cannot pass the evidence requirement.

children.title: Relaxation Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Inspection of relaxation gaps and fractional structural patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization and fractional-pattern inspection diagnose relaxation strength for a minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a mixed-integer feasible set and \(R\supseteq F\) its continuous relaxation. Given an objective \(c\), solve \(z_F=\inf_{x\in F}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(z_R=\inf_{x\in R}c^{\mathsf T}x\), recording an optimal relaxation point \(x^R\) when attained. Report the additive gap \(g=z_F-z_R\ge0\), and, when \(z_F\ne0\), the normalized gap \(g/|z_F|\). For each integer-indexed component, report \(\delta_j=\min_{k\in\mathbb Z}|x^R_j-k|\). Large gaps or structured nonzero \(\delta_j\) identify weak relaxation behavior for the tested objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare integer and relaxation optima, then inspect distances of relaxed integer variables from integers. Large gaps or systematic fractional patterns indicate a weak relaxation for the tested objective.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem and \(F\subseteq R\).
Both optimal values are finite; fractionalities require an attained relaxation optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_R\le z_F\), while \(g\) and \((\delta_j)\) quantify objective and integrality weakness for the tested instance.

notation.meaning: mixed-integer feasible set and its continuous relaxation
distance of relaxed component j to the nearest integer

children.title: Infeasibility Conflict Diagnosis
children.top_down_role: Support for irreducible conflicts, feasibility relaxation, and diagnostic subsystems.

children.title: Irreducible Infeasible Subsystems
children.top_down_role: Minimal or reduced conflicting subsystems used to localize infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Irreducible Infeasible Subsystems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite constraint systems; irreducibility is inclusion-minimality, not minimum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of constraints over a common domain \(X\), and for \(J\subseteq I\) define \(F(J)=\{x\in X:x\text{ satisfies }C_i\text{ for every }i\in J\}\). A subset \(J\subseteq I\) is an irreducible infeasible subsystem if \(F(J)=\varnothing\) and \(F(J\setminus\{j\})\ne\varnothing\) for every \(j\in J\). Equivalently, the subsystem is infeasible and every proper subset is feasible. An irreducible infeasible subsystem need not have minimum cardinality among infeasible subsystems and need not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An irreducible infeasible subsystem is an infeasible constraint subset that becomes feasible whenever any one member is removed. It need not be smallest by size or unique.
assumptions_latex: The constraint index set \(I\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J\text{ is irreducibly infeasible}\iff F(J)=\varnothing\text{ and }F(J\setminus\{j\})\ne\varnothing\text{ for all }j\in J\).

notation.meaning: points satisfying the constraints indexed by J

review_flags: Standard-field definition; supplied locators do not directly address irreducible infeasible subsystems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is exactly appropriate, and the finite-family formulation correctly distinguishes inclusion minimality from minimum cardinality. No inspectable source locator is supplied for the IIS definition and its nonuniqueness and nonminimum-cardinality qualifications.

children.title: Conflict Refinement Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Solver facilities for isolating constraints, bounds, or domains implicated in conflicts.

knowledge_statements.title: Conflict Refinement Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A solver-facing refinement contract returns a locally minimal conflict over eligible model elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an infeasible model with eligible constraints \(C=\{C_i\}_{i\in I}\), optional variable bounds represented as constraints, and protected indices \(P\subseteq I\), initialize \(J=I\). For each removable \(j\in J\setminus P\), test feasibility of the subsystem indexed by \(J\setminus\{j\}\); if it remains infeasible, replace \(J\) by \(J\setminus\{j\}\). Repeat passes until no removable member can be deleted. Return \(J\), the membership status of every eligible element, and the feasibility tolerances used. The output satisfies infeasibility and deletion minimality relative to the eligible, unprotected elements and the employed feasibility oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteratively remove eligible constraints whose deletion preserves infeasibility. Return the resulting conflict, element statuses, and tolerances; minimality is relative to the exposed elements and feasibility oracle.
assumptions_latex: The initial eligible subsystem is declared infeasible by the feasibility oracle.
Every protected index remains in the returned subsystem.
The deletion process continues until a complete pass removes nothing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned \(J\) is infeasible and \(J\setminus\{j\}\) is feasible for every \(j\in J\setminus P\).
review_flags: No supplied locator documents a solver conflict-refinement interface or its exact guarantees.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is suitable for the interface-oriented container, and the deletion procedure is coherent relative to a consistent feasibility oracle and protected elements. No cited source documents the proposed interface outputs, eligibility semantics, tolerance reporting, or deletion-minimality guarantee, so the exact contract remains unsupported.

children.title: Feasibility-Relaxation Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Controlled violation information used to identify sources of infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Relaxation Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted violation minimization identifies a minimally penalized repair, not necessarily a minimum-cardinality repair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\), introduce violations \(s_i\ge0\) and choose penalties \(w_i>0\). Solve \[\min_{x,s}\ \sum_{i=1}^m w_i s_i\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i+s_i\ \ (i=1,\ldots,m),\quad x\in X,\quad s\ge0.\] If an optimum \((x^*,s^*)\) exists, return its objective value and the support \(V=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\). A zero optimum certifies feasibility of the original system over \(X\); a positive optimum quantifies the least weighted additive relaxation under this diagnostic model, and \(V\) identifies constraints relaxed by the selected optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize weighted nonnegative constraint violations. Zero cost certifies original feasibility; positive cost measures the cheapest modeled repair, whose positive slacks identify relaxed constraints.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation problem has an attained finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i w_i s_i^*=0\iff\{x\in X:a_i^{\mathsf T}x\le b_i\text{ for all }i\}\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports feasibility-relaxation diagnostics.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the diagnostic container. With positive weights and an attained finite optimum, the zero-objective equivalence and the interpretation as a least weighted additive relaxation are mathematically consistent; the statement also correctly avoids claiming minimum-cardinality repair. No supporting source and locator are supplied.

children.title: Diagnostic Coverage Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on what conflict tools can expose under presolve, reformulation, or numerical ambiguity.

knowledge_statements.title: Diagnostic Coverage Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conflicts and feasibility relaxations provide local diagnoses whose coverage depends on eligibility, tolerances, and penalties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) index all model constraints and let \(E\subseteq I\) be the elements exposed to a diagnostic. A conflict finder returning \(J\subseteq E\) certifies only that the selected subsystem is infeasible under its feasibility oracle; it does not establish uniqueness, minimum cardinality, or involvement of every modeling error. Likewise, a weighted feasibility relaxation minimizes \(\sum_{i\in E}w_i s_i\) only over its permitted relaxation family. Changing \(E\), the weights, admissible slack directions, or numerical tolerances can change the reported diagnosis. Therefore absence from a returned conflict or violation support does not certify correctness or irrelevance of a model element.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagnostic results depend on exposed elements, tolerances, weights, and allowed repairs. Omission from one conflict or relaxation support does not prove that a constraint is correct or irrelevant.
assumptions_latex: The diagnostic examines only eligible elements \(E\).
Conflict and relaxation results use fixed but interface-dependent numerical settings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned diagnosis is valid only relative to \(E\), the diagnostic oracle, and its configured relaxation and tolerance rules.
review_flags: No supplied source establishes the stated coverage limitations of diagnostic interfaces.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the limitations described are plausible and appropriately relative to eligibility, oracle settings, tolerances, and relaxation design. No source with a specific locator supports these interface-dependent coverage claims.

children.title: Alternative-Formulation Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Controlled comparison of equivalent formulations across representative regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Formulation Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent integer projections should be compared using relaxation strength and controlled computational measurements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_1}\) and \(Q_2\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p_2}\) be formulations with integer-feasible projections \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_1\cap D_1)=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_2\cap D_2)=F\). Let \(R_k\) denote the continuous relaxation of \(Q_k\). For a minimization objective \(c\), formulation \(1\) is at least as strong as formulation \(2\) when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(R_2)\), which implies \[\inf_{x\in\operatorname{proj}_x(R_1)}c^{\mathsf T}x\ge\inf_{x\in\operatorname{proj}_x(R_2)}c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Computational comparisons additionally require identical instances, objectives, correctness tolerances, resource limits, and solver settings; otherwise observed performance differences are not attributable solely to formulation choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulations can be ordered by projected relaxation inclusion. Fair empirical comparison additionally fixes instances, objectives, tolerances, resource limits, and solver settings.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations project to the same integer-feasible set \(F\).
The displayed relaxation optima are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(R_2)\) implies that formulation \(1\) has no weaker minimization bound for any common linear objective.

notation.meaning: common intended feasible set in original variables
